Reminds me of young Timothy Hargrave, wanted to become a professional badger watcher. Said it was a vitally important, yet overlooked, profession. Oh, this family. You both have the most wonderful stories. It's a wonder any of your students became anything practical. Practicality isn't everything, El. Though I will say, trying to navigate the car park at the Trafford Centre yesterday felt like a rather quixotic endeavour in itself. Absolute gridlock. Took nearly an hour just to find a space. The Trafford Centre… a concrete monstrosity. I simply refuse to go. I get everything delivered. Honestly, the queues! I heard Mrs. Higgins was stuck in a queue at the butcher’s for nearly forty-five minutes last week. Forty-five minutes! For a sausage! People will queue for anything these days. It’s a national pastime. When I was a boy, a queue meant something was truly worth waiting for. Now, it seems people queue just to  be  in a queue. I saw Brenda posting on Facebook about the butcher’s queue. She was live-streaming it! Apparently, Mr. Peterson had a new shipment of Cumberland sausages in. She called it “Sausage Saturday.” The internet is a strange place. Brenda and her Facebook. Honestly. Sometimes I think she lives for the likes. Remember when she posted a photo of her toast? The toast! With the perfectly symmetrical buttering! I commented, naturally. Had to acknowledge the artistry. Though, I did wonder if she’d spent longer arranging the butter than she did eating the toast. Speaking of artistry, have you seen the latest issue of  Uncut  magazine?

Oh, this is lovely. Just what I needed. All that talk about bylaws and membership drives… gives me a headache, it does. Though, bless ‘em, they mean well, don't they? Proper dedication, the TME lot. Dedication bordering on obsession, perhaps, Margaret. Though I’ve always admired people who throw themselves into things. Myself, I preferred observing. Keeps you out of trouble, mostly. And allows you to see the  patterns , you know? Patterns, aye. You always were the observant one, Arthur. More the thinker than the doer, weren’t you? Which, considering what you  did  all those years, is rather remarkable. Printing systems… sounds terribly complicated. Complicated is… one word for it. It started, believe it or not, with a rather irritating offset lithography process. Everything was just so…slow. And wasteful. I thought, there  must  be a better way. Spent years fiddling, building prototypes in the shed, much to my wife’s dismay, of course. She kept finding ink everywhere. Oh, I can imagine! My gallery always looked like a bomb had hit it after a particularly busy Saturday. Dust sheets and chipped porcelain, the lot. But a better way… that’s what drives us, isn’t it? What  was  the better way, if you don’t mind me asking? Trying to picture all these gears and levers… Well, the core of it was a modular system, really. Interchangeable printing heads, automated ink distribution. It dramatically sped up the process, reduced waste, and allowed for far more intricate designs. The first sale was to a packaging company in Leeds. They took a gamble, but it paid off. Then things…well, they took off rather quickly. Goodness me. And all from a shed in Guiseley? Sounds like something out of a Dickens novel! Did you stay involved with the manufacturing side, or did you sell it off? I stayed with it for twenty years, Margaret. Built a team, expanded. It got to the point where I was spending a good deal of time over in Germany. Specifically, Düsseldorf. The Drupa exhibition was…essential. A monstrous affair, really. Halls the size of aircraft hangars, filled with the latest printing technology. Düsseldorf! Oh, I remember those exhibitions. I used to go to a smaller one, focused on antique prints and engravings. Terrible coffee, but the connections were invaluable. Always a bit tense, those German exhibitions, though. So much…precision. Everything had to be  just so .

Honestly, Dad, I’m  dreading  this English Language coursework. Mrs. Davison is making us dissect the history of, like, every single word. It's exhausting. Aye, sounds a bit keen, doesn't she? Though, it’s not a bad thing, lass. Understanding where words come from… it's fascinating. Remember when we were arguing over whether it was ‘aluminium’ or ‘aluminum’? Oh god,  that  was a saga. You were adamant it was ‘aluminium’ because that’s how  you  learned it. Well, it  is ! It’s the proper British spelling, isn't it? Though I’ll admit, seeing it the American way a lot in films… makes you wonder. Speaking of counties and spellings… Worcestershire. Try saying that five times fast. Worcestershire! Okay, challenge accepted. Worcestershire, Worcestershire, Worcestershire… I can’t even look at it without tripping over my tongue. It looks like someone just mashed the keyboard. Exactly! And then there’s Leicestershire… hardly rolls off the tongue, does it? Makes you wonder who came up with these names. Probably some ancient Brit with a mouthful of rocks. Speaking of ancient, Mrs. Davison was going on about proto-Germanic roots today. Honestly, I zoned out after ‘Indo-European’. It all feels so… abstract. What's the point of knowing where ‘the’ came from? Well, it’s about understanding how language evolves. How meaning shifts. And it shows you how connected everything is, really. Like, did you know ‘quinoa’… I only learned this a few years back…comes from the Quechua language? From the Andes? Quinoa? Seriously? I just thought it was…a healthy grain. Mum's always trying to make me eat it. It's a bit bland, if you ask me. It is a bit, isn’t it? I’d rather have a proper chip butty, myself. Right, we’re getting near Birmingham. Should be a service station coming up soon. Need a loo break and I’m parched. Definitely. And maybe some chocolate. That coursework is draining my energy. Are we still on for visiting that farmer’s market near Padstow when we get there? Absolutely. I heard they have some proper good Cornish pasties. And hopefully, some decent bacon. Although, I saw something on the news about a pig escaping from a farm near there yesterday. Caused a bit of a kerfuffle, apparently. A runaway pig? That's brilliant! Maybe we'll see it. Imagine. “Holiday ruined by rogue swine!”

Right, so, Dad, you’re  absolutely  sure you don’t want me to do less onion? Last time you said it was too strong and then moaned there wasn't enough flavour. Honestly, it's like walking on eggshells. Now, now, lass. I just said it needed…adjusting. A bit of subtlety, you know? It weren’t  bad , just…robust. And don’t go calling me Dad, you know I prefer Anthony. Makes me feel a bit…ancient. Robust is a nice way of putting it, Anthony. It smelled like you were trying to gas the whole street last time. No offence, Beth. None taken, Liam. It’s a family tradition, apparently. My grandma made everything with enough onion to ward off vampires. And honestly, Anthony, you know I’m just trying to help. You haven’t cooked a proper meal in years, have you? That’s a bit harsh, isn’t it? Used to be a dab hand at a Sunday roast, back in the day. Before…well, before things changed. Besides, your mother always did the bulk of the cooking. She was a marvel in the kitchen, your mother. Speaking of your mum, Beth, how’s she doing? Haven’t seen her since Christmas. Still badgering you about settling down and finding a nice lad? Oh, don't even  start  with the ‘nice lad’ thing. It’s a constant refrain. Last phone call was dedicated entirely to a neighbour’s grandson who apparently ‘works with computers’ – which, in Mum-speak, could mean anything from building rockets to fixing the printer. She sent me his Facebook profile, too. It’s mostly pictures of him flexing in the gym. Sounds charming. Mothers will be mothers, won't they? Mine was always trying to marry me off to the vicar’s daughter. Didn’t quite work out. She liked me a bit  too  much, apparently. Said I had discerning taste. Right, that's a story I need to hear sometime. So, this is a nice change of pace for you, Anthony, isn't it? Being cooked for? It is, it is. Though I do miss your mother’s Yorkshire puddings. She had a knack for them. Light as a feather. Yours are good, Beth, perfectly edible, but they lack that…oomph. Oomph?! They’re Yorkshire puddings, not a fireworks display! Honestly, the criticism! You’ve never even  attempted  a Yorkshire pudding in your life.

Right, you made it! Thought you might be dodging me after I nearly spilled a pint down your new coat last Friday. Oh, don’t be silly, Leo. It was a near miss, and honestly, that coat  needed  washing. It's just… busy. End of term rush with the students. They’re all suddenly desperate for detailed feedback on their dissertations. You wouldn’t believe the stress. What about you? Still wrestling with demanding customers and sticky floors? You have  no  idea. Last night was quiz night. You get all sorts. One bloke tried to argue that the capital of Australia was Sydney. Sydney! I swear, sometimes I wonder if people even pay attention in school. It’s a good laugh though, mostly. Pays the bills, allows for the occasional pint. What are you teaching at the moment? Still French and Spanish? Mostly. I’ve picked up a few Italian beginners this term, which is nice. It's a bit of a change. Though, honestly, the grammar is… robust. It feels like learning a whole new set of rules every week. You did languages at uni, right? How did you end up behind the bar? Yeah, I did. French and Spanish, same as you. Spent a year in Spain, which was brilliant. But the whole ‘career’ thing… didn't quite pan out. I realised I didn't want to be stuck in an office. This is… freer, you know? Plus, the tips are alright. Did you ever think about going abroad to teach, after your Masters? Oh, constantly. I applied for a few placements in France, even a couple in Argentina. But then my mum got ill, and I just… couldn't bring myself to go. Staying close to family felt more important. It's funny, isn’t it? How life throws things at you. Totally. I was all set to apply for a translation job in Brussels, then my Nan had a fall, and everything changed. I ended up staying in Brum to help out. No regrets, though. It’s good to be close to family. Speaking of which, are you still seeing…what was his name… Ben? The musician? We’re… taking a break. A very prolonged break. It’s complicated. He’s… intensely focused on his music, which is amazing, but it means he’s also… not very focused on anything else. It started to feel a bit one-sided, to be honest.

Cor, this is a good cuppa, Margaret. Not quite as good as what Doris used to make, mind you. She always had a knack with the Tetley’s. Though I reckon she put a little something  extra  in it sometimes… a drop of sherry, perhaps? Don't tell anyone I said that! You and your stories, Arthur! Doris didn’t need sherry, she just cared about making a proper brew. You’re late for break time, you know. I was starting to think you'd fallen asleep in your chair again. Now, now, let the man enjoy his tea. He's earned a bit of relaxation. Been puttering about with those banners all morning, hasn't he? They looking alright, Arthur? Need a hand with the lettering? Right as rain, they are, David. Though my hands aren’t what they used to be, you know. Shake a bit when I’m trying to do the fine work. Still, “Bell Ringing for Gambia” is clear enough, I think. Reminds me, did you ever manage to sort out that donation box? The little wooden one? Yes, already done. It’s over by the window, with a little sign. Looks quite smart, if I do say so myself. Though I'm still not entirely convinced about this whole Gambia thing. All those stories you tell about it... seems a bit… intense. Intense? It  is  intense, David! It's a beautiful country, desperately needing help. I told you about Old Man Hemmings, didn't I? Went out there with his wife, bless 'em, thinking he could build a school with his own two hands. Ended up nearly bankrupting himself. People don’t understand the challenges over there. Arthur, dear, you do have a tendency to… exaggerate. Remember what the doctor said about not getting yourself too worked up? You get all agitated talking about it. Agitated? I’m  passionate , Margaret! There's a difference! And it's not exaggeration, it’s… well, it’s about people needing help. It's like that Mrs. Henderson down the road. Always complaining of feeling poorly. She's a bit of a case, if you ask me. Mrs. Henderson? Oh, you mean the one who's always turning up at the hospital with different ailments? That’s the one. My Elsie – God rest her soul – used to say she had a touch of… well, she called it Munchausen’s something.

Honestly, this is exactly what I needed after that day. Work was… a  situation . Honestly, spreadsheets are my nemesis. Tell me about it. I spent three hours this morning trying to get that Gantt chart to cooperate. Gantt charts should be illegal, they're actively designed to induce stress. You two and your office woes. At least you  have  offices. I was on the road all day, chasing leads that turned out to be…well, let's just say enthusiastically uninterested in our widget offerings. Oh no, a bad sales day? Rough. Did you at least find a decent coffee shop to sulk in? That's my coping mechanism for bad shopping trips. Speaking of, I downloaded this new app…it’s supposed to find all the best deals on clothes, but it just keeps showing me things I already own. That's… incredibly unhelpful. What's it called? I'm always looking for new time-wasters, I mean,  useful  apps. It's called 'Style Scout'. Honestly, it's more 'Style Disappointment'. I’m deleting it after dinner. Sounds about right. I downloaded one that promised to teach me a new language in five minutes a day. Five minutes of repeating the same five phrases. Highly effective. You’re both easily parted from your data, aren’t you? I stick to the classics: Instagram and doomscrolling through TikTok. Speaking of which, did you see Chloe’s holiday pictures? Bali looks insane. Ugh, don’t even get me started. Bali! She’s making me seriously rethink my summer plans. I was thinking a quiet week in Cornwall, maybe. Now I’m feeling decidedly…under-adventurous. Cornwall is lovely! Much less Instagram pressure, right? Plus, pasties. Although, Bali  does  look amazing. I saw a video of someone swimming with manta rays and I nearly cried. Manta rays are cool. Although they're massive, aren't they? Like… underwater winged monsters. Actually, that leads me nicely onto something. Has anyone seen that new horror film, "The Hollow"? Oh god, no. Absolutely not. I tried to watch the trailer and I was already having palpitations. I’m a lightweight when it comes to scary movies. I need everything to be sunshine and rainbows, or at least mildly amusing. I saw it last week. It's proper unsettling. Really gets under your skin. There’s this scene in the woods… honestly, I slept with the lights on for two nights.

…and then young Timmy, bless ‘im, decided the handbrake wasn’t for applyin’. Rolled right into Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning roses. A right mess, it were. She weren’t ‘appy, not one bit. Still, gives you a story, don’t it? Roses, eh? That’ll learn ‘im. Though Mrs. Higgins  does  take those roses rather seriously. Remember when old man Peterson’s dog… well, never mind. Different story for another day. Good cup of tea, Anon, mind. Proper brew. It is lovely, thank you, George. Though honestly, a biscuit would’ve made it perfect. Frank, you always did have a knack for making a good cuppa. Though you spent more time tinkering with those cars of yours than anything else. Tinkering is a kind word, Maureen. 'Restoring', I’d call it. And a proper hobby, it were. Unlike some folks I know who just… sat. . Oh, here we go. Don't start on me about the "sitting", Frank. I 'ad interests! I enjoyed a good read, the garden, watching the cricket. Not everyone needs to be under the bonnet of a motorcar, pulling it to bits and putting it back together again. Made the shed smell of oil for decades, it did. Now, now, you two. No need to bicker. It’s lovely to have you both here, and I don't want to hear about sheds and roses. I was just thinking, it’s getting on a bit. George, are you managing alright with the bus these days? I worry about you getting home on your own, especially in the dark. The bus? Oh, it's alright, Maureen. Though they changed the route again, didn't they? Takes me all the way round Costessey before it heads back towards the city centre. Adds a good twenty minutes to the journey, it does. And the youngsters these days… no manners, not a single one. Blocking the aisle with their rucksacks, loud music… Honestly. Twenty minutes? That’s a disgrace. They cut the 26 route years ago, remember? Said it wasn’t ‘economical’. Economical for  who ? Not for folks trying to get to the shops, that’s for sure. I used to drive you, George, remember? Before me knees went. I do indeed. You were a right chauffeur, Frank. Always complaining about the state of the roads, though. "Potholes the size of craters," you’d say. Because they  were ! They still are!

Honestly, this traffic is dreadful. Reminds me of trying to get out of Dublin on a Friday evening. Though, admittedly, Dublin traffic had  character . This is just…gridlock. You said it. I’m starting to regret suggesting we drive. The train would have been less stressful, even with the airport transfer on the other end. Aye, but the train’s a fortune now, isn't it? And then lugging everything to Manchester Piccadilly… No, this is better. Slower, granted. But we've got biscuits. And Mary’s complaining is a comfort, in a strange way. She always finds something to grumble about. Oh, hush you, Arthur. I’m not  complaining . I’m merely observing. Though, thinking about Manchester…are you  sure  about this house, love? It just feels…small. It’s perfect for what we need, Mum. Less to manage. Remember what the doctor said about you needing to take things easier? A huge garden is just going to be more work. And it’s closer to the hospital, which is important. I know, I know. You’re right, of course. It’s just…leaving everything in Stratford. All those memories. Old Man Hemmings next door, always with a story… even if half of them weren’t true. Hemmings and his tales of being a wartime spy! Good lord. He swore he single-handedly prevented a V2 rocket from hitting Birmingham. He did. Or at least, he believed he did. And the garden…I spent decades perfecting those roses. You can definitely have a rose garden in Manchester, Mum. A smaller one, perhaps. We can even bring some cuttings. I’ve been researching varieties that do well in the northern climate. You and your research. Always the practical one. That's why I’m glad you're helping with all this. I'd be lost without you. Arthur’s…well, he provides moral support. And biscuit consumption oversight. I resent that! I have been offering insightful commentary on the state of the M6 for the last hour. It’s a vital service, really. Absolutely vital. Speaking of vital services, have you both remembered to pack your travel documents? I don't want a repeat of the Heathrow debacle last year. Oh, don't remind me. That was  your  fault, you know. Rushing me through security like a criminal! I was trying to make sure we didn't miss our flight to Malaga!

Oh! Is… is that it? Is that  the  helmet? It is, love. It is. And the bike’s safe and sound too, thankfully. Just… a bit worse for wear. No way! Seriously?! Where did you find it? I thought it was gone for good. I checked all the usual spots near the pier every day. I even asked Old Man Hemmings at the bike shop, thinking maybe someone'd pawned it. Well, it's a long story. Apparently, a lad – only about your age, actually – was trying to sell it on Facebook Marketplace. Listed it for, get this, fifty quid! Fifty quid?! After I saved up for  months  for that bike? The cheek! Did you… did you recognise him? From his profile picture, vaguely. Turns out he lives just up on Priory Road. The police went and had a word – a very firm word, I gather – and it was returned this afternoon. They said he claimed he’d ‘found’ it leaning against the bowling alley. Honestly, the stories some people come up with… Found it?! Right. And I suppose it magically unlocked itself too. I’m so glad you kept checking Marketplace, Mum. I’d basically given up hope. I was looking at those electric bikes online, but they’re miles out of my price range. I wasn’t giving up on your old faithful. It’s a good bike, and you loved it. It’ll need a good clean, and the gears are a bit sticky, but nothing a bit of TLC can't fix. Your dad can take a look this weekend. He's been itching to get his hands dirty with something. Perfect. I really need to get back to cycling. It’s the only way I can clear my head with all this college stuff looming. Open day at Brighton Uni is next week, and I'm already stressed. Brighton’s lovely! It's a good choice to look around. Are you still leaning towards Marine Biology? I think so. It's just... the thought of actually choosing something  now , something that’s going to pretty much define what I do, is terrifying. What if I hate it? What if I'm terrible at it? Oh, darling. Everyone feels like that. It’s a big decision, yes, but it's not written in stone. You can change your mind, you know. And Marine Biology is fantastic. You’ve always been brilliant at science, and you’ve always loved the sea.

Right, that completes my route from Plymouth to Penzance. Honestly, this game is deceptively strategic. It  looks  like just colourful trains, but it’s all about blocking people, isn't it? Deceptively is the word. I’ve been hoarding blue cards for ages hoping to snag that long coastal route, but Rhodri keeps scooping up all the locomotives! It’s a conspiracy, I tell you. A Welsh conspiracy to dominate the railways of England. Hey! I’m just being efficient. Someone has to build the infrastructure, you know? Though, I’m slightly distracted by the fact that we’re playing a train game…in Hereford…when the journey  here  was an absolute saga. Oh, don't even  start  on the trains. It was biblical. Delayed leaving Cardiff, then a 'points failure' somewhere near Newport. Points failure! It sounds so…vague. Like a general malaise affecting the railway lines. Points failures are rarely vague, my dear. Usually, it’s a mechanical issue with the switch that directs the train from one track to another. I used to volunteer with the railway preservation society, you know. Fascinating stuff, the engineering behind it all. Though modern railways…they've lost some of the character. Character, and reliability, from what I hear. My sister was stuck on a train for five hours last week. Five hours! She said they gave them a voucher for a coffee as compensation. A coffee! For five hours of their lives. Honestly! It’s insulting. It’s the sheer lack of communication too. You’re just…there. Sitting. Waiting. With no idea what’s going on. I remember once, travelling back from London, we were stuck outside Reading for two hours, and the announcement was just on repeat: “We are experiencing a slight delay.” A  slight  delay? Two hours is not a slight delay! “Slight delay” is British understatement at its finest. It's a national sport. You could write a whole book on the euphemisms used by train companies! Speaking of food... anyone else fancy another scone? These are incredible. Where did you get them, Liz? From that little bakery in the village. Old Mrs. Higgins makes them. Absolutely legendary. She insists on clotted cream  before  jam, though. Says it’s the Cornish way. Blasphemy! Jam first,  always  jam first. It’s a hill I am prepared to die on. It creates a barrier to the cream, you see. Prevents it from squelching everywhere.

Right. “Quixotic.” Twenty-two points. Sorry, darling. I think that pretty much seals it. Quixotic? Seriously? Where do you  find  these words? It’s like you secretly have a dictionary implanted in your brain. I'm doomed. Twenty-two points is brutal when I'm staring at a rack of vowels. It's a lecturer's curse, I think. We’re forced to ingest language for a living. Besides, you were doing so well earlier with that triple word score on ‘Zephyr’. Don't pretend you aren’t competitive. Touché. Zephyr was a moment of fleeting glory. This, however, is scholastic domination. So, your mum’s roast was incredible as always. She really outdid herself with the Yorkshire puddings. Oh, absolutely. She knows exactly how to bribe us with food. It's her superpower. It’s just… nice, isn’t it? Being back here. It feels a million miles away from marking essays on post-structuralism. It really does. London feels… frantic, all the time. Even when it’s quiet. Here, it’s just fields and birdsong. It’s almost… unsettlingly peaceful. Although, I'm beginning to suspect your dad deliberately sets the wifi password to something ridiculously complicated just to force conversation. He does enjoy a good analogue evening. He worries we’re all glued to our screens too much. Which, let's be honest, is valid. Speaking of "glued to screens", have you noticed how board games seem to be having a Renaissance? A renaissance is putting it mildly. It’s a full-blown revival. Everyone's into complex strategy games and escape room style stuff now. It’s a far cry from Monopoly and Cluedo, isn’t it? Which, incidentally, always ended in arguments when we played as kids. Oh,  always . You always accused me of cheating at Cluedo. Because you  were ! You had a very suspicious habit of knowing who did it and where before you’d even asked half the questions! But seriously, I think it's connected to that wider thing of people actively seeking out offline experiences. A pushback against constant connectivity. Perhaps. Or maybe it’s just that people are bored. And realise spending an evening actually  talking  to each other is surprisingly…enjoyable. It’s interesting comparing it to drinking cultures, isn't it? The British obsession with the pub… that’s a  very  different social ritual. Totally. Pubs are built around a very specific kind of social lubrication.

Honestly, this shepherd’s pie is  amazing , Kerrie. You’ve outdone yourself. Is there a secret ingredient? It’s not just the lamb, it’s… something else. Proper Welsh cooking, that's what it is. No secret, just good quality ingredients and a bit of love, apparently. It’s miles better than anything I can manage. I burnt toast this morning.  Toast . Oh, don’t be so hard on yourself, Rhys. You're a project coordinator, not a chef! Though I still maintain you should learn to make a decent cuppa. Remember that time you tried to make me one with milk  first ? The horror. In my defence, I was stressed about the Henderson account! And it wasn’t  that  bad. It was. Terribly bad. Anyway, back to the pie. Kerrie, you really should consider doing this professionally. You’d be brilliant. Oh, darling, I've had my fill of professional life, thank you very much. Accounting is enough excitement for one lifetime. Speaking of filling things… have you two made any progress on the house hunt? It feels like ages since you started looking, Elara. It  has  been ages. It’s just… everything is either a complete fixer-upper and way over budget, or a soulless new build with postage-stamp gardens. We saw one yesterday that had… beige everything. Beige carpets, beige walls, beige curtains. It was depressing. And the estate agent kept going on about “neutral palettes” like it was a  good  thing. I want some colour! Some personality! Beige is the enemy. Absolutely the enemy. Though, truthfully, finding the right place is a nightmare these days. Especially with interest rates the way they are. And then you’ve got the council tax to think about. Honestly, it's scandalous. Tell me about it. We’ve been looking mostly in the outskirts of Bristol, trying to get a bit more for our money. But even then, it’s competitive. Rhys' mum offered to help with a deposit, which is amazing, but then you feel even more pressure to find  the one . She's a gem, my mum. Though she did immediately start suggesting we paint the living room magnolia. Which, naturally, I vetoed. Magnolia? Oh dear. Progress, Rhys, progress! You’re standing your ground! Good for you, love. You need to be firm. You’re the ones living there, after all. It reminds me of when I moved here, years ago.

Honestly, Mum, this traffic is mental. We've barely moved since Canary Wharf. I swear, every single person in London decided to go to Hampstead at exactly the same time. It's a Sunday, darling. Hampstead Heath is always busy on a Sunday. And honestly, you’re just like your father, always complaining about the traffic. Though he usually accompanied it with… well,  stronger  language. Yeah, I get the road rage gene from him, don’t I? I’m trying to be better though. Deep breaths. Thinking of nicer things. Like… not being stuck behind that white van doing 30 in a 40. That's good. Though imagining nicer things isn’t always enough, is it? Sometimes you just need to accept the inevitable. Speaking of inevitable… have you thought any more about what you're getting your Aunt Carol for her birthday? It's next month, you know. Ugh, Aunt Carol. Right. I've been trying to avoid that thought. She’s impossible to buy for. She either already  has  it, or she pretends to hate it to be polite. Last year’s cashmere scarf got a… lukewarm reception, to say the least. She did say the colour was ‘challenging’, didn’t she? I think a book might be best. Something literary. I can give you some suggestions. I’ve been wading through a lot of submissions lately for the  TLS . The  Times Literary Supplement  still going strong, then? I thought everyone just got their book reviews from blogs now. Is print still… a thing? Oh, it’s very much a thing. Don’t underestimate the pleasure of proper typesetting and a substantial binding, darling. There’s a sensory experience that a glowing screen just can't replicate. It’s also about authority, credibility… things that are easily lost in the digital noise. Though, naturally, we  have  a comprehensive online presence as well. It’s about balance. Fair enough. I guess I'm just used to everything being instant. Everything’s digital for uni work, you know? It's all PDFs and online journals. Makes a proper book feel… luxurious, I suppose. Exactly! That’s a lovely way to put it. And it’s important to preserve that. Speaking of preserving things… I was thinking we could possibly go to France this summer. Haven't been in ages. Your father used to adore Brittany. France? That sounds… amazing. I haven’t been since I was a kid.

…and then, honestly, the seagull  dive-bombed  me for my chips. Not just swooped, dive-bombed. Full-on kamikaze seagull. Right over the harbour in Whitby. You and your chips, Rach. It’s a documentary waiting to happen. “Rachel vs. the Seagulls: A Chip-Related Saga.” Shut up, Liam. They were  good  chips. Proper chunky, really fluffy inside. It was worth risking life and limb. And you screamed like a banshee, didn’t you? Mum was mortified. I did  not  scream like a banshee! I made a… startled exclamation. A perfectly reasonable reaction to aggressive avian behaviour. Sounds chaotic. Whitby’s lovely though, isn’t it? I went a few years back with me grandma. We did the Dracula tour. Dracula tour? Really, Chloe? That sounds a bit… cheesy. Oh, it was! Absolutely ridiculous. But grandma loved it. She’s obsessed with Bram Stoker. She was convinced she saw the ghost of Dracula wandering the abbey. Your grandma sounds brilliant. Better than battling seagulls, anyway. Speaking of chaotic, you will  not  believe what happened to me in Amsterdam… Oh, here we go. Liam and his “Amsterdam adventures.” Prepare yourselves. It wasn’t what you think! I swear. I was cycling, right? Trying to be all Dutch and adventurous, and I ended up in a canal. A very small canal, admittedly, but still. You fell  in  a canal? Well, ‘fell in’ is a strong phrase. I… gently lowered myself into the canal whilst attempting a particularly ambitious turn. “Gently lowered”? Liam, you’re making it sound like you were taking a leisurely dip! Was there a bike involved? Because I'm imagining a spectacular slow-motion fall. There was a bike! Thankfully, a very kind Dutch gentleman fished me, and the bike, out. I was soaked, covered in algae… not my finest hour. Did anyone get photos? I dread to think. I saw a few people pointing and giggling. I just pedalled away as fast as my soggy legs could carry me. It’s just like you, Liam. Always finding a way to get into trouble. Remember that time in Skegness when... Oh, don’t even  go  there, Sarah! Skegness is a sacred, forgotten memory we agreed never to speak of! What happened in Skegness?! I need to know. It involves a donkey, a rogue ice cream cone, and a very angry beach vendor. It's a long story… Sounds promising. We've got time.

…and honestly, the silence. That's the biggest thing. Utter, complete silence. Not like the countryside where you get tractors and sheep, this was…absolute. Just the wind, sometimes. And the snow, of course. Crunching under your boots, that’s a good sound, mind you. Sounds… bracing, Arthur. Bracing is a polite word, isn’t it? I mean, you’re deliberately seeking out discomfort. In  winter . I'm a nurse, I’ve seen enough hypothermia cases to last a lifetime, thank you very much. Oh, come now, Moira. It's not about seeking discomfort, precisely. It’s about stripping things back. Everything you need to survive, you carry on your back. No telly, no phone signal – well, barely – no distractions. Just you and the elements. It focuses the mind something fierce. Dad’s got a point, actually. There's something about needing to actively  maintain  your comfort that's… restorative. It’s the opposite of passive consumption, you know? We spend so much of our lives just… having things done  for  us. Restorative? You two are romanticising frostbite! Honestly, I'm picturing you both looking like blue Smurfs, huddled around a tiny stove. Not quite, though there was a bit of a chill in the toes one night, I’ll grant you. Proper kit is essential, of course. Layers, proper insulated boots...and a good stove. Can't beat a hot cuppa in those conditions. That’s a definite necessity. This last trip was up near Cairngorm, exceptionally beautiful. Everything coated in proper, thick snow. The visibility was awful on the second day, though. Dad nearly walked straight into a snowdrift that was easily six feet deep. I had to haul him out. A slight miscalculation, that was all. I underestimated the depth. It’s the white-out conditions that can get you. Makes discerning the landscape… challenging. You rely on map-reading and compass work a lot more. It's good practice. Good practice for getting lost! Look, I’m fascinated by the psychology of it, I truly am. This intentional confrontation with… potential danger. Is it about control? Proving something to yourselves? I see a lot of that in my practice, people pushing boundaries. Hmm. Control, maybe a little. Certainly, a test of self-reliance. I spent years in a lab, Moira. Surrounded by equipment, procedures, other people telling me what to do. This...this is the opposite. It’s just  you .

Right, that was a proper brew, wasn’t it? Needed that after wrestling with those XML tags all day. Honestly, sometimes I think the corpus is actively  trying  to break me. Sounds stressful. XML, eh? Still sounds like gobbledygook to me, even after all these years of using computers. My code’s all Python these days, thankfully. Much more…readable. Although, debugging is a whole separate circle of hell. So, did you manage to finish that article I sent you about the whole ‘auteur theory’ debate? Nearly. Got about halfway. It’s… dense, innit? All very academic. I get the gist – that it’s a bit dodgy to say  one  person is solely responsible for the art of a film, especially when you’ve got cinematographers, editors, composers… the whole lot. But the way they were writing about it was making my head spin. Kept throwing around words like ‘dialectical materialism’. Oh, they  love  their jargon, those film studies lot. My flatmate did a masters in it. He could talk for hours about mise-en-scène and diegetic sound. Drove me mad, honestly. I preferred it when he just watched the films and enjoyed them. Did it change your thoughts on, say, Wes Anderson at all? You're a big fan, aren't you? A bit, yeah. I mean, I still love his films. They’re beautifully crafted and so distinctive. But it makes you think, doesn’t it? He’s got a very particular style, very controlled. How much of that is  him , and how much is the collective effort of everyone else involved? It's just...different when you think about something like, I dunno, early Kurosawa, where you’ve got a really powerful vision but it feels more… collaborative, y’know? That’s a good point. Kurosawa felt…rawer, more visceral, even with the incredible technical skill. It's like the personality of the whole production team is visible. Anderson feels…polished. Almost manufactured. Speaking of manufactured… Have you seen any good food reviews lately? I’m trying to find somewhere decent for a proper Sunday roast. Somewhere with  Yorkshire puddings  that aren’t just pathetic little discs. Oh, you and your Yorkshire puddings. You’re a southerner, you're allowed to be fussy. Up north, we’re happy with anything vaguely resembling one. Though, on that note, there's this little place in Seaburn, 'The Italian Farmhouse'. They do a roast, and the gravy is next level.

…and then the dragon, honestly, it just  sneezed  a whole castle into existence! A fully formed castle, with flags and everything. Can you believe it, Elsie? Wow! Was it a sparkly sneeze? Dragons are  always  sparkly in my stories. It wasn’t described as sparkly, no. It was more… a dusty, ancient sneeze. Very impressive, though. It’s from the book I was reading to your Dad last night. He was quite taken with it. Dusty sneezes are rubbish. Sparkly sneezes make everything better! Even grumpy goblins. That’s very true, Leo. Sparkly sneezes  do  improve things. You know, your Gran used to say something similar. She had an expression, "a bit of sparkle never hurt anyone." She used to say it when I was making a mess, actually. Gran says loads of funny things! Like “butter someone up” – what does that  mean ? Is she trying to put butter on people? Oh, Elsie! No, darling, it doesn’t mean actually putting butter on someone. It means being nice to them to try and get them to do something for you. It's a bit…silly, really. Old-fashioned. Like when I ask Dad for another biscuit? Is  that  buttering him up? That's exactly it! You’re a little expert. So, what amazing structure are you two building? It looks…intricate. It's a spaceship to go and find sparkly dragons! It needs lots of engines. And a laser. And a control room! I’m making the control room. It has… …buttons. Lots of buttons. And a screen. A very important control room. You know, it's funny… building things like this. When I was little, I didn’t have Lego. We had… typewriters. Typewriters? What are  those ? They were… like computers, but without the screen. You hit the keys, and the letters appeared on the paper. Really clunky and noisy. Imagine trying to design a spaceship on a typewriter! That sounds…slow. It  was  slow. Now you can design anything on a computer, or even on a PlayStation. Did you have fun playing Minecraft earlier? Yes! I built a house for a unicorn. It has a rainbow roof. I was building a city! A really big one. With a monster in it. A monster? A friendly monster, I hope? Sometimes. It depends if he gets enough snacks. Of course. Monsters need snacks. You know, I spend all day at work helping children with… well, with things like Excel spreadsheets.

…and honestly, Arthur, you wouldn't  believe  what young Tim turned up in yesterday. Tracksuit bottoms - and not the posh kind, mind - and a t-shirt with a hole in the shoulder. For a job interview! I nearly fainted. My mother would’ve tanned his hide. Ah, the youth of today. No sense of occasion. Though, to be fair, I remember my own interview outfits weren’t exactly Savile Row material. More… practical. Did he get the job? Not a chance. Said he’d “made an impression”, alright. A lasting one, the poor lad. Though the manager did look rather amused. Speaking of impressions, this jam’s lovely, Brenda. Did you make it yourself? Brenda makes everything, doesn’t she? Except perhaps the electricity. No, that’s Betty down the road. Aye, she’s a marvel, our Brenda. This is proper stuff, not like that gloopy supermarket nonsense. Reminds me of my Auntie Maggie’s. She used to grow her own fruit, you know. Had a little farm down near Pickering. Used to take us kids picking strawberries in the summer. Sunshine and sticky fingers. Fruit farms… bring back memories. We used to go apple picking in Kent, though it wasn’t quite the same atmosphere as a Yorkshire farm, I imagine. More… organised. Less likely to fall into a ditch full of nettles. Oh, you’d find a ditch full of nettles anywhere in Yorkshire, Arthur, given half a chance. It’s part of the landscape. You know, I was reading an article the other day about deserted medieval villages. Right here in this county, there are dozens. Whole settlements just… vanished. Wonder what happened to all those folks? Probably succumbed to the plague, or moved to the cities for work. Or just… faded away. Life was different then. Less forgiving. Though, speaking of vanishing, have you driven through the centre of Bradford recently? The roadworks are a nightmare. Took me forty minutes to get from the ring road to here. Forty minutes! Don't  start  me on the roadworks. It's a conspiracy, I tell you. They create them just to keep the consultants like yourself in business, Arthur. Honestly, it's a scandal. And they never seem to finish them. Always "essential maintenance"... for twelve months. It’s a living, Brenda. A living. Though I sometimes wonder if they actually  have  a plan. It looks remarkably… ad hoc.

Honestly, darling, you look exhausted. Another late night battling the algorithms? You practically live on that laptop these days. Pretty much, Auntie Carol. Client wanted a complete revamp of their social media strategy  yesterday . New Year, new marketing push, you know the drill. It’s relentless. And honestly, Facebook’s algorithm is actively trying to make my life difficult. Facebook. Don’t get me started. Brenda keeps sending me those… motivational cat pictures. It's enough to drive a man to drink. Speaking of which, Carol, are we still on for a nice glass of wine later? After young Amelia’s gone to bed, of course. Absolutely, Geoff. I’ve got that lovely Pinot Grigio chilling. Though, I’m trying to be a bit careful at the moment. Dr. Patel wants me to keep an eye on my blood pressure. Said the readings were a little…enthusiastic, after Christmas. Oh, Auntie Carol! You and Christmas biscuits. It’s a love story for the ages. They  were  rather good biscuits, to be fair. Mrs. Higgins from number 7 always makes far too many. They call to me, they really do. Anyway, I’ve got those tablets, the Losartan, and I’m trying to be good. It’s just… hard! And I keep forgetting to take them in the morning. Honestly, having everything scheduled on my phone helps, even if the reminders are annoying. Phones… another modern marvel I’m struggling to master. My mobile keeps asking me to update something. I just press ‘remind me later’ until it stops. It’s a system that works for me. Though, it’s impossible to get directions now without one. Remember when we used to fold out maps? Vaguely. I think I saw a map once in a museum. Feels like ancient history. Though, I do sometimes miss the feeling of… discovering things. Google Maps just  tells  you where to go. It's true. I remember getting utterly lost in the Lake District with your Uncle Barry ages ago. He insisted he knew the way, despite me having the map. Ended up asking a farmer for directions, and he just looked at us like we were completely daft. Barry and his sense of direction. A match made in… well, nowhere particularly accurate. He was convinced he could navigate by the stars. Did you guys get a chance to properly look at the presents Amelia sent?

Honestly, this Earl Grey is… underwhelming. You’d think a decent pub in London could manage a proper cuppa. It tastes like they steeped it for five seconds. You and your tea standards, Liv. It's fine! Perfectly drinkable. Though, knowing you, you'll be analysing the tannins and bergamot levels before you’ve even finished the first mouthful. How  is  work, by the way? Still battling rogue semi-colons and clients who think ‘synergy’ is a personality trait? Oh, don’t even  start  me on the clients. I had one yesterday, honestly insisted his garden centre needed to “disrupt the horticultural landscape”. Disrupt it! It’s petunias and compost, Barry, not a tech startup. And the semi-colons… they breed overnight, I swear. It's exhausting. At least the pay is good, which is… necessary. Have you managed to avoid any catastrophes with the survey programming? Relatively. It’s mostly just endless bug fixing. The professor keeps changing his mind about the weighting, which throws everything off. It's a bit frustrating, but honestly, it's a welcome break from actually  thinking  about my thesis. Thinking about post-structuralist feminism and the representation of female labour is… draining. Speaking of draining, how are things with… well, with Mark? You’ve been a bit quiet about him lately. Oh, Mark. It's...complicated. We're taking a 'pause', as he so eloquently put it. A pause? Is that code for broken up? Not  broken up , exactly. More… indefinitely postponed. He got offered a job in Manchester. A really good job, actually, head chef at some fancy new restaurant. And he wants me to move with him. Manchester? That’s… a fair distance. And you really like your job here, don't you? I do! And I love my flat, and I’ve got all my friends here. It’s just…everything feels a bit suddenly. We only moved in together six months ago. It's also, I think, we just want different things. He’s so focused on his career, and I’m… well, I'm trying to figure out what  my  big career thing is, you know? Copywriting is good, it pays the bills, but I don’t know if it’s ‘it’. That makes sense. It's easy to get swept up in someone else's trajectory. Do your parents know? They seemed pretty keen on him. Mum’s already started subtly suggesting I reconsider.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of paperwork is getting to me. They’ve switched systems again, haven’t they? It's like they actively try to make our lives harder. Anyway, enough about work. How was your walk with Angus this morning? Did you manage to drag him beyond the park gates? You know Angus. He  tolerates  the park. Anything further and it’s a protest involving sitting down and refusing to move. It was… brisk. The wind coming off the Water of Leith was something else. I’m starting to think I need to invest in some proper walking gear, not just a glorified fleece. Oh, the wind! Yes, it’s been dreadful. I tried a potter in the garden yesterday, just to deadhead some roses, and nearly lost my hat twice. Honestly, it feels like autumn is here already. Which, thinking about it, is probably why I’m craving soup. Soup sounds  perfect . I made a butternut squash one last week, absolutely divine. Though, honestly, everything tastes better when you’re not staring at spreadsheets all day. Speaking of things that improve life, have you seen what’s happening with house prices around here? It’s utterly ridiculous. Don’t even  start  me. I was looking at properties online, just out of morbid curiosity, and a semi-detached on Elm Street - the one that needed a new kitchen and had a garden the size of a postage stamp - went for over £600,000. It’s bonkers! Utterly bonkers. I saw a flat – a  flat  – near Richmond station advertised for nearly that. And it’s not even a particularly nice flat! It’s all down to people moving out of London, isn’t it? Pushing the prices up everywhere. My niece is trying to buy, and she's genuinely thinking she might be priced out forever. It’s heartbreaking. I remember when we bought this place… it feels like a lifetime ago. And we were complaining then! Still, at least we’ve got a garden, even if it’s constantly needing weeding. Have you been doing much gardening, Helen? A bit. Mostly battling slugs. They've no respect for delphiniums, you know. It’s therapeutic, though, isn’t it? Getting your hands dirty. Gets you out of your head. Much better than endlessly scrolling through Rightmove, depressing yourself. You’re right there. Actually, talking of getting out of your head, I’ve been trying to get back into running.

Aye, this is proper nice, innit? Beats staring at spreadsheets all day, that’s for sure. Though, spreadsheets are looking more appealing than thinking about the Budget right now. Definitely a step up from concrete and steel, even if I do secretly enjoy a good spreadsheet myself. You’re right about the Budget though. It’s just… depressing. Did you catch Rishi’s speech? It felt like a load of rearranging deckchairs, didn’t it? Catch it? I had it on in the background while I was tagging part-of-speech data. Honestly, it all washes over you after a while. Something about tax cuts and investment… and everyone still seems skint. Honestly, I’m just trying to figure out how I'm going to afford to go to that new musical next month. Oh, the one about the scandalous queen? "Six", isn’t it? I’ve heard good things. A bit outside my usual taste, maybe, but I’m up for something different. I'm more of a Sondheim man myself, you know?  Into the Woods  is a masterpiece. “Six” is a right laugh, apparently. My cousin went last week and said it's proper energetic. I'm worried it'll be full of hen dos though. And Sondheim… aye, good, but a bit…heavy for a Tuesday night, isn't it? More of a weekend thinker. What are you working on at the minute, anyway? Still battling with bridge designs? Pretty much. I'm on a project in Peterborough, designing a replacement for an older railway bridge. It’s… complicated. Lots of ground investigation, dealing with Network Rail, the usual. It’s far more practical than it sounds - a lot of Excel to be honest. Ironically, even though I used to think I escaped spreadsheets with engineering, they follow you everywhere. What about you? Still wrestling with bits of text? Wrestling is a good word for it. I’m basically making sure a language model doesn’t go rogue and start saying daft things. It’s… fascinating, actually. We’re building a corpus of Northern English dialect, trying to teach it to understand things like "bairn" and "owt". It's a nightmare sometimes, getting consistent tagging when everyone spells things differently! It’s a brilliant project, though, trying to preserve some of that, you know? It feels important. That  is  important. Language changes so quickly. My grandma, she’s got this incredible Kentish dialect that barely exists anymore, except in her stories.

Right, another coat on this bit, eh? Honestly, this fence has seen better days. Though, looking at it, it's probably older than half the new builds going up around here. Everything's got to be 'new', doesn’t it? No appreciation for a bit of character anymore. Tell me about it. They’re tearing down Old Man Hemmings’s place next month, you know. The pub. 'Progress', they’re calling it. Gonna be another block of flats. All identikit, same as the ones over on Prescot Road. Hemmings'? No way! That’s… that’s a proper loss. Used to be a cracking little boozer. Remember when we used to sneak in there, pretending we were old enough for a swift half after the football? Sneak? We were bloody brazen! Old Hemmings knew exactly what we were up to, just didn’t care as long as we weren't causing trouble. Good bloke, he was. So, what's all this 'progress' supposed to  be  then? More expensive places for students who won’t even appreciate the history? Essentially, yeah. They say it’s about ‘regenerating the area’, attracting investment. But it feels like they’re just squeezing out the people who  made  this area what it is. It's like they're trying to erase everything that isn't shiny and new. Makes you think, eh? Reminds me of a play I was lecturing on last term – "Death of a Salesman." All about being discarded when you're no longer 'useful'. Plays. You and your plays. I'd rather watch a good film, something with a bit of action. Speaking of which, did you see that new one with… what’s his name? The fella who played Hannibal Lecter? Really good stuff. Hopkins? Anthony Hopkins? Yes, I did. Very good, unsettling as always. Though, I find myself increasingly drawn to… quieter films these days. More character driven. There was this Scandinavian film I saw recently… beautifully shot, really minimal dialogue. It felt more like a painting than a film, you know? A painting? Sounds a bit… slow for my tastes. I like a bit of a bang, a bit of a chase. Though, I do appreciate a good bit of art. My nan used to paint, landscapes mostly. Awful, mind you, but she loved it. Always had me fetching her different shades of green. Always wanting that 'perfect' shade for the fields.

Oh, look at that. Fields of rapeseed. Just…sea of yellow. It’s almost vulgar, isn’t it? In a really lovely way. Reminds me of Constable, though he probably never saw anything quite  this  bright. Vulgar is a strong word, Aunt Carol! Lovely is definitely more accurate. It  is  pretty intense though. Makes the landscape feel… warmer. Are you tracking the fuel consumption on this beast? We're burning through diesel. Fuel consumption? Honestly, I try not to think about it, darling. It gives me anxiety. You're the sensible one, keeping tabs on the practicalities. Just tell me when we're nearing bankruptcy and I’ll start rationing the biscuits. Though, given your penchant for those Polish chocolate wafer things… Hey, they’re essential road trip provisions! And I  am  keeping track. It’s not too bad, considering. But Tarnow’s going to mean another fill-up. And we really should start thinking about a campsite. I’ve been looking at a few online, some near the Old Town. A campsite…yes. Sounds…organised. I was rather hoping we’d just find a nice lay-by. A bit of wild camping, you know? Though I suppose that's frowned upon here. Frowned upon and potentially illegal. We’re pushing our luck enough as it is, driving this van with a questionable MOT. A proper campsite’s safer, and we’ll have access to showers. Trust me, after a week in the mountains, you’ll thank me. Showers are good. Though truthfully, I’m rather enjoying the…rustic charm of things. It’s liberating, isn’t it? Downsizing to this. All that decluttering before we left…it felt  good . Years of accumulated junk, just…gone. Liberating until you realise you forgot your favourite scarf. Or, in my case, the adapter for my phone charger. That was a pain. You know, it's funny, I was talking to Liam – remember Liam from Uni? – and he’s thinking about selling everything and doing something similar. Living in a van. Liam! Goodness, has he finally decided to escape the corporate grind? He always seemed so…stuck. It suits you, though. You’ve always been adaptable. Plus, you have a useful job that you can do remotely. Teaching English to the world, eh? Pretty much. It’s kept me afloat, certainly. Though I do miss having a proper classroom sometimes. The energy of the students… it’s different online.

Honestly, this traffic is  mental . Thought getting out of St Anne’s would be easier on a Tuesday. It's always a bit dodgy around this roundabout, isn’t it? Google Maps says another five minutes of this, then we should be flowing onto the A522. Are you alright, love? You seem a bit…off. Aye, she’s been a bit quiet since breakfast. You alright, petal? Exams stressing you? You’ve not said much about ‘em. Just…tired, I think. And a bit overwhelmed. The English lit exam is next week and I feel like I haven’t retained  anything  about Victorian poetry. It all just blurs into grey, miserable men in top hats. Oh, darling. Victorian poetry can be like that. It’s a mood. Remember that time we went to the Hay Festival? Mrs. Davies - that poet, the one who wrote about the Welsh coastline – she explained it beautifully. Said it was all about repression and longing. Makes a bit more sense when you frame it like that, doesn’t it? Hay? That’s a trek, innit? Never been meself. Too many…books. Gives me a headache just thinkin’ about it. Give me a good footie match any day. Dad! Seriously? Books are amazing! And Hay was brilliant. Remember the amazing little bookshop with the cat? And the stall selling hand-bound journals? I wanted to buy them  all . It was lovely, wasn’t it? And that cafe… the lemon drizzle cake was heavenly. Speaking of things I wanted to buy, did you remember to put washing powder on the list for Preston? We’re completely out. Got it covered. And loo roll. Can't forget that. Though, honestly, I still think we should be going to Booths. Tesco’s just isn’t the same. The quality…it's all gone downhill. Oh my god, not the Booths debate  again . We’ve been over this! It's twice as expensive! I’m a student, remember? My budget is basically dust bunnies and hope. He's just a Booths man, darling. It’s in his DNA. Honestly, it's a Lancashire thing. He still remembers when they used to deliver! They  did  deliver! And the fruit and veg were proper good. Not like the plastic-wrapped rubbish you get now. You wouldn’t get a decent plum at Tesco’s to save your life. It’d be hard as rock.

Oh, this is lovely. Just lovely. It's good to be out of Kendal, even if it is just for a few days. Though, frankly, Thirsk isn’t  that  different, is it? Still fields, still sheep… still people who look at you funny if you ask for a proper cuppa. Now, Mum, don’t be like that. Thirsk has its charms. And I  always  make a proper cuppa for you. It’s a standing order. Besides, it’s been too long. I was so surprised to get your call yesterday. Just… appearing like that! Well, I got bored. Honestly. Kendal’s very peaceful, yes, but peaceful can quickly become… empty. Old Mrs. Higgins next door keeps trying to get me into embroidery. Embroidery! I have a Masters in History, for goodness sake! Embroidery? That  is  bad. What are you watching, Leo? Honestly, you've been glued to that thing since you arrived. Leo, put the phone down for five minutes and say hello to your grandmother! She’s travelled all this way to see you. Hi, Grandma. It’s… uh… this comedian. He’s doing a bit about AI. It’s hilarious. It’s like, the robots are taking over and… AI? Honestly. What  is  it with children and these… machines? I still struggle with the television remote. It feels like it has a mind of its own. It's artificial intelligence, Mum. Basically, getting computers to think like humans. It's used in everything now – your online banking, the recommendations on streaming services… Sounds utterly terrifying. Getting machines to  think ? That’s asking for trouble. Like in those science fiction films. Remember ‘The Day the Earth Stood Still’? That gave me nightmares for weeks. It's not like that, Grandma. It’s just algorithms and stuff. It learns from data. It’s kind of cool, actually. This comedian is pretending to be a robot trying to understand sarcasm. Leo, please. Mum, have you been sorting through things at home? You mentioned on the phone you were starting to clear out the attic. Oh,  that . It's dreadful. Absolutely dreadful. So many memories. Boxes and boxes of photographs, letters… your father’s old army things. It's brought up all sorts, you know? Things I’d forgotten. Like what? Anything interesting? Well… I found a bundle of letters from Aunt Millie. She wrote to me a lot after… well, after Michael.

Right, so… what do you reckon, then? Pretty tidy, innit? Got it for a steal online. Though the delivery took  ages . Not bad, not bad at all, Liam. Solid state drive, I presume? Looks pretty quick just booting up. What are you hoping to do with it? Beyond, you know, browsing memes and watching YouTube compilations. Looks alright. Is that one of them fancy gaming laptops? You finally giving up on the desktop? That thing was a beast… when it actually  worked . Remember trying to get that graphics card sorted for, like, a week? Yeah, solid state. And yeah, Noah, mostly YouTube and… work stuff, actually. I'm doing a lot more digital illustration now, and the old laptop was choking on the bigger files. And Jamie, the desktop  was  a beast, but it was also a constant headache. Honestly, more time was spent fixing it than actually using it. Remember that time the power supply went and smoked the whole room out? Mum nearly killed us. Oh, good times. Though, speaking of headaches, have you updated the antivirus yet? Don’t want to be downloading anything dodgy. Remember that virus Ethan got last year? Lost everything. Nah, not yet. That's what I wanted to test, actually. You're the tech wizard, right? Can you give it a once-over? Make sure it’s all shipshape? And maybe show me how to back everything up properly this time? I still haven't learned my lesson, clearly. Backing up is a faff. I just… don’t. If it goes, it goes. It's mostly pictures of prize-winning marrows anyway. No one wants to steal those. Jamie, that’s… incredibly irresponsible. You need backups! Imagine losing all your plant lists, your grafting schedules… the horror! I happily installed a cloud-based one for my mum last month and she actually thanked me. A  thank you ! See, Noah? You're a hero. Anyway, have you two been keeping up with the MMA? Saw Adesanya fight the other night, absolute clinic. Yeah, watched it down the pub. Proper brutal. I've been trying to get back into training, but… well, gardening takes it outta ya, you know? Constant bending, lifting… it’s a workout in itself. My back's been killing me. It is surprisingly physical. I’ve started doing some beginner’s yoga to try and counteract all the sitting. It’s… humbling.

Honestly, I’m so glad we found this place. It's a little bit…unexpected, isn’t it? Tarnow doesn't exactly scream ‘trendy bistro’. But this is lovely. The decor is actually quite sophisticated. Mmm, this is  amazing . And you’re right. It’s a complete departure from the usual pierogi places. Old Man Kowalski down the street was muttering about ‘fancy foreign rubbish’ when it opened. He’s clinging to the past, that one. Though, to be fair, his pierogi  are  pretty good. Kowalski’s is an institution. But sometimes…sometimes a girl just wants a decent croissant and a cappuccino without feeling like she’s committing some sort of cultural faux pas. It's nice to have options. It makes you feel…less isolated, I think. Definitely. Being here long-term, even with a good job, you start to feel the… sameness. That’s why I make a point of exploring when I can. It’s good for the soul. Speaking of which, how are your lessons going? Still tutoring that Polish businessman? Yes, Mr. Nowak. He’s…challenging. He understands the grammar perfectly, but his pronunciation! It's like he’s actively trying to avoid the ‘th’ sound. And he keeps wanting to talk about football. I’ve learned more about Polish football in the last month than I have in my entire life. Oh, the joys of TEFL! You get a crash course in everything. I'm teaching a group of high school students at the moment. They’re obsessed with TikTok. It’s exhausting trying to keep up with the slang. It’s a whole other language, really. It’s funny, isn’t it? Language is so intrinsically linked to identity. And how we  present  our identity. I was thinking about that recently…you know, about how my identity feels… fractured, I suppose. After, well, after everything. Are you okay? You don’t have to talk about it if you don’t want to. No, it’s alright. It just… feels like so much of my life was built around a certain version of myself, and then… that version just sort of dissolved. Being largely unemployed for so long, it's not exactly conducive to self-worth, is it? It feels ridiculous to even admit that, but it's true. It’s not ridiculous at all. Work doesn’t  define  you, you know? It’s just… a thing you do.

Honestly, Grandad, you wouldn’t  believe  the queues for the Dorset Steam Fair tickets online. I’ve been trying since yesterday! They’re selling fast, apparently. Dorset Steam Fair, eh? Haven't been to that thing in… well, decades. Used to go with your nan, back when it was just a field and a few blokes with oily rags. Still sounds good though. Is it still at Blandford? Yep, still at Blandford. And it’s  huge  now. Loads of stalls, demonstrations, everything. Mum's really keen, and I thought it’d be a nice day out for all of us. But getting the tickets is proving a nightmare. They have different tiers too, like camping options and VIP… honestly, it’s a whole thing. Ooh, that sounds lovely. I haven’t been in years. Is it good for… well, for someone with dodgy knees like me? Are there places to sit, decent pathways? I don’t want to be stuck in a muddy field all day. That’s a really good point, Mum. I’ve been looking at their website, and they  do  have accessibility information. They offer disabled parking, and loan out wheelchairs. The ground is generally quite flat, apparently, but can get churned up if it rains. I'll call them tomorrow and specifically ask about the best routes for someone with mobility issues. Good thinking, love. Can’t be having your mum stuck, that's for sure. Remember when we took her to that garden centre in Wimborne, and the paths were all gravel? She was moaning for days! Oh, don't remind me! It felt like walking on broken glass! Still, I’m not letting a bit of gravel put me off a steam fair. It's just... everything’s an effort these days, isn't it? It is, Mum. But we’ll make sure you’re comfortable. Right, back to these tickets. I think I’ve found a package that might work. It's a bit more expensive, but includes parking and access to a covered seating area. Covered seating sounds perfect. Especially in England. You never know what the weather’s going to do. Speaking of things that need covering... have you given any more thought to that furniture you're trying to move into your new flat, Chloe? That sofa looks like it won’t fit through the door. Don't even get me started, Grandad!

Honestly, this Yorkshire weather is doing my head in. One minute it’s sunshine, the next it’s threatening a downpour. Reminds me of the Lake District, really, but even Kendal seemed to have more…predictability. Though, thinking about it, maybe I just  felt  more prepared for it there. Familiar, like. It is a bit changeable, isn’t it? Still, better than the constant drizzle we had last week. And Thirsk  is  lovely. You haven't complained about it too much since we moved. Though I know leaving Kendal was hard. Hard is an understatement, love. But you two convinced me it was a good idea. Closer to Leo, you said. And a bit more…life. Kendal was getting a bit quiet for an old bird like me. Though quiet has its charms. Grandma, you wouldn't understand the ‘life’ here. It’s all TikTok and Fortnite. He’s exaggerating, Mum. Thirsk has a thriving little theatre scene, remember? And that lovely artisan cheese shop? We’re taking you there tomorrow. Oh, the cheese shop! Now  that  sounds promising. Though I still don't understand this obsession with…Twitter. You showed me, Sarah, and it just seems like everyone shouting into the void. It can be, but it’s also a good way to keep up with the news, and connect with people. I use it for my school updates mostly. It's easier than endless emails. Emails are perfectly good enough! Less…aggressive. And all these notifications. It’s a wonder anyone gets any peace. Though, I suppose I’m just showing my age. Remember when we had to  wait  for letters? And a phone call was a real event? It does feel different now. Speaking of events, Leo has a drama club rehearsal tonight. They're working on 'A Midsummer Night’s Dream'. It’s going well! I'm Puck. It’s a really good part, lots of mischief. Mr. Henderson says I've got a natural stage presence. Puck! Oh, lovely! You always were a little rascal. This is wonderful, dear. Your grandfather would have been so proud. He always loved the theatre. Did I ever tell you about the time he tried to build a set for the local amateur dramatics group? It nearly brought the village hall down. You’ve mentioned it a few times, Mum. It’s become a family legend. Well, it’s a good story!

Honestly, Leo, please don’t try and incorporate the chocolate fingers into the structural integrity of that…thing. It’s going to collapse. And you’ll have sticky fingers. It  needs  support, Mummy. It's a castle! Castles need strong walls. My bunny needs glitter. Lots and lots of glitter. It’s for Easter! Of course it does, darling. More glitter it is. Right, so, the dentist appointment. Ashaad’s mum called. She says little Ashaad is absolutely  terrified  about going. Apparently, he’s convinced the dentist will drill all the way to his brain. ALL the way to his brain?! That’s what  he  thinks. I told Ashaad’s mum that’s definitely not how it works. Bit dramatic, that one. Reminds me a little of someone else I know... Is Ashaad in my class? He likes drawing dinosaurs. I believe so, yes. He does love dinosaurs, doesn't he? Anyway, it got me thinking about your hearing test next week, Leo. You haven't said much about it. Are you worried? Nah. It’s just…sitting still is  boring . And I have to wear headphones. It won’t take long. And they'll give you stickers afterwards, I promise. Speaking of boring, has anyone thought about what they want to  do  for their birthdays? It’s creeping up on us. Both of yours so close together – honestly, it’s madness having siblings with birthdays practically on top of each other. It’s a logistical nightmare. I want a unicorn party. With a real unicorn. A real unicorn. Right. We’ll see about the real unicorn. Perhaps a very convincing inflatable one? Leo? Any demands? A Lego Death Star! A  really  big one! The one with all the minifigures! We'll discuss Lego options. Perhaps we can tie it into your school trip? They're going to that Impressionist exhibition, aren’t they? Monet, all the water lilies. Monet is…pale. Pale? It’s beautiful art, Leo! It's all about light and colour! Mummy, can I have another biscuit? A pink one? Absolutely, darling. One more. Honestly, you two are going to be bouncing off the walls before bedtime. Now, about this Monet trip…it could link to Lego, honestly! Building structures, design… You mean I could build a Monet garden out of Lego? With the bridge? Possibly! We could explore that. It's all about making connections. Maths…art…it all fits together.

Honestly, this is  exactly  what I needed. Proper builder’s tea and a catch-up with you. It feels like ages, doesn't it? Since uni, properly ages. Everything’s been so… hectic. Tell me about it! Work's been absolutely mental. Acute stroke ward, you know? It’s rewarding, don't get me wrong, but draining. And then trying to actually  live  a life on top of that… It’s a struggle. Though, your flat is looking lovely, by the way. Did you finally get around to painting the living room? I did! Took me three weekends, and I’m still finding bits of magnolia paint in strange places. Worth it though, isn’t it? Makes it feel… less like a student hovel. Speaking of which, did your mum finally stop hinting about you buying a house? She was relentless last time I spoke to her. Oh god, don’t even  start  me. It’s a weekly occurrence now. "Darling, all your friends are settling down, are you sure you wouldn't like a viewing?" as if I haven’t explained about the deposit, and the general impossibility of affording anything in Ashford these days! It's even worse than when we were trying to decide on universities. Remember the pressure then? Oh,  definitely . Mum was convinced I’d made the wrong choice going to Brighton. “Too… bohemian,” she said. As if a bit of independence was a terrible thing. I still think Brighton was the best thing for me, though. Forced me to grow up a bit. And the copywriting job’s good. Challenging, but good. Although, honestly, sometimes I stare at a blank screen for hours and wonder what I’m doing with my life. I know that feeling. Some days at work, I’m dealing with incredibly complex cases, and I feel like I’m actually making a difference. Other days… it’s just paperwork and hoping I haven’t missed something crucial. It's the responsibility that gets to me, I think. Especially with older patients. It’s funny, isn't it? We both went off and did these ‘serious’ jobs, and I sometimes wonder if we overthought things. Do you ever have moments where you just wish you’d become a florist or something less… weighty? Constantly! Honestly, I had a serious daydream about opening a dog grooming salon last week. Just fluffy dogs and happy owners.

…and honestly, the audacity of it! Saying it’ll 'enhance the landscape'. It looks like a solar farm  is  the landscape now, doesn't it? Especially after last night’s decision. I still can't believe they approved it. Ghastly. Utterly ghastly. They say it's progress, but it's progress at the expense of everything that makes the area…well, the area. Though, I suppose young Timmy – you remember Timmy from the village shop? – he’s got a job lined up maintaining it. So there's that. Timmy always was a practical lad. Good for him. Though a field of shimmering blue isn't exactly postcard material, is it? It reminds me, actually, of a story Old Man Hemmings used to tell about when he first qualified as a surveyor. He was sent to assess a proposed industrial estate, apparently, and he described it as ‘a visual assault on the senses’. Perfect phrasing, I always thought. Hemmings! Now  there  was a character. Always smelled faintly of pipe tobacco and disapproval. Speaking of assaults on the senses... remember the state of this town thirty years ago? Before the “improvements”? It was genuinely grim. And now they’re trying to ‘rebrand’ it, as if a new logo will fix decades of bad planning. It's true. It was rough around the edges, but it had  character . That wonderful old Victorian architecture, the market… they’ve replaced it all with beige boxes and chain stores. They knocked down The Grand Hotel to build that monstrosity of a car park! Absolute vandalism. And the High Street. It’s all nail bars and phone repair shops now. Whatever happened to proper butchers and bakers? I remember when you couldn’t move for the smell of freshly baked bread on a Saturday morning. It was bliss. Before all the European… influence, if you will. Now, now, let’s not descend into that territory, shall we? Though I do agree, the homogenization of towns is a tragedy. It's all part of this relentless drive to make everywhere look the same. It stifles any sense of local identity. I was in Prague last year, you know, and it was a breath of fresh air. Prague, eh? I've been meaning to go. They do some remarkable deals on city breaks these days. Managed to snag a week for Margaret and myself – all inclusive – for just under six hundred quid.

…Right, so, the initial feedback on the ‘Historical Figures Reimagined’ TikTok series is… surprisingly good. More than just teenagers are watching, apparently. A lot of comments from university students saying they're using it as quick revision. That’s brilliant, isn’t it? You really nailed the tone - informative but not  dry . It’s the visuals, I think. Those little animated bits you add. Way more engaging than just me lecturing about Henry VIII for 50 minutes. Aye, well, that’s the power of short-form video. Attention spans are… challenged, let’s say. And it's not just Henry, the Elizabeth I one is doing really well too. It got me thinking though…this could be bigger than just a fun side project. What if we actually developed a suite of these? Like, targeted learning modules for different key stages? You mean… a business? Properly? While house-sitting in Australia? That feels a bit…ambitious, even for you, Ben. Ambition is my middle name, darling. No, seriously though. Think about it. There’s a huge gap in the market for visually engaging, easily digestible educational content. Especially post-pandemic. Kids and young adults are used to learning in different ways now. And schools are scrambling for resources. We could focus on history, initially, given the initial traction, but expand. History is definitely your wheelhouse. Mine's more… pedagogical theory and curriculum design. I can map things to learning objectives, assessment criteria, all that jazz. But building the actual content…that's where it gets trickier. And expensive. That’s where we dovetail nicely, doesn’t it? You do the ‘what’ needs to be taught, I do the ‘how’ it’s presented. Content creation wouldn't need to be  huge  initially. We could freelance animators, voiceover artists. Focus on quality over quantity. And the TikTok/YouTube revenue streams…they’re not nothing. It’s the legal side that worries me. Copyright, educational permissions, safeguarding… the minefield of working with young people, even indirectly. My head’s already spinning imagining the risk assessments. Fair point. We’d definitely need to consult with someone knowledgeable about educational law. But we can mitigate. We focus on public domain figures, historical events, stick to factual information… That sort of thing. Besides, many universities now use YouTube as a study tool. It's already 'acceptable' on some level. Hmm. You're starting to wear me down, you know.

Honestly, this is exactly what I needed. Just… walking. And not talking about marking essays for five minutes. You were starting to resemble a particularly stressed-out owl last night, you know. Eyes wide, muttering about referencing styles. Glad to get you out of the house. And beautiful evening for it, isn’t it? That light on the water…it’s almost otherworldly. It is. It reminds me of that trip to Cornwall with Mum and Dad. When I was, oh, maybe ten? We went to St Ives, and the sea was exactly this colour. All shimmering silver and grey. Cornwall…right. The one where you were convinced you saw a mermaid? I  did  see a mermaid! It had long, flowing hair and…and a sparkly tail! Though, looking back, it was probably just a particularly sleek seal, and my imagination running wild. Dad fuelled it, though. He absolutely played along, making up stories about mermaid kingdoms under the waves. Your Dad’s a master storyteller. Always has been. Speaking of stories, have you heard anything more from Eleanor? She was supposed to be back from her sailing trip a week ago. That’s what I was going to ask  you ! I texted her a few days ago, just a quick ‘hope you're having a blast,’ and got nothing back. Which is… unusual for Eleanor. She usually replies instantly, even from the middle of the Atlantic. Exactly. I tried calling yesterday, went straight to voicemail. She was so excited about this trip, though. Said it was a solo sail, just her and the open water. A real 'finding herself' sort of thing, apparently. Right. Finding herself. Sounds a bit cliché, even for Eleanor. Still, a week of radio silence is concerning. Maybe there’s just been bad reception? Though knowing her, she’d have a satellite phone or something. You’d think. She’s obsessively prepared for everything. Remember when she went backpacking through Southeast Asia and had a spreadsheet detailing every potential illness and the corresponding medication?
