Oh, don’t remind me. It was… thorough. I admire her ambition, though. Just throwing herself into things. It's a world away from us, isn't it? Content with our academic bubbles. Bubbles that are currently overflowing with student essays, yes. But true. She really  lives . It makes you wonder, doesn’t it? If we're missing out on something. On a potentially terrifying solo sailing trip?

Ooh, look at ‘er shoes! Honestly, what  is  that? Like somethin’ a magpie dragged in, innit? All glitter and… feathers? It’s… avant-garde, I think they'd call it. Though, yeah, it’s a  lot . She’s trying to make a statement, clearly. Doesn’t mean it’s a  good  statement. Honestly, I think she's aiming for ‘shock value’ rather than ‘style’. It reminds me of that time I tried to bedazzle a pair of wellies for a school fair. It didn’t end well. Glitter  everywhere . Bedazzled wellies? You were a wild child, weren't ya, Liv? No, seriously though, I just don’t get it. Back home, people want somethin' practical. A good pair of boots for walkin' the dog, that sort of thing. All this…fuss… It's different here, though, isn’t it? Cambridge is a bit of a bubble, and London even more so. People are more willing to experiment, I think. Plus, the fashion scene down there is completely different. Honestly, sometimes I feel a bit…underdressed even going to the supermarket! I get that. Being around so many students definitely influences things. They're all trying to find their 'look', even if it's a bit…out there. I try to keep it sensible for school, obviously. Can't exactly turn up to Year 3 in something that looks like it walked off a runway. Sensible’s good. I like sensible. Though, I do love a good bargain. Found a cracking coat in Doncaster market last week, proper wool, for a tenner! You wouldn’t find that kinda deal round here, would ya? Tenner? That  is  a bargain! Everything in Cambridge is overpriced, especially clothes. I mostly shop online now, or in the sales. I actually saw a dress I liked on ASOS the other day… it’s kinda midi length, floral print… I was thinking of getting it for Hannah’s birthday drinks. Oh, Hannah’s birthday! When is that again? I’ve completely lost track. Next Saturday, isn't it? Gonna be at that new bar, The Velvet Heron, apparently. Fancy, sounds it. I'm dreading having to figure out what to wear. I've got nothin' 'fancy'. Ooh, The Velvet Heron’s supposed to be good. A bit pricey, though. That dress I mentioned, it's floral but not  too  floral, you know? Maybe I could send you a link?

Ugh, this Physics homework is  brutal . Honestly, Mrs. Davies thinks we have nothing else to do but calculate the trajectory of… I don’t even know  what  anymore. Some hypothetical projectile. Sounds delightful. Physics was never my strong suit, even at A-Level. Though, to be fair, A-Level wasn’t  that  long ago, it just feels like it. Milk and sugar as usual? Thanks, Mum. And yeah, you know me. Honestly, I’m starting to think I want to drop it. Maybe just focus on Art, English Lit, and History. Dropping Physics is a big decision, love. Have you spoken to your guidance counsellor? Perhaps it’s just a tricky topic, and a bit of extra help would make all the difference. I have, briefly. She just said I need to ‘persevere’. It’s so… unhelpful. Anyway, I took some photos down by the Stade this afternoon. I think some of them actually turned out okay. Oh really? Let me see! You’ve been getting quite into photography lately, haven’t you? It’s lovely you’ve found a hobby you enjoy. Much better than just staring at TikTok all day. Hey! I do other things. But yeah, I really like trying to capture the light on the fishing boats. It’s really hard actually, getting it right. I’m trying to do a series on Hastings, like, the real Hastings, not just the tourist stuff. That sounds ambitious and lovely. You’ve got a good eye, you always have. Remember when you were little and you’d ‘decorate’ everything with glitter glue? A different kind of artistry, perhaps, but the dedication was there! Don't remind me! Grandma still finds glitter in the sofa cushions. Speaking of which, how was work today? Anything exciting happen at the dentist’s? Oh, you know. The usual anxieties about root canals and the price of veneers. Old Mr. Henderson nearly fainted when I told him the cost of whitening. Bless him. It’s… a lot of people-ing. It can be draining, if I’m honest. Sometimes I just want to hide in the stationery cupboard. Sounds stressful. You deserve a holiday. Actually, talking of stressful… I saw online that Maisie Peters is doing a gig in Brighton next month. Oh, yes! She’s good, isn’t she? Do you want me to look at tickets? It might be a nice little outing.

Right then. Lovely cuppa, Doreen, thank you. Though, I still reckon you put too much milk in it. Makes it…well, milky. Oh, don’t be daft, Arthur. You always say that. It’s just how I like it. And you drink it all the same. How’s the application form comin’ on, then? Still stuck on that bleedin’ “achievements” section? Stuck as a limpet, I am. Achievements! What achievements 'ave I got? Watched a lot o’ football? Argued the toss with the telly? I tell you, they make it sound like you need to 'ave single-handedly cured cancer to fill that form in. Morning, you two. Sounds like Arthur’s grappling with the bureaucratic nightmare again. What form  is  it this time? Some sort of community grant, David. He wants to get one of those… what d’you call ‘em… 3D printers. Says he wants to make little models of boats. A 3D printer? That’s…ambitious. Though, I suppose it’s a productive hobby. Better than staring at the garden all day, Arthur. Speaking of which, how’s the cockerel doing? Still crowing at ridiculous hours? The menace! It’s a plague, I tell ya. Five in the mornin', right under my window. Drives me spare. I swear it looks at me when it crows, proper defiant, that bird. And Doreen keeps tellin’ me I shouldn’t complain, says it’s a “beautiful sound of the countryside.” Beautiful! It’s a racket! Now, Arthur, be nice. Old Mrs. Higgins loves hearing him. Reminds her of her farm days, apparently. And the baby birds seem to be thriving in the apple tree, haven’t they? I saw the mother feeding them earlier. That’s good. Though I had a bit of trouble with some of my Year 9s yesterday. Absolute nightmare class. One of them, little Liam, just… completely shut down during the maths test. Wouldn't write a thing. It's heartbreaking, y’know? You try and reach them, but sometimes… Problem children, eh? Always ‘ad ‘em. Reminds me of young Kevin next door, back in Costessey. Absolute terror. Set fire to old Mr. Henderson’s shed, he did. Little blighter. Though, he turned out alright in the end, became a builder. Funny, that. Didn’t learn from his mistakes, did he? Speaking of builders, have you seen the work they did on the new houses down by the old mill?

…and honestly, the paperwork is just relentless, isn’t it? I thought teaching prepared me for bureaucracy, but this is a whole other level. Visas, proof of funds, accommodation checks… it’s like she’s applying to Oxford, not coming to live with her own mother! You always did make a dramatic flair of things, Elsie. But I can imagine. It’s not like it was when  we  travelled, is it? Just a passport and a bit of luck. Everything’s so… regimented now. How's Amelia coping on her end? Is she getting stressed about leaving everything behind in Australia? She’s putting on a brave face, of course. She’s always been a strong one, my Amelia. But I can hear it in her voice, you know? That little wobble. She’s leaving friends, a job she actually enjoyed… a life she built. And while she  says  she’s excited to be closer to me, I know it’s a big upheaval. Especially after all this time. Ten years is a long time to build a life somewhere. Ten years  is  a long time. But you’ve been talking about this for a while now, haven’t you? She knew it was on the cards. And Brighton’s a lovely place, Elsie. She’ll settle. It’s not the Outback, that’s for sure, but it’s got a vibrancy… a good energy. It’s not the  place  I’m worried about, George. It’s the… readjustment. She’s very independent, fiercely so. She’s used to managing everything herself. I don’t want her to feel like I’m suffocating her, trying to wrap her in cotton wool because I’m suddenly feeling maternal after all these years of letting her fly. You wouldn't. You're far too sensible for that. And she knows you. She knows you wouldn't do anything to stifle her. It’s just… you've missed her, haven’t you? That's what this is really about, under all the visa applications and housing concerns. Don't be so perceptive, George. It's terribly irritating. Of course, I've missed her! She's my daughter! We’ve always been close, but distance… it does things. Phone calls and video chats are all well and good, but they're not the same as having a cup of tea with her, are they? Or just… knowing she’s down the road if I need her.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the Scottish referendum again… it’s just exhausting, isn’t it? Feels like we’ve been having this conversation every decade for the last thirty years. Did you catch Humza Yousaf’s speech yesterday? Quite fiery. Exhausting is the word, David. Absolutely exhausting. I did see snippets of it. He’s a good speaker, that boy. Though I still think it’s all a bit of a distraction, to be honest. From the real issues, you know? The cost of living, the NHS… Scotland’s got its own problems too, independence won’t magically fix them. I was talking to Margaret down at the bowling club about it - she's fiercely pro-independence, always has been, but even  she  admitted things are a bit grim just now. Grim is putting it mildly. Though I suppose a lot of people feel a sense of… well, a need for  something  to change. That’s where the appeal lies, I think. It's just, the practicalities seem so insurmountable. Anyway, enough about politics. How did the interview go for the Head of Department role? You sounded fairly optimistic last week. Oh, don’t even ask. It was… a disaster. Not a complete train wreck, but definitely derailed. It was Professor Armitage and that new woman, Dr. Chen, on the panel. Chen grilled me for a good twenty minutes about ‘dynamic leadership’ and ‘leveraging synergy’ – corporate jargon, frankly. I felt like I was applying for a job at a marketing firm, not an educational institution! Ah, the modern university. I know the feeling. Armitage has a real fondness for buzzwords, doesn't he? He probably read a Harvard Business Review article and decided he was a management guru. Precisely! And then they asked me about my experience with ‘digital transformation’. Digital transformation! I've been using interactive whiteboards since they were the size of a small car! It feels like they want someone who's never actually  taught  a class. I think they’ve already got someone in mind, someone younger, more… ‘disruptive’. That's a shame, John. You’d be brilliant at it. You've got decades of experience, you know the department inside and out. It's those shiny new faces they always seem to favour. It's maddening. Tell me about it. Keeps an old man on his toes, though, I suppose. Keeps me remembering I'm not spring chicken anymore.

Honestly, Arthur, are you  sure  this is remotely safe? It feels…precarious. Like a Rube Goldberg machine designed by someone with a distinct lack of engineering skill. Which, admittedly, might be me. Oh relax, Penelope. It's a mousetrap game, not a structural engineering project. A bit of precariousness is the  point . Think of the drama! Besides, young Leo here has been surprisingly good at the build. It’s mostly following instructions, Dad. Though I did suggest the pulley system with the biscuit tin. That was all me. Biscuit tin's good. Strategic bait. Though I reckon cheese is better. Mice like cheese, right? They certainly do, Leo. Though I've heard peanut butter works wonders too. Though then you risk attracting  other  things... like squirrels. We had a squirrel incident in Connecticut, you wouldn't believe. Connecticut! Oh, do tell, Margaret. It always fascinates me, the differences between American children and ours. They seemed so…forward. Confident. Almost aggressively polite. Aggressively polite? That’s a new one, Penelope. It’s true! Little Timmy, the boy next door, just  marched  up to me and asked if I needed help carrying groceries. Before I could even acknowledge him. Here, a child would shuffle their feet and mumble something. Maybe it's the culture? They're brought up to be more independent? Like, encouraged to speak their mind? I think so. And the schools are very different. A lot more emphasis on presentation and self-promotion, even at a young age. My niece, Emily, was in debate club from the age of ten. Ten! Can you imagine? Debate club? Sounds…intense. I just wanna make a mousetrap game. A very important aim, indeed. Now, Margaret, you were saying about the squirrel incident? Oh, it was a nightmare. We'd left the bird feeder out, and this incredibly brazen squirrel was systematically dismantling it, piece by piece. It would sit on the patio table, stuffing its cheeks, and  look  at you. Like it owned the place. They have no fear, those American squirrels. No fear. Perhaps that's it. Children and squirrels. A distinct lack of British reserve. It's rather refreshing, in a way, isn’t it? Though slightly exhausting. Dad, can I try the biscuit tin pulley again? It almost worked last time, but the string snapped. Go for it. Just be careful with the hammer, Leo. Your grandmother's right, we don’t want a hospital trip over a mousetrap.

Right, operation “wardrobe refresh” is officially underway. Honestly, it was a  mission  out there today. The markets were absolutely heaving. Oh, good! I thought I heard a rustling of plastic from the lift. Successful haul then? You look… triumphant. And slightly stressed. A bit of both, definitely. Triumphant because I found  the  dress. And stressed because battling for a silk scarf feels like a competitive sport these days. Honestly, the aunties are fierce. The aunties are always fierce when it comes to good quality silk. Let me guess, floral? You've been eyeing up those silk scarves for weeks. You know me too well. It's a beautiful one, deep burgundy with little cream blossoms. But that’s not even the best bit. Look! This is why I was so excited. Is that… a qipao? A proper one? It is! I found a little shop just off the main shopping street, run by an elderly woman who clearly takes immense pride in her craft. It’s hand-embroidered. Look at the detail on the sleeves! Wow. That’s… stunning, actually. The embroidery is exquisite. And the colour suits you beautifully - that deep teal is amazing. You weren’t planning on going down this route, were you? I thought you were just after a few new sweaters for the colder weather. I  was . Honestly! I walked past the shop and just… got drawn in. It felt a bit silly at first, thinking about wearing a qipao, being a… well, being me. A foreigner. But she was so lovely, the woman running the shop, and she explained all about the different styles, the history… and it just felt… right. I understand. It’s beautiful, and wearing something like that is a lovely way to show respect for the culture. It's… it’s ambitious though, isn't it? You usually lean towards more… understated things. Exactly! And that's what made me hesitate. But she encouraged me. She said it’s wonderful when people appreciate the craftsmanship. Plus, I thought, when are we ever going to have the opportunity to wear something like this  here , surrounded by the real thing? Back in Norwich, it'd just feel... a bit performative, wouldn't it? It certainly wouldn’t get the same reception at a pub quiz. So, the aunties didn't get  everything  then? What else have you got in those bags of wonder?

Ah, that was a match and a half, wasn’t it? Absolutely brutal out there. Sexton was lookin' a bit rattled towards the end, I thought. Nearly cost us, that last penalty. Brutal is an understatement! My Dad was  screaming  at the telly. Said the ref was blind as a bat. He kept saying "Forward! It was clearly forward!" like, twenty times. Your Dad’s always like that during the rugby, isn’t he, Oisin? It's part of the experience. Honestly, I was just relieved we pulled it off. My nerves are shot. Ach, a good win is a good win. Though, I’ll admit, all that scrummaging does me in. Reminds me too much of trying to keep thirty seven year-olds behaving in the dinner hall. Same pushing and shoving, just less mud! You always have a way of putting things into perspective, Moira. Still, it’s good to see the boys playin' with that kind of heart. It's a long time since we’ve seen Ireland play like  that . Can we talk about something else now? It’s making my head hurt thinking about all the tackling. I’ve got a history test tomorrow and I need to actually, like, study. Of course, darling. Anything to avoid rugby analysis with your Dad and Moira. What about your birthday plans? Are you still keen on laser quest? Yeah! Definitely. Finn invited Jamie and Leo, so it should be good. Though Finn reckons he’s, like, a pro at laser quest. He’s been watching YouTube videos. YouTube videos, is it? Back in my day, we practiced our tactical maneuvers in the schoolyard with sticks and stones! Times have changed, surely. Speaking of school, how's PE goin’, Oisin? Still enjoyin’ the sports? It’s okay. We're doing basketball at the moment. It's alright, but I’m not very good. I keep missing the basket. Everyone else is already, like, doing layups and stuff. Don't worry about that, love. It takes time. Just have fun. Remember when I tried to teach you to ride your bike? That was a bit of a disaster! Oh, that  was  a disaster! You were convinced you'd broken your arm, darling. A scraped knee was a tragedy! Right, well, it’s gettin’ on. Oisin, you should be thinkin’ about headin’ up to bed soon. Big test tomorrow, aye? Ugh, but I wanted to finish my drawing!

Honestly, I’m starting to think everyone I know is having a baby. It’s a proper epidemic! Sarah just announced, didn’t she? Third one. Three! She did! Mental, isn't it? Proper breeding machine, that one. Though, she always did want a big family. Still, it makes you think, doesn’t it? Especially with everyone getting married… It's the next logical step, I suppose. Don’t even  start  with the logical steps. I’m barely managing to keep my houseplants alive, let alone a tiny human. Though, I did spend ages cooing over little Leo at the Christmas do. He’s Maisie’s, remember? Oh, Leo! He's a little cherub. Maisie's loving it, even if she is utterly exhausted. She was saying just yesterday she hasn't had a full night's sleep since, well, since Leo arrived. It’s good to see her so happy though, isn't it? Definitely. It just…feels a long way off. Speaking of long ways off, have you made any progress on finding a place in Cambridge? Still stuck with your parents in Lincoln? Ugh, don’t remind me. It’s…complicated. Viewings are a nightmare. Everything’s either falling apart, ridiculously overpriced, or already gone by the time I enquire. Mum’s starting to hint I’m perfectly comfortable there, which, you know, isn’t the vibe I’m going for. I really want my own space. I can imagine. Lincolnshire's lovely, but… Cambridge is Cambridge. It's so different. Have you tried looking beyond the city centre at all? Like, out towards Histon or Impington? Bit further out, but potentially more for your money? I have! A little. But commuting is a pain, and honestly, I want to be able to cycle everywhere, like we do here. It's just… frustrating. I keep getting outbid. It's like the whole city is being bought up by students’ parents. Tell me about it. It's the same trying to buy a decent coffee table. Honestly. Anyway, chin up. Something will come up. You're relentless when you want something. Remember how long you searched for those Dr. Martens? Okay, fair point. That was a saga. Speaking of relentless searching… I was having a clear-out at my parents' and found a bunch of clothes I haven’t worn in ages. Loads of stuff that would totally fit you.

…and honestly, Mrs. Higgins nearly had a fit when I told her I was painting a mural of a badger playing the banjo. Said it was 'unsuitable for a dental practice waiting room', can you believe it? Like what’s unsuitable about a badger with musical inclinations? Typical Mrs. Higgins. She probably thinks anything remotely cheerful is ‘unprofessional’. Though, a banjo-playing badger  is  a bit…specific. You’ve been on that folk instrument kick for a while now, haven’t you? Still got that cheap acoustic you picked up from Gumtree? Nah, sold that one. Found a proper Gibson, secondhand, up in Cambridge. Bit of a steal, actually. Needed a bit of work, the action was miles off, but I’ve been tinkering with it. You wouldn’t believe the tone now. You should come round, I'll play you something. A Gibson, eh? Proper bit of kit. More useful than a banjo, if you ask me. Though, I suppose even a badger needs a hobby. Oi! Don’t diss the banjo. It’s a beautiful instrument. And what’s with the knife, Liam? Planning a hostile takeover of my mum’s biscuit tin? Always prepared, mate. You never know when you’ll need to, uh, liberate a digestive. Seriously though, been doing a bit of self-defence stuff. Mixed martial arts. It's good to know how to look after yourself, innit? Especially working alone like I do. Some right dodgy characters about. That’s sensible, Liam. Though I always figured a well-worded sentence was the best defence. Years of explaining grammatical nuances to teenage language learners has given me a pretty intimidating glare, apparently. You and your linguistics, Ben. You can explain the subjunctive mood to someone, but can you take ‘em down in a clinch? Point taken. Though I suspect most attackers would be baffled into submission by a discussion of phonemes. Speaking of baffling, I was reading this article about regional dialects… apparently, even within Bedfordshire, there’s a massive variation. You two, being proper Bedford lads, have you noticed that? Luton’s different, definitely. A lot more… direct, shall we say? People don’t beat around the bush. My old man always said it’s from the Romany influence. Got a bit of Cyprus in the blood too, so that changes things. Yeah, Bedford's a bit… softer. More rounded vowels. I’ve noticed people from further out, like the Fens, sound completely different.

Honestly, this Bolognese is taking  ages . I swear, every time I try to cook something proper, it ends up being a three-hour ordeal. Dramatic, much? It smells amazing though, so worth it. And hey, at least you're not wrestling with car insurance quotes again. That was a genuinely stressful afternoon. You’re not wrong. That was… something. Still can’t believe how much it’s gone up. Fifteen percent! Fifteen! And for what? Apparently, everyone in Peterborough is crashing their cars on a Tuesday now. Ridiculous, isn’t it? I think they just see young drivers and automatically assume we're all Lewis Hamilton in disguise. Though, admit it, you  do  drive a bit fast sometimes. I do  not ! I just… appreciate efficient travel. Especially on the A1. It’s a motorway, it’s meant to be used! Anyway, that brings me back to my original point about things being expensive. Insurance, petrol… it’s all eating into the ‘Saving for a Flat’ fund. Tell me about it. I'm trying to put some money aside too, but every month something else pops up. The car needed a new tyre last month, and before that it was… oh, what  was  it? Something equally annoying and costly. It’s never ending, is it? You know, sometimes I really wish I hadn't decided to learn to drive. I thought it would give me freedom, and it does… but at what cost? The commute is still awful, just with more responsibility. Right? Before I got the car, I was convinced the bus was a nightmare, but now… now I almost  long  for the days of reading a book on the way to work instead of actively trying to prevent road rage. And fighting for a parking space! Don't even  start  on the parking. It’s a blood sport. Especially around the office. I’ve seen grown adults practically wrestling over a space. You're exaggerating! …slightly. Have you thought about cycling maybe? Just for the days when the weather is decent? Cycling? In Peterborough traffic? Are you mad? I'd be roadkill within five minutes. Plus, I'd arrive at work looking like a drowned rat. No thank you. I'm German-born, I appreciate practicality, and arriving looking presentable  is  practical. Fair enough. Though, I am seriously considering getting one of those electric scooters. They seem a bit less terrifying.

Right then, who wants a Yorkshire Tea brew? Proper strong, like we like it. Arthur, you look like you could do with one after that journey from Hull. Aye, Dorothy, you read my mind. My bones ache just  thinking  about that A63. Congestion’s terrible these days. Used to fly down that road, we did. Fly is a strong word, Margaret. More like a brisk walk, even back then. Though it were quieter, mind. Not all these fancy cars… and roundabouts! Give me a simple crossroads any day. Thanks, Gran. This is good. Can I have two sugars, please? Two sugars for our young mathematician. Honestly, Leo, you’ll rot your teeth. Though I suppose a bit of sugar helps the brain work, eh? Busy with your A-Levels, are you? Yeah, pretty busy. Physics is killing me. Honestly, I think I'd rather mark GCSE papers than do another integration question. Oh, don't say that! You think  my  job is easy? Trying to decipher what these kids are  trying  to write sometimes... It’s like reading hieroglyphics. Honestly, last paper, one lad tried to solve an equation using… well, I don’t even know  what  he was trying to do. Looked like advanced squiggles. Oh, the youth of today. No respect for a good, solid method. When  I  was young… Now, now, Margaret. Don’t start on the ‘when I was young’ stories. We’ll be here all day. Though, truth be told, things  were  simpler. More community spirit, you know? What was Hull like when you were kids, Grandad? I only know it as… well, a city with a really big bridge. Ah, Hull. A proper working city it was. All shipyards and fishing trawlers. The smell of the sea and fish… could knock you sideways, it could. Your grandmother worked down at the fish market for a bit, she did. She could fillet a fish faster than you can blink! Don’t exaggerate, Arthur! It weren't  that  fast. Though I did have a knack for knowing a good herring. You couldn't get away with anything, mind. Old Man Hemmings, he ran the market, knew everyone’s business. And the dances at the City Hall! Remember those, Arthur? Your grandmother could waltz like a dream. Though you always stepped on her toes, if I recall correctly. A little white lie, Dorothy. She was a bit clumsy herself, let's be honest.

Right, who finished all the biscuit crumbs? Honestly, it looks like a tiny pirate crew had a raid on the biscuit tin.  I  did! I was Captain Bluebeard, and I needed energy for… for sailing! And fighting! And  I  was First Mate! Captain Bluebeard made me eat all the crumbs so I’d be strong enough to steer the ship! Oh, you two. A very important job, steering the ship and consuming all evidence, clearly. Although, a real pirate would have shared the plunder, wouldn't they? Maybe… but Captain Bluebeard was  very  hungry. Fair enough. Now, finish your vegetables, both of you, and  then  we can talk more about pirates. We need fuel for our own adventures this week - especially if we're going to tackle Shakespeare. Shakespeare? Is that like a pirate? Does he have a ship? Not exactly a pirate, darling. He wrote plays. Stories, with kings and queens and fairies and… well, sometimes pirates actually  appear  in Shakespeare! Remember when Mrs. Davies read us ‘The Tempest’ last year? Prospero used magic to create a storm… a bit like a pirate storm, perhaps? Oh! With Ariel? And the scary bits? That's the one. And this week is Shakespeare Week at school, so we’re going to try and learn a bit more. We’re even talking about going to Stratford-upon-Avon next weekend. Stratford? What’s there? Just Shakespeare? Not just! There's his house, and we can see a performance, maybe. And lots of lovely gardens. It'll be a bit of a day trip. Think of it as a quest, like going to find buried treasure… but instead of treasure, we find… words! Beautiful words. Will there be… sparkly things? Possibly! Sometimes they decorate the theatre with sparkly things. More sparkly things than a pirate's chest, maybe? Though pirates do love a good gem. I want to see the circus! Yes, the circus. Remember we booked that workshop? The one in the REAL circus tent? With the trapeze! And the clowns! That's the one. It's next Wednesday after school. It’s going to be amazing. They said we'll learn some basic circus skills – juggling, maybe some tightrope walking... Can I be a lion tamer? We'll see. Perhaps we can  pretend  you're a lion tamer. It’s just a workshop, not a real circus with actual lions! Can we take pictures?

…and honestly, the look on the harbourmaster’s face! Absolutely priceless. He kept repeating, “But  why  Cyprus, Madam?” As if it wasn’t obvious - sunshine, reasonably priced tavernas… and a complete escape from another damp English November. Good Lord, Margaret. Sailing from Jeddah to Cyprus? You always were a bit of a rogue, weren’t you? I vaguely remember you mentioning teaching out in Saudi. Was that before or after the…incident? Oh, before. Many years before. 1982, it was. Newly qualified, full of youthful bravado… and utterly naive, of course. Saudi was… an experience. Very hot, very conservative. The students were lovely, actually, desperately eager to learn English. Though explaining idioms was a nightmare. “Break a leg”? Utterly baffling. I can imagine. I did a short stint in Kuwait myself, back in the late 70s. Similar challenges. The cultural differences were… significant. Though, I found the coffee astonishing. Strong enough to stand a spoon in. Speaking of strong stuff, reminds me of a time in Morocco. Trying to get a gin and tonic was like applying for a visa. Everything’s mint tea, or something suspiciously sweet and fizzy. No subtlety. Saudi was dry, naturally. Completely. Which, for a while, wasn't too bad. I wasn’t a huge drinker then. But after a year… oh, you start to dream of a proper pint. We’d get little smuggled bottles in, whispered about like state secrets. The compound we lived on was ringed with security, but somehow, the stuff always got through. Risky business. Risky indeed. Still, a bit of rebellion is good for the soul. It’s what kept things interesting, I suppose. Though, sailing from Jeddah sounds a  lot  riskier than a clandestine gin and tonic. What exactly was the issue with the harbourmaster? Was it the boat? The route? You smuggling anything  in  this time? Oh, none of that! It was the paperwork, apparently. Or rather, the complete lack thereof. I’d chartered a little yacht – perfectly seaworthy, no problems there - and foolishly assumed a British sailing certificate would be enough. It wasn’t. They wanted… everything. Proof of ownership, insurance, detailed charts, a letter from the Saudi government… it was a bureaucratic nightmare. And I hadn’t anticipated needing any of it. They ended up detaining me for questioning. Effectively arrested. Good grief! Detained? For wanting to go sailing? This is getting better and better. How long were you held?

Honestly, Maureen, I’m starting to think this bathroom re-do is a complete folly. Fifty shades of beige just aren't inspiring me. Remember when we talked about that teal? Teal? Oh, love, you know David would have a fit. He's a man of… neutral tones. And frankly, after the kitchen debacle, I'm not arguing with him about colour schemes. Though, it  was  a bit much with the orange. It was  terracotta , Maureen. And it brightened the place up! But alright, alright, no teal. It’s just… everything feels a bit… blah. And now young Leo's locked himself in his room again. Honestly, what  is  going on with that boy? Teenage angst, Sheila. Plain and simple. He's eleven going on twenty-five. Probably agonizing over some girl at school. Or a video game. Or both. Remember when our Sarah used to slam doors and declare we ‘just didn’t  understand ’? Oh, I remember. Vaguely. It feels like a lifetime ago. Though, different, wasn’t it? Sarah’s rebellion was more… theatrical. Leo just withdraws. He barely said two words at dinner. And he used to love lamb. Lamb’s boring. And you were talking about me? Well, we were wondering why you’ve decided to become a hermit. And why perfectly good lamb is 'boring'. It's just… school. And Ben’s being a bit of a… well, he’s being Ben. Ben? That boy who’s always causing trouble? The one with the bright blue hair? Yeah. He's saying stuff. About… forgetting a homework assignment and blaming it on me. Everyone thinks I copied his work. Oh, Leo. That sounds awful. Have you told a teacher? No. It just makes it worse. They always take Ben’s side. He’s… good at talking. Right. Well, sometimes, you just have to rise above it, love. Let him have his moment. It won't last. Though, remember when I was working at the factory? Old Mr. Henderson used to spread rumours about me and Stan, saying we were… well, it wasn't pleasant. Best thing I did was ignore him. That’s good advice. Maybe you could talk to Mrs. Davies, Leo? She seems a fair teacher. We  are  thinking about a summer holiday, by the way. Nothing fancy, probably just Cornwall again. Cornwall’s okay. But it’s always Cornwall. Well, it’s easy, isn’t it?

Oh, this is lovely, isn’t it? Proper sunshine. Beats Bolton grey any day. Though I do miss a good chippy, mind you. You always miss a chippy, love. Even in Barbados you were moaning about needing a bit of mushy peas. It's a  need , not a moan! A fundamental human right, I reckon. Right, Leo? You understand the importance of a good chippy tea? Uh-huh. Yeah. Definitely. Is there Wi-Fi near that truffle place we’re going to? Leo, put the phone down and look at the view. We’re driving through  Istria . It’s gorgeous. And no, I doubt there’s a strong signal for much longer, we’re heading into more rural areas. This truffle hunting experience, apparently, is with a family who’ve been doing it for generations. Very authentic. It’s supposed to be amazing. Old Man Miro, they call him. Apparently, he can find truffles with his eyes closed. His dog, Bella, is the real star though. They say she’s a genius. A genius dog, eh? Sounds good. I'm worried it’ll all be a bit…fancy. You know me, I’m happy with a sausage sandwich. Truffles seem a bit poncey, don't they? They are a bit, aren’t they? But apparently, the Croatians use them in everything. Pasta, scrambled eggs…even ice cream, I read. Ice cream?! That sounds disgusting. Don’t knock it ‘til you’ve tried it, Leo. Though I agree, it’s an odd pairing. Remember that time your Auntie Maureen put black pudding in her trifle?  That  was a culinary disaster. Oh god, don’t remind me! I still have nightmares. It smelled like…well, black pudding in trifle. She was trying to be all experimental after watching Rick Stein. Rick Stein. Now there’s a chef. I met him once, at a conference in London. Perfectly pleasant man, a bit obsessed with fish, unsurprisingly. Very down-to-earth, considering. Speaking of chefs, have you seen that new show, ‘Kitchen Inferno’? It's awful, but I'm hooked. That Gordon Ramsay is such a shouty man! I swear he gets half his energy from yelling. It's pure drama. But it's good drama. I watched a bit when I was at Uni, just to unwind after all the essays. God, Uni feels like a lifetime ago. All those late nights and instant noodles… Uni?

…and honestly, the phonetics of it are  fascinating . People just don't realise how much shifts even within, like, a ten-mile radius. Old Aylesbury dialect is almost… gone, isn’t it? Drowned out by everything else. Mmhmm. It is, isn’t it? My Nan used to talk about Cambridge having a slightly different accent again, even just forty years ago. Something about the colleges influencing pronunciation. I never really paid attention, to be fair. Too busy trying to work out if I sounded posh enough for university. Posh enough? That’s the story of everyone here, isn’t it? Except me, I probably sounded too… normal. Everyone else had boarding school voices and stories about gap years in Patagonia. Oh, don’t sell yourself short, Leo. You’re brilliant at what you do. And you definitely don’t  sound  normal. I mean, ‘normal’ is a really loaded term anyway, linguistically speaking. It implies a standard, which… well, doesn't really exist. That’s what I’m researching, actually. The constructed idea of ‘received pronunciation’ and how it impacts perceptions of intelligence and trustworthiness. Right, your job, yeah? You mentioned it briefly at the Christmas do. Language Research Coordinator. Sounds… intense. I just push ads onto the internet. Much less philosophical. Although, having to write ad copy that resonates with different demographics  is  a bit of a linguistic puzzle sometimes. It's trickier than people think. You wouldn’t believe how much A/B testing goes into a single sentence. Like, “Discover our amazing new product!” versus “Unleash the power of…” and the difference it makes to click-through rates. It’s bonkers. See! It’s all language. Even marketing. It's manipulation, essentially, and relies on deeply ingrained assumptions about how words  should  be used. It’s all about power, really. Who gets to define 'correct' language? Who’s listened to, and who isn't? That’s… a bit bleak when you put it like that. I usually just think of it as trying to get people to buy things. Well, yes, that's the end goal! But the  how  is what I'm interested in. I've been looking at regional accents in job interviews, particularly. The bias is insane. So many studies show candidates with ‘non-standard’ accents are perceived as less competent, even when their qualifications are identical. I can imagine. I had one interview where the guy kept asking me to repeat myself, even though I wasn’t mumbling.

Oh, this is lovely, isn’t it? Just…seeing the Polish countryside drift by. It’s so much greener than I expected. Though, admittedly, everything looks greener after the M25. You’re telling me! I think I aged about ten years just  thinking  about the M25 this morning. This is massively better. Though, honestly, navigating these little lanes is a bit stressful. Thanks for being the driver, Auntie Val. My nerves wouldn’t cope. Nonsense, darling. I enjoy driving. Keeps the mind active, you know? Besides, you’ve been prepping lessons for that online class all morning. You’ve earned a passenger seat. How are those students doing, by the way? Still mostly Japanese, are they? Mostly, yeah. A couple of Brazilians joined last week, which is good. They’re really enthusiastic, but their pronunciation… it’s a challenge. I’m trying to get them to focus on the th- sounds. It’s just…not a thing in Portuguese, apparently. Oh, dear. Sounds familiar. I had a Spanish student years ago who couldn’t grasp the difference between ‘sheep’ and ‘ship’ to save his life. He kept ordering boats of wool. It was hilarious, looking back. Oh, bless him! Honestly, sometimes I feel like a linguist, a psychologist, and a comedian all rolled into one. It's exhausting but rewarding. Are we nearly there yet? Google Maps is being…optimistic. Optimistic is a kind word. It rather assumes these roads haven’t been the same since the Middle Ages. I’d say another twenty minutes, maybe? Kasia sent a really detailed set of directions, but I’m not sure even she truly understands the Polish road system. She’s been laughing about it on Facebook. Apparently, her husband, Marek, refuses to navigate. Says it’s a matter of national pride. Oh, that’s so Kasia. Always with the drama. I'm looking forward to seeing them both. It's been too long. And honestly, it’s good to  be  somewhere. This whole campervan thing is fun, but I miss having a proper shower. I wholeheartedly agree on the shower front. Although, this campervan is remarkably comfortable, isn’t it? A bit compact, perhaps, but perfectly serviceable. I'm still amazed your cousin, Leo, managed to find such a gem. He's surprisingly resourceful. Apparently, he restores them as a hobby. It's a bit unusual, considering he's a dentist. Do you think Kasia will have made her pierogi?

…and then he just  flopped . Honestly, it was embarrassing. Like a beached whale. Did you catch that bit, even with the sound off? Roughly. I could tell by the dramatic flailing. Is it still 0-0? I haven’t really been paying attention. This paper on the commodification of leisure is… absorbing, to say the least. Fitting, considering what we were  just  talking about. 0-0. Predictably boring. I swear, some of these games feel… manufactured. Like they  want  a goalless draw for the viewing figures. More talking heads, more analysis. Cynical, much? Though you're not entirely wrong. And speaking of manufactured… did you see Man U’s new kit? It’s just… stripes.  More  stripes. They’ve gone back to basics, apparently. Stripes are classic! But yeah, it  is  a bit unimaginative, innit? Like they ran out of ideas after ten minutes. Remember when Newcastle had that grey and black one? Proper controversial. My dad nearly had a fit. Said it wasn't ‘proper black and white.’ Oh god, the grey one. That ignited a national debate. My mate Dave was vehemently against it. Said it looked like they were mourning. It's all about branding, though, isn’t it? They’ll sell buckets of the things regardless. Especially to tourists. Exactly. Speaking of branding, I saw an ad for the sponsorship deal with… Hold on, was it Visit Rwanda on Arsenal’s shirts? Honestly! It feels a bit…icky. It  is  icky. ‘Sportswashing’ plain and simple. Trying to polish a slightly tarnished image with millions in football funding. It's a textbook case for my research, actually. The ethical implications are fascinating - and deeply worrying. It just feels…wrong. Like enjoying a nice meal knowing it was made with questionable practices. Though, I suppose that applies to a lot of things, doesn't it? Like… McDonalds. I feel guilty every time I go, but then a McFlurry just  calls  to me. The siren song of the McFlurry. A powerful force. That’s a perfect example of brand loyalty overriding ethical concerns – cheap, convenient, nostalgic. They’ve built an empire on reliable pleasure. And aggressive marketing. Reliable pleasure is a good way to put it. My mam used to take me for Happy Meals after swimming lessons when I was little. It’s totally ingrained now. Do you think football sponsorships  actually  make people think differently about these companies?

Honestly, it’s just… draining, isn't it? Another day, another saga with the Job Centre. They’ve sent me a referral for a ‘digital marketing assistant’ role. Digital marketing! Me? I can barely work the smart TV without Dad explaining it. Tell me about it. Everything's a referral. They think chucking a load of links at you is actually  helping . Last one was for a forklift driver. A forklift driver, Ana! You know I haven’t driven anything bigger than your Fiesta. See? It’s just… pointless. And the woman on the phone was all chirpy, like it's a privilege to be considered for a job I’m utterly unqualified for. Did you manage to sort out that eBay order, by the way? The one with the… what was it, a miniature Dalek? Oh, yeah. Finally. Seller messaged apologising, apparently their kid 'accidentally disassembled' it. Honestly, the state of some people. Offered me a tenner off. Like a tenner makes up for little Leo being heartbroken he didn't get his Doctor Who villain. Leo will be alright. He’s already planning on building his own out of Lego, isn’t he? They grow up so fast. It feels like yesterday he was obsessed with Thomas the Tank Engine. Remember that day trip to the Bluebell Railway? Total chaos. Chaos is an understatement. Nearly lost him in the steam engine shed. Thought I’d had a heart attack. Little terror. But yeah, good times. Speaking of day trips, I was thinking, if I ever…you know,  get  anything sorted…maybe we could take the kids to Margate? It’s not far. That sounds lovely. Actually, really lovely. We should definitely look into that. But focus on getting things sorted first. Have you actually told Mum and Dad how bad things are with the JSA? They keep asking how the “job hunting” is going. No. Not really. I just… I don’t want to worry them. Especially Dad. He’s already got enough on his plate with the gas bill going through the roof. It’s ridiculous, isn't it? How much everything costs now? Electric's the same. I practically live in the dark to save money. It  is  ridiculous. And don't worry about Dad, he'll find out eventually. He always does. Remember Uncle Derek getting that inheritance? And just…blowing it on a caravan? Mum was fuming.

Honestly, Mum, the traffic getting here this morning was  atrocious . Sat nav kept trying to reroute me through those tiny village lanes. Absolutely not! I stuck to the A47, even if it meant crawling. Crawling’s a good word for it, dear. Used to be you could fly down that road. Now it’s just…stop, start, stop, start. All these people moving  to  Peterborough. Never used to be like this. It’s alright on a bike, missus. Gets you where you need to be, and you don't 'ave to worry about parking. Though I wouldn’t cycle on the A47, not in this weather. A bike! You’re braver than me, Doreen. It’s just…everything seems so congested. And the roadworks! They’re always doing roadworks. I swear they just invent them to keep people busy. They just don't  plan  things properly, do they? It's all reactive. Remember when they built that bypass? Took them ten years, and it disrupted everything. Speaking of disruptions, did you ‘ear about that plane crash in the news? Awful. Makes you think, don’t it? Flying in a metal tube, miles up... Don't, Doreen. I’m already stressed enough about the traffic. Planes are the only way I’m visiting Aunt Carol in Florida next year, though. She's insisting. She says the orange juice is to die for. Carol always did ‘ave a sweet tooth. Remember that Christmas she made that trifle with  three  different types of sherry? Old Man Hemmings nearly passed out. Oh, goodness, yes! And then blamed it on the mince pies! Speaking of food, I’m thinking of doing a roast this Sunday. Would you two like to come? I was thinking chicken, maybe? That’d be lovely, missus. Thank you. I could bring a pudding maybe? I made a nice apple crumble last week. Chicken’s nice. Though last time you did a roast, Sarah, you nearly set the smoke alarm off. Remember that? Burnt the Yorkshire puddings to a crisp. It was one Yorkshire pudding! And it was a very enthusiastic oven. I’ve learned to lower the temperature since then. Honestly, Mum. I'm just saying, missus, you’ve been a bit busy at work lately, haven't you? Always on the phone. Is everything alright? Work’s…work. It’s a new client, quite demanding. They’re a big logistics company, want everything yesterday.

Honestly, I think Mrs. Davies is actively trying to fail us all. Dramatic much? What’s she done  now ? Is it the poetry analysis again? Because I swear, she looks for symbolism where there absolutely isn't any. Like, a blue curtain is just a blue curtain, Mrs. Davies! It doesn't represent the sadness of the protagonist's childhood! Worse. Way worse. It’s the practice tests for the GCSEs. She’s giving us ones from… 2008. 2008, ANON! They ask about things that aren't even  on  the syllabus anymore. And the questions are phrased like they’re trying to trick you. No way! Seriously? That’s… actually a bit dodgy, isn’t it? Old tests are fine for practice, but not if they’re completely irrelevant. Has anyone said anything? Loads of people. Leo actually tried to politely point out that the structure of the questions was different now, and she just told him he wasn’t “applying himself rigorously enough.” Rigorously! Who even  says  that? It’s like she’s auditioning for a Victorian novel. Oh, Mrs. Davies. She  is  a bit… unique. Remember when she brought in a stuffed raven for the Edgar Allan Poe lesson? Said it helped “channel the atmosphere.” How could I forget? It was shedding feathers all over everyone's work! And then Mr. Harrison, the trainee teacher, spent ten minutes trying to vacuum them up, looking mortified. Poor Mr. Harrison. He's trying so hard, isn’t he? He’s a bit flustered, but he seems genuinely nice. Way nicer than Miss Peterson, who just sighs at everything we say. He's alright. He asked me for help with the lab setup yesterday, and it was actually…pleasant. He didn't assume I was completely useless, like some of the other teachers do. Though, I did nearly cause a small explosion with the bunsen burner. You  what ?! It was a tiny explosion! Just a little whoosh of flame. I sorted it. But yeah. He didn’t yell, just calmly showed me how to adjust the air vent. He's definitely his brother's keeper - Mr. Reynolds is head of science, right? Makes sense he'd be good at it. Yeah, that's right. They're both super clever, but Mr. Reynolds is…intense. He’s always going on about quantum physics and the universe. It goes right over my head. Speaking of clever, have you seen Freya’s art project?

So, you’re  sure  about the nuns, Mum? Like, really sure they… chose that life? It just seems a bit… extreme, doesn’t it? Giving up  everything ? Extreme to  us , maybe, Leo. But for some people, it’s what feels right. It’s about dedicating yourself to something bigger than yourself. It’s faith, love… a calling. It’s not about  giving up  everything, it's about exchanging one set of things for another. Think of it like… giving up playing Fortnite to focus on your schoolwork. It’s a sacrifice, but one you make for something you value more. Fortnite’s nothing like becoming a nun! That's just a game. They, like, can’t get married or have kids or… go to the cinema! Cinema! Dino-saur! Roar! Yes, darling, dinosaurs are very exciting. And Leo, you’re right, it's a massive commitment. But they believe they are serving God, and finding fulfilment in that. It's not for everyone, obviously. But what if they  change  their mind? Is there, like, a nun return policy? A…nun return policy? Honestly, Leo, sometimes you ask the most outlandish questions. It’s not exactly like returning a faulty toaster. It's a very difficult process if someone feels they made the wrong decision, but it can happen. They can leave the order, but it’s a huge thing, with a lot of support needed. It just makes me think of… you know, that documentary Mr. Harrison showed us in RE? The one about Scientology? That was  weird . Everyone looked so… happy, but in a really creepy way. Like robots. Scientology  is  very different. That's a controversial one. It's not a traditional religion at all, it’s more… a business disguised as a religion, in my opinion. They charge a lot of money and there have been accusations of manipulative practices. I wouldn’t compare nuns to that at all. The nuns at St. Mary’s, where your Grandma volunteered, were genuinely kind, dedicated women. But isn’t it all the same thing? Just… believing in something you can't  prove ? Like, what if it's all just… the Matrix? What if we’re all living in a computer simulation, and the nun’s ‘God’ is just the programmer? Oh, Leo, here we go. The Matrix. You’ve been watching too many films. That’s philosophical speculation, darling. It’s interesting to ponder, but it doesn’t invalidate people’s genuine beliefs.

Right, I’m properly knackered after that. Honestly, three hours of quickstep is… a lot. My feet are screaming. Told you. You underestimated the quickstep. It's deceptively tiring. You were flying though, honestly. Much better than last week. Are you actually enjoying it though? You looked a bit…grim at times. Enjoying it? It’s…challenging. And embarrassing. Old Mr. Henderson kept giving me that look like I was ruining the lineage of ballroom dancing. Honestly, the man takes it  very  seriously. It's less about fun and more about precision, apparently. He sounds lovely. Seriously though, are you going to stick with it? We did book a block of ten lessons. I think so. Mam's already talking about us doing a proper foxtrot at Christmas. She’s envisioning the whole thing, twinkling lights, a string quartet... Honestly, the pressure. Speaking of Christmas, have you even  thought  about holidays this year? I was looking at maybe a week in the Lake District? Bit closer to home, saves a fortune on flights… The Lakes sound nice. Quite sensible, actually. I was idly browsing Croatia, purely because of the  Game of Thrones  filming locations. Don’t judge me. It's a terrible idea logistically, and probably expensive, but…King’s Landing! Oh, you and your  Game of Thrones . It's a bit much, isn't it? Still, Croatia  is  beautiful. Though I'd rather not spend all my time searching for where they filmed something. What about something a bit…different? I was reading about some of the old Anglo-Saxon sites, Lindisfarne, Jarrow…proper history stuff. Anglo-Saxon? Bit niche, even for you. You’ve been doing a lot of reading for your work, haven't you? All that corpus linguistics must be making your brain go all historical. It does bring up odd things, actually. I was looking at some Old English texts, trying to tag verb conjugations, and it's  wild . Like, completely unrecognisable. It makes modern English look like a simplified toddler version. It's fascinating but my brain hurts. Sounds…intense. My brain's been fried by structural analysis all week. Trying to model the stress distribution on this new bridge design. It’s less poetic, admittedly. Are you still watching that awful reality TV show?  Glamour & Grit  or whatever it’s called? Don't you  dare  mock  Glamour & Grit ! It’s a guilty pleasure. It's so wonderfully, spectacularly awful.

Oh, this is lovely, isn’t it? Proper sunshine. Beats Bolton grey any day. Though I do miss a good brew, mind you. You always miss your tea, love. Even in Barbados you were craving a cuppa. And honestly, relax, we've only been driving for an hour. We'll be at that olive oil farm before you know it. Can we stop for ice cream soon? I saw a thing online about this place near Pula that does, like, massive sundaes. Pula can wait, young man. We’ve got a schedule, remember? Olive oil, then wine tasting, then finding somewhere decent to eat in Rovinj. It’s all planned. Efficiency, that’s the key. Oh, let the lad have an ice cream, Dave. You’re always so…structured. We’re on holiday! It’s about spontaneity, yeah? Besides, I fancy a gelato myself. That little market in Grožnjan looked like it had some good stuff. She’s right, Dave. Live a little. You’d think you were still managing that merger back in London. Honestly, you were buzzing about “synergies” even  before  we left the driveway. I just like things to run smoothly. Especially when coordinating four people and a frankly terrifying rental car on Croatian roads. Have you  seen  how people drive here? It's a bit like Sons of Anarchy out there sometimes. Sons of Anarchy?! You watch that? I thought you only watched documentaries about train spotting. I have eclectic tastes, thank you very much. It’s…research. Understanding different organisational structures. Oh, aye, and Jax Teller’s a master of workflow optimisation, is he? You’re unbelievable. Speaking of unbelievable, did you see that pottery in Motovun? The colours! I was thinking maybe a little vase for Mum… That’s a nice thought, love. Everything in Motovun was gorgeous, though expensive. Reminded me of that arts festival we went to near Kendal a few years back. Remember that chap who made the sculptures out of driftwood? Oh, aye! Proper artistic. This is different though. More…Mediterranean. All those blues and yellows. It makes you want to paint. I've not touched a brush since uni, mind you. Mum, can we go to a water park? They have loads near Poreč, apparently. With slides and everything. We discussed this. Water parks are not on the itinerary. We are here to experience  culture , understand? Istrian history, local culinary delights…

…and then, honestly, Liam  insisted  on bringing his keyboard to the pub quiz. A keyboard! Said he needed it for the music round. It was just embarrassing, like. Everyone was lookin’ at ‘im, proper weird. Oh,  god , Liam. That sounds… classic Liam. He's always been a bit extra, hasn’t he? It’s endearing, in a deeply frustrating way. Did you at least win? He didn’t even  use  the keyboard. Just carried it around like a precious baby. And no, we lost. The Red Lion beat us again. Old Man Hemmings knows  everything  about 80s power ballads. Seriously? Liam and the keyboard? I'm picturing it and I can't stop smiling. Makes a change from revising, that’s for sure. I’m so stressed about these upcoming exams. I feel like I’m drowning in information. Tell me about it. I’m supposed to be writing an essay on Victorian literature, but my brain feels like mush. Honestly, I’d rather be listenin’ to Liam’s keyboard escapades. Still, easier than that, innit? Speaking of… easier… I was chatting to Chloe yesterday. She was telling me about this… game. Apparently, it's getting quite popular. It's all about truth or dare, but… with a twist. Oh, don't tell me it's one of those "spicy" ones going around on TikTok. I saw a few of them, honestly terrifying. Well, she said it's… customizable. You set the boundaries beforehand. It was her boyfriend who mentioned it, actually. He’s really into… well, he’s a bit of a tech whiz. He was showing her how you can even… record the dares. Record the dares? What for? Showin’ off to his mates? Sounds a bit… much. Maybe it’s for accountability? Like, proof you actually did the dare? Or… … something else? That's what I thought! Chloe said it gets a bit… adventurous. Apparently, some people are using it for, like, really personal challenges. She didn't go into specifics, thankfully. She just mentioned someone got dared to… well, it involved something rather  intimate . You mean… like…? Oh,  no . Please no. I’m officially scared of the internet. Cor, that’s a bit grim, that. Sounds like someone’s askin’ for trouble. I mean, recording somethin’ like that… that’s just not right. Restricts your choices, doesn’t it? And puts a load of pressure on.

Right, I’m tellin’ ya, there's nae substitute for a proper bacon butty. None. Especially after a mornin' wrestling with Windows updates and folks who think "the cloud" is a fluffy white thing in the sky. You and your bacon butties, Dave. It’s a daily obsession. I had a perfectly good avocado toast this morning, thank you very much. Healthy  and  satisfying. Avocado toast? Sounds a bit… fancy for a Tuesday, doesn’t it, Chloe? I just had a bowl of porridge. Quick and easy. Gets the job done. Porridge?! Good lad, Mark. Sensible. Keeps ya goin'. But it's nae a  treat , is it? A bacon butty is a treat. Proper crispy bacon, brown sauce... maybe even a bit of black pudding if you're feelin’ wild. Oh, here we go. The black pudding debate. Last time you mentioned black pudding, Dave, you nearly started a fight in the staff room. Old Mr. Henderson nearly had a coronary. He just doesn’t understand the finer things in life, that man. Honestly. Thinks it’s made of…I dunno…evil. I said to him, “It’s just blood and oats, Albert!” He went pale. You’re terrible, Dave. Though, I have to admit, a good full English  is  hard to beat. My grandma used to make the best. Proper sausages, like, the kind that actually tasted of pork, not just… filler. See, Dave? Mark gets it! It's all about quality ingredients. That's what makes the difference. I tried to get a decent breakfast roll in town last week and it was… tragic. Soggy bread, anaemic bacon, and a single, lonely sausage. Tragic is right. It’s a criminal offence, that is. A proper breakfast roll needs structure! You need a good, sturdy cob. Granary, if you’re feelin' fancy. And the bacon has to be stacked… strategically. You can’t have it all floppin’ about. Strategic bacon stacking. Now  that  should be a training module. "Advanced Breakfast Roll Construction." I’d actually sign up for that. Honestly, it's a skill. I was in Berlin last month, and they don't  do  breakfast. At least, not like we do. It’s all meats, cheeses, and bread rolls. Fine, but where’s the fried egg? Where's the baked beans? Baked beans are essential! They’re the glue that holds it all together. And you need tomato, too.

…and honestly, I still don’t get TikTok. My daughter, bless her, tries to explain it. "Dad, it’s just short form video," she says. Short form of  what , I ask? Short form of wasting time, apparently. Tell me about it. My nephew is completely hooked. He's started trying to do those dances. It’s… a sight. Though, you have to admit, some of the book recommendations on BookTok are actually decent. I’ve added a couple to my ‘to read’ pile. BookTok, eh? Is that the one where people film themselves crying over books? I saw a news report about it. Seems… intense. Though I suppose anything is better than the doomscrolling I see everyone getting up to on X. Honestly, that platform is just a shouting match these days. Intense is one word for it. My daughter showed me one where a girl was absolutely  devastated  because the love interest died. Like, full-on sobbing. I just… offered her a biscuit. Seems a sensible response to me. But X… you're right. It's just… draining. I used to find it useful for keeping up with industry news, library stuff, but now it’s all politics and outrage. I deactivated my X account last year. Best decision I ever made. It became an echo chamber of negativity. I've switched to following library-related hashtags on Instagram mostly. It's a bit more visual, and generally a more positive vibe. And you see lovely photos of library cats, which is always a win. Oh, library cats! Excellent. We had a resident cat at the university library back in Wellington. Old Man Fitzwilliam, we called him. He’d wander the stacks, judging everyone’s reading choices, I swear. He was a menace, but everyone adored him. We put his picture on all the library policies. "Fitzwilliam’s Rules of Silence," that sort of thing. That’s brilliant! We had a… well, we  have  a resident mouse. Doesn’t quite have the same gravitas, does it? He’s more of a stealth operative. Rarely seen, often suspected. A mouse?! Oh dear. We have a strict ‘no pets’ policy. Although, I'm fairly certain Brenda in acquisitions sneakily brings in her chihuahua, Princess Fluffybutt the Third. She says it’s for emotional support. Princess Fluffybutt the Third? Oh, that  is  good! You librarians are a colourful bunch. Back home, we had a student who tried to claim their emotional support animal was a… a saltwater crocodile.

…and honestly, Richard, the sheer volume of responses from the consultation is a bit overwhelming. I’ve barely scratched the surface of the detailed feedback forms. People  clearly  have strong opinions about where this new hospice should be. Yes, well, a good consultation  should  elicit strong opinions, shouldn't it, Eleanor? It means people feel invested. But overwhelming is…unhelpful. Have you had your team start collating the key themes? We need to distill it down to something manageable for the Business Case. We are, we are. But it's not just  where , Richard. It’s  what kind  of hospice. There’s a definite split emerging between those who want a very traditional, almost domestic feel, and those pushing for something more modern, integrated with technology. And the debate about in-patient beds versus increased day care provision is…robust. Robust is a polite way of putting it, I imagine. Look, the Business Case, as you know, is going to hinge on demonstrating value for money. And demonstrating that we've genuinely listened. The location is pivotal, obviously, but we can't get bogged down in pleasing everyone. Tunbridge Wells, frankly, makes the most sense geographically. Access to the A21, relatively central within the Kent and East Sussex catchment... Geographically, yes. But the Rotherham model – your previous hospice there – benefitted from being on a major bus route, easily accessible for families without cars. Tunbridge Wells… isn’t quite the same. We've had several comments about the reliance on private transport, particularly for those visiting frequently. Point taken, Eleanor. But land prices in those areas are astronomical. And honestly, trying to navigate the planning permissions for a larger site on a busy road… it’s a nightmare. We secured a good deal on the land just outside the town centre. It’s near the Pembury Hospital, which gives us potential synergies with their palliative care services. That’s a strong selling point for the commissioners. Synergies are good, but ensuring truly integrated care is more complex than simply being geographically close. Are we confident Pembury are genuinely on board with a collaborative approach? I’ve had…mixed experiences with hospital-hospice relationships in the past. Too often it's a one-way street. I’ve had a preliminary meeting with Dr. Sharma, the Head of Palliative Medicine. He’s enthusiastic. He recognises the gaps in their current provision, particularly regarding psychological support for families.

Oh, look at this one! Remember Sarah’s hen do? Absolute chaos. She nearly fell in the harbour trying to take a selfie with that seagull. Good Lord, I'd forgotten about that. Sarah always was a bit of a daredevil. She’s still got that spark, hasn’t she? Did you hear she’s trying to convince Mark to go to Royal Ascot this year? Ascot? Really? That’s… a choice. She’s never been one for hats and formality. Though, knowing Sarah, she’ll probably find a way to make it incredibly entertaining. I saw a post she tagged you in, Mum, about matching fascinators. Don’t even. She sent me about six links to, and I quote, “absolutely divine” creations. One involved feathers and a miniature replica of the Eiffel Tower. Honestly, the woman. I told her I'd rather wrestle a badger. You tell her. She needs someone to keep her grounded. Speaking of grounded, how’s the new agency treating you, love? Still churning out brilliant copy? It's alright, actually. They’re… busy. Really busy. Lots of briefs, very quick turnarounds. It’s good experience, I suppose. I’m learning a lot about SEO and content strategy. I’ve got an interview next week for a slightly more senior role, though. At a smaller agency, a bit more focused on ethical branding. Oh, that sounds wonderful, dear! Ethical branding is important. What’s the interview like? Is it a panel or just one-on-one? It’s a panel, apparently. Which is terrifying. They said they’ll be asking about my experience with developing brand voices, and my approach to measuring campaign success. Basically, all the things I’ve been furiously Googling for the last three days. You’ll ace it. You’re a naturally gifted writer. Remember that poem you wrote for your grandmother’s 80th? Brought a tear to everyone’s eye. You’ve got a knack for capturing emotion. Absolutely. Just remember to breathe, darling. And don’t be afraid to ask them questions. Shows initiative. What are you wearing? Have you got something suitable? That’s the next crisis. Everything I own seems either too casual or too… trying too hard . I was thinking navy trousers and a cream blouse, maybe? Do you think that’s safe? Safe is good. Smart and professional. You don’t want to be remembered for a daring fashion choice, do you?

Right, honestly, I still can't believe you made me watch that.  The Autopsy of Jane Doe . Proper messed with my head, that did. Oh, come on, it wasn't  that  bad! It was atmospheric. And the mystery was really well done. You just don't like anything remotely unsettling, do you? Unsettling? Elsie, it was terrifying! That final scene with the… the thing in her chest. I had to hide my face for a good ten minutes. Honestly, I thought I felt a draft when they opened her up, and there wasn’t even a window open! Dramatic much? It’s a  film , Liv. Special effects and clever sound design. It's not real. Though, I admit, the practical effects were genuinely creepy. Much better than all that CGI rubbish you get these days. Remember that film,  The Descent ? Now  that  was proper scary. Oh, don’t even  start  on  The Descent . Claustrophobia is my biggest fear, thank you very much. Those caves…and the creatures... Nah. Absolutely not. That’s the one I actually had nightmares about for a week. I kept dreaming I was trapped. It was awful. See? You  do  appreciate a good scare! You just deny it. What about  Hereditary ? Did you find that one disturbing? Disturbing is an understatement. That one wasn't even jump scares, it was just… pervasive dread. Like something awful was lurking just beneath the surface the entire time. And Toni Collette's performance? Incredible, but terrifying. The miniatures… ugh. That was seriously unsettling. Though, to be fair, I think anything involving demonic possession messes with me. It's just… too close to things I don’t want to think about. You and your anxieties. But that's why it's  good ! It preys on those things. It taps into the primal stuff. It’s like…catharsis, almost? Facing your fears… in a safe environment. Catharsis? I'd describe it more as a week of checking under the bed and refusing to turn the lights off. Though, I will admit, after watching something truly terrifying, normal life feels… quite pleasant, you know? Like facing a spider and then just being glad it's gone. Exactly! It gives you perspective. So, are we doing another one then? I was thinking maybe  It Follows ?  It Follows ?! Elsie, no. Absolutely not. That one’s just…wrong. The concept is genuinely disturbing. That slow walk… the inevitability… it’s just relentlessly bleak.

Right, Dad, nearly bedtime for me too. Just wanted to quickly chat before I head off. How was your day? Did you manage to get out to the garden at all? Garden was… ambitious. The weeds are winning, Penelope, winning I tell you. Spent most of the afternoon trying to decipher how to reply to Margaret’s email about the family reunion. Honestly, these computers… Oh, emails. I know the feeling. I had a whole class of Year 5s trying to send me pictures of their pets today. Chaos. Is Margaret still trying to organise it for August? That's the plan. She’s suggesting we rent a big house somewhere. An Airbnb, she called it. Says it'll be cheaper than a hotel. I don’t know, Penelope. Sounds awfully… modern. And what if something goes wrong? Who do you complain to? A  website ? It's not as scary as it sounds, Dad. It's essentially someone renting out their home. There are reviews, pictures, everything. And Airbnb themselves have customer service if something isn't right. I've used them a few times, actually. Remember when I went to Italy last year? Stayed in a lovely little apartment in Florence through Airbnb. Italy… Yes, yes, you did. Lovely photos. But still. A stranger’s house. It all seems a bit risky. Back in my day, you booked a hotel, spoke to a person, and that was that. Reliable. Times change, eh? Speaking of bookings… I was thinking of getting a new iPad. This one’s getting a bit slow. Mostly for school stuff, marking, lesson planning… But also for video calls with Leo. He’s been loving FaceTiming. An iPad, is it? What's wrong with a good book? I finished that biography of Churchill you lent me. Absolutely fascinating. Though, I had to get young Thomas to show me how to… enlarge the print on my Kindle. My eyes aren't what they used to be. I know, Dad! I keep trying to get you to have your eyes tested. But Leo loves seeing my face, and it’s just easier sometimes. Honestly, ordering one online is so simple. You just…click a button. Though, I did spend about an hour looking at different pizza places last night. I was craving a proper pepperoni one. Pizza, eh? Reminds me of your mother. She used to make the most divine pizzas.

Aye, it’s grand tae be oot here, isn’t it? Brucefield’s a wee bit o’ paradise. Beats the city any day, even Edinburgh with all its… bustle. Though, I did manage tae snag a first edition o’ MacDiarmid’s ‘First Hymn to Lenin’ while I was in town last week. A real find. You and your books, Alistair. Always on the hunt. Lenin, eh? Bit of a shift from your usual travel writing obsession. Though I suppose both involve a certain… exploration. This farm is bliss though, isn't it? Reminds me of summers as a bairn at my Gran’s. No wifi, just fields and the smell of hay. Exploration in different forms, aye. MacDiarmid’s exploration of ideology, my own o' landscapes. They're not sae different, really. Both trying tae understand the world, just through different lenses. And it  was  a steal. The bookshop owner didn’t even realise what he had. Said it was just “some auld poetry”. Honestly! They rarely do. That’s half the fun, isn’t it? Unearthing a bit o’ cultural history. Speaking o’ unearthing, have you given any more thought to that trip tae Georgia? We were talking about it a few weeks back. I’ve been reading about the Svaneti region… those medieval towers… it’s extraordinary. Och, Georgia… It’s still high on the list. I've been poring over some travelogues – Patrick Fermor’s ‘Between the Woods and the Water’ has just rekindled the wanderlust. The way he describes the Balkans… it’s almost poetic. Though, the political situation there’s a wee bit worrisome, isn't it? It is. Always a consideration, unfortunately. But Svaneti is fairly remote. The Georgians are fantastically hospitable folk, and the mountains…they’ve protected them, culturally and physically, for centuries. I read an account from a botanist who spent a year cataloguing the wildflowers up there. Apparently, species you won’t find anywhere else. That sounds… incredible. I’ve been trying to reconcile adventure with responsible tourism, y’know? I hate the idea o’ just being a passing face, contributing tae the disruption of local lives. I was reading Bill Bryson's ‘In a Smaller World,’ and it really hit home how much impact we have, even unintentionally. It’s a valid point. And Bryson's a good voice on it. I think the key is to slow down. Really engage with the place, the people.

Honestly, Mum, this job description is…intense. “Lead Architect on a mixed-use development, requiring extensive experience in sustainable design and BIM Level 2 proficiency.” It feels like they want a miracle worker, not a…well, not someone who’s only been qualified for a year. Oh, don’t be so hard on yourself, darling. A year is plenty. You were top of your class at uni, weren’t you? And that internship at Foster + Partners… that’s got to count for something. It’s a competitive field, of course, but you're a bright girl, Elara. I  was  top of my class, yes. But internships are different. This is leading a team, making huge decisions… It's a completely different ballpark. And everyone applying for these roles will have five, ten years' experience. I feel a bit like I'm sending my CV into a black hole. Well, you won’t know until you try, will you? And honestly, even  applying  is good practice. Polishing up your statements, thinking about how to present your skills… it’s all useful. What specifically is worrying you? Is it the BIM Level 2 part? That’s part of it. I used it during my master’s, obviously, but it wasn't… central. It wasn’t like, ‘If you don't know this inside out, don't bother applying’. This feels like that. They want someone who  lives and breathes  it. Right. Well, could you maybe… highlight the parts of your master’s projects where you demonstrably used it effectively? Focus on the outcomes, not just the fact you  used  the software. Think about how it helped the design, improve efficiency, whatever. Sell yourself, love. That's what I always told your father when he was interviewing. He was terrible at selling himself! You always say that. He was a brilliant history teacher. He didn't  need  to sell himself. People knew he was good. Being an architect is… different. It’s all about presenting a vision, convincing clients, competing. True enough. It's a world away from a classroom. Still, the principle remains. Focus on your strengths. And don't downplay anything. Remember that sustainable design project? The one with the community garden roof? That was brilliant. Yes, but… it was a theoretical project. It never actually  happened . It feels a bit pointless to put on my application. “Designed a revolutionary green roof that exists only in CAD drawings.”

…and then young Thomas, bless ‘im, tried to tell me that a roundabout isn’t technically a circle. Said somethin’ about the mathematics of curves. Honestly, you’d think he was buildin’ the bloody thing himself, not drivin’ round it! Thomas and his learnin’. Always was a clever one, that lad. Bit too much bookin’ and not enough common sense if you ask me. Still, better than bein’ glued to that phone all day like some of ‘em. Oh, don't start on phones, George. My granddaughter, Lily, she practically  lives  on hers. Says it's how she keeps in touch with all her friends. Keeps  me  in touch with her, thankfully, but… it’s a different world. Different it is, Brenda. Different it is. Remember when keepin’ in touch meant a proper letter? And waitin’ a week for a reply? You appreciated it more then, I reckon. Aye, you did. And you  knew  who was writin’ it. None of this anonymous online nonsense. Though, I must say, that Facebook thing helps me see what Maureen’s up to. She’s always postin’ pictures of that new dog. Little fluffball. Maureen’s enjoying retirement, then? Good for her. She worked hard enough all those years at the bakery. She does. Though, she keeps complainin’ about the price of dog food. Everything’s goin’ up, innit? It's scandalous. I was lookin' at the gas bill this morning...utterly ridiculous. This government… Don't get me started on the government, Arthur. They promise you the world and deliver… well, not much at all. Always fiddlin' with things, are they. Remember when they were talkin’ about buildin' more houses? That was ages ago, George! And look around. Still not enough, are there? Especially not affordable ones. Young people haven’t a hope of gettin’ on the ladder these days. It’s a crime, it is. My grandson, David...he and his wife, they’re savin’ like mad, but it’s just never enough. And the houses they  are  buildin'… all tiny boxes, crammed together. No garden, no space. Not like the houses we grew up in. You’re right about that. We had a proper garden in Costessey, back then. Enough room for a vegetable patch, a swing, everything. I used to spend all my summers out there. Used to have an old Austin… a proper motor, that was. Never broke down, touch wood.

Right, so the youth club wants the entire back hall for Tuesdays now, not just half. It's… a good problem to have, I suppose, demonstrating demand, but it really throws a spanner in the works regarding the pottery classes Mrs. Patel was hoping to run. Tuesdays, eh? That's a bummer for Mrs. Patel. She's been building up a good following with those classes. Did you explain the situation to the youth club folks? Maybe they could shift to Wednesdays? I did, love. Absolutely. But it’s peak time for them, apparently. They say getting the kids from school is easier then. They’re very insistent. And honestly, the youth club brings in a decent chunk of consistent income, which, as we both know, is…precious. You’re right about that. Every pound counts.
