Speaking of circling back…I was looking at those photos on your phone again, the ones of you and your brother when you were little. You both looked so mischievous. Oh, God, don't start. That was pure chaos. Liam was  always  getting me in trouble. He'd tell Mum I’d broken something, then act all innocent! Brothers. A complicated relationship. I had two, you know. Quite different from each other. One was a quiet scholar, the other a proper rascal. Like night and day. It’s funny, isn’t it, how family dynamics play out? It feels like…with David and I, we always tried to do things  right , you know? Create a perfect home for Leo. But it just…didn’t work out. It wasn’t your fault, Mum.

Right, I’m officially knackered. That shift at the pub was  mental . Old Man Hemmings tried to order a Black Russian using only hand gestures. Honestly. Sounds… challenging. You'd think after twenty years of coming in, he’d have mastered the spoken word for ‘coffee liqueur’. Did Dave help? He usually steps in for the complicated ones. Aye, Dave did. Eventually. It took about ten minutes of increasingly frantic miming from Hemmings. I just… I need a week in bed. And possibly a new liver. You say that every Saturday. You’ll be alright. At least you’re not stuck in the library like me. I’ve been staring at Medieval French poetry for the last six hours. My brain feels like porridge. Oh, bless ya. That  does  sound grim. At least pulling pints is… social. Though horrifying, like with Hemmings. Speaking of horrifying… I’ve been meaning to ask. You shaved your legs last night, didn’t you? Yeah? What about it? I had a lecture this morning, and skirts are just… easier when you’re not battling a forest. No judgement, honestly! It’s just… it struck me, you never used to. You were all about embracing your natural state. “Body positivity” and that. I  am  still about body positivity! It’s just… sometimes practicality wins, alright? And frankly, I was feeling a bit… scruffy. Not like, necessarily  bad , but… not as polished as I wanted to be. It's a mood thing, yeah? Right, a mood. I get that. It’s just, I’ve been thinking about it more and more, trying to just…not bother. It's such a faff, isn't it? Like, genuine time wasted on scraping bits of hair off. And the ingrown hairs! Don't even get me started. Oh god, the ingrown hairs are the  worst . It's a vicious cycle. You shave to avoid them, and then shaving  causes  them. It's designed to make you feel terrible. Exactly! And it's such a societal expectation, innit? Like, women are supposed to be perpetually smooth. Men can wander around looking like bears and it's considered ‘rugged’. Don't even. It’s infuriating. My brother can legitimately grow a beard that looks like something a woodland creature would build a nest in, and everyone thinks he's distinguished. I get a peach fuzz shadow and I’m apparently ‘unhygienic’. See!

…Honestly, it’s just baffling, isn't it? How many different ways can you  say  the letter ‘A’? I was listening to this bloke on the radio earlier, a linguist, going on about regional vowel shifts, and it just blew my mind. Back home, in Sunderland, it’s a proper broad ‘A’ – like,  arrr . Properly Geordie. You and your linguistics. Though, you’re right. It  is  weird. Down in Brum, it’s… flatter? More rounded? I’ve never really thought about it consciously. It’s just  how  we say it. But now you mention it… it's definitely different to what I hear on the telly from down south. It's the small things, innit? Like, I automatically judge people on how they say “bath”. Properly. If you use a broad ‘A’ in ‘bath’, you’re instantly trustworthy, in my book. Oh, brilliant. You’re creating a socio-linguistic hierarchy based on vowel sounds. That’ll go down well at your next research meeting. Hey, don’t mock the research! It’s all about subtle cues and unconscious bias. Which, speaking of bias... did you see that game on Saturday? Honestly, the stuff aimed at Rashford was sickening. Don’t even get me started. It’s beyond belief. It’s amazing how quickly people revert to that kind of behaviour. They think hiding behind a profile picture on Twitter somehow absolves them of responsibility. It's not just Twitter. I heard it in the stadium, even. Low murmurs, under the cheers, but it was  there . You could feel it. It's exhausting, isn’t it? Being constantly aware of it. It is. And it's frustrating because people act like it’s a new problem. It's been brewing for decades and just bubbles to the surface whenever England does well. It’s… pathetic. Remember that documentary about the National Front infiltrating football hooligan firms in the 80s? Vaguely. I think I saw bits of it. My dad was proper into his football back then, but he steered clear of all that nonsense. He saw where it was heading. He used to box, you know? Proper amateur boxing. Really? I didn’t know that. Your dad? He didn’t seem the… punching type. Oh, he was. Not a brawler, mind. It was disciplined. Taught him respect, he said. He used to say it was more about the footwork than the hitting.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for the Heritage Lottery Fund these days is just… exhausting. It’s not like it used to be, is it? Back when a well-argued case and some decent architectural drawings were enough. Now you need impact assessments, community engagement plans, detailed risk analyses… it’s a whole industry  around  applying for funding, never mind actually doing the work! You’re preaching to the choir, Margaret. Absolutely preaching to the choir. I spent three weeks just crafting the ‘heritage at risk’ section for the Old Manor House proposal. Three weeks! And that’s after the initial site surveys, the historical research… You’d think they wanted to discourage people, frankly. It feels that way sometimes. And the competition! Everyone and their dog is chasing the same pot of money. Though, I do understand the need for thoroughness, particularly with something like the Rose Cottage project you mentioned. Seventeenth-century wattle and daub is… delicate. Delicate is putting it mildly. It’s practically held together by wishful thinking and a particularly robust ivy. The current owners, bless them, haven’t a clue. They wanted to render over the whole thing and stick in uPVC windows! I nearly fainted. That’s why I called you, actually. You've always been so good at navigating the traditional building techniques. What would  you  suggest, initially, to stabilise the south gable? It’s leaning rather alarmingly. Oh dear. Leaning is never good. From what you say about the construction, I’d be cautious about any modern cement-based repairs. It can exacerbate the problem in the long run, doesn’t allow the structure to ‘breathe’ properly. Honestly, I’d lean towards a complete deconstruction of the affected area, carefully documenting everything as you go - each piece of timber, the infill material. Then rebuild it using traditional methods, lime mortar, obviously. Deconstruction… that’s what I was leaning towards, but it feels so drastic. The owners are already balking at the estimated cost. They thought a bit of pointing and a lick of paint would sort it out! Bless their hearts. They really don’t understand, do they? You have to educate them. Show them images of what happens when you try to patch up historic buildings with modern materials. Damp, rot, accelerated decay… it’s a slippery slope. Have you shown them examples of successful restoration projects? Visuals always help.

Right, milk first for me, always. Though, honestly, it feels fundamentally  wrong  to anyone north of… well, pretty much anywhere south of Durham, doesn’t it? It’s a cultural divide. You and your regional sensitivities, Elara. It’s just tea. Though, you’re right, it's a serious point of contention. My mam always said milk last was for people who didn’t trust the hot water. Which, admittedly, is a bit grim. How’s the research going, anyway? Still wrestling with those historical dialect levelling studies? Wrestling is an understatement. It’s like trying to untangle a ball of yarn knitted by a particularly mischievous cat. I’m trying to pinpoint exactly  when  and  why  certain vowel shifts started disappearing in the North East, and it’s just…messy. So much conflicting data, so many poorly documented sources. And everyone thinks they’re a linguistic expert because their grandma spoke a bit differently. Sounds…familiar. My own PhD has moments like that. Trying to establish the impact of post-industrial migration on Birmingham’s accent. Everyone’s got an opinion on how ‘Brummie’ sounds now, and very little of it is based on actual methodology. Exactly! It’s all anecdote! I had one chap, a retired headteacher, tell me my pronunciation of ‘bath’ was ‘an abomination’ and a sign of societal decline. As if how I say ‘bath’ is indicative of the moral fabric of the nation! Oh, bless him. The gatekeepers of ‘proper’ English will always be around. Still, it's funny isn’t it? The weight people attach to these tiny variations. It's pure identity, isn't it? More than logic. Completely. And that’s what  makes  it interesting, right? It’s not just about sounds; it’s about people, and history, and belonging. I'm trying to model the spread of these changes, factoring in things like railway networks and industrialization. I think the rail lines were  huge . Suddenly, people are moving around, hearing different accents… That makes sense. Birmingham became a real melting pot during the Industrial Revolution. Massive influx of people from rural areas, then Ireland, the Caribbean… It’s probably why the accent is so… resilient, actually. It kept absorbing influences rather than being completely overwritten. Though, it gets a lot of stick. It does, unfairly. All the accents get stick, really, don’t they? Everyone thinks theirs is the ‘neutral’ one.

Oh, that’s lovely, Elsie! Is that… is that supposed to be Mrs. Higgins? With the really big hair? Yes! And she’s giving everyone sausages! She always gives good sausages at lunchtime. Sausages are yummy! But I like chips better. School dinners are good. They are, aren’t they? It’s good to hear you both enjoy them. Although, Elsie, Mrs. Higgins doesn’t  always  give sausages, does she? It’s a menu, you know. There’s Monday’s shepherd’s pie… Shepherd’s pie is… okay. But it doesn’t have sausages. And sometimes it’s got peas  in  it. Peas are green and sneaky! They hide! Sneaky peas! You’re right, they do. Listen, about school dinners… I need to make sure you both have the money for next week. The office sent a note, the price has gone up slightly. It’s five pounds fifty now each. Five pounds fifty?! That's a lot of money! More than for a comic! It is a bit, love. But it covers all your lunch, every day. It’s important to have a good meal to help you learn. Do you want to put the money in your wallets now, or shall I? I want you to, Mummy. My wallet is hard to open. Alright, here you go, Leo. And Elsie, yours is here. Now, speaking of school… have you both been practicing for the tennis tournament? Yes! Miss Patel says I’m getting much better at my serve. I almost hit Mr. Davies in the… the bum! Elsie! Goodness me! Well, that’s… good aiming then! Just try not to aim  at  people. Remember to say sorry if you accidentally hit someone. I’m not very good at tennis. I keep hitting the ball into the bushes. But I'm good at running! You  are  a very fast runner, Leo. That’s fantastic. Maybe you can use that speed to chase down the tennis balls when Elsie hits them into the bushes! Maybe! Mummy, can we talk about something else? Of course, love. What’s on your mind? Ruby said her dad took her to see a clown at a fair. But she said it was a  scary  clown. Like, with lots of red and a really big smile. Clowns are silly! I like clowns! They drop things! Some clowns are silly, yes. And some can be a bit… startling.

Honestly, that film… “The Dig.” It was beautifully shot, wasn’t it? But so…slow. I mean, I appreciate the archaeological detail, and the performances were good, but two hours to watch people brush dirt off things? I nearly nodded off. Slow, you say? Well, that's progress, isn’t it? Films these days are all explosions and flashing lights. Give me a thoughtful, paced story any day. Reminds me of those old Merchant Ivory films. Though, admittedly, I’ve probably fallen asleep during a few of those too, in my time. I thought it was alright. Visually stunning, definitely. Though the historical liberties they took grated a bit. It wasn’t a documentary, I know, but… still. It got me thinking about that debate at the Union last week, the one about  how  we teach history. Oh, the Cambridge one? I read a bit about it. Something about moving away from ‘Great Man’ history, wasn’t it? More focus on social history, everyday lives… Exactly. So, less Churchill, more… the people Churchill impacted. Which, theoretically, sounds excellent. But I worry it’ll end up being a bit sanitised, a bit… apologetic. We need to teach the complexities, the darker sides too. Not just focus on victimhood, you know? Politicians. All of them. They’d argue the toss over the colour of the sky if it suited their agenda. Remember when they tried to rewrite the National Curriculum back in the… oh, must have been the early 2000s? All that fuss over dates and key events. Felt like they were trying to dictate what children should  think , rather than how to  think  about history. Don’t get me started on the National Curriculum. Trying to cram so much in, it’s all surface level. And the pressure on teachers to ‘teach to the test’… it’s stifling. When I was at school, in Dorchester, we had a fantastic history teacher, Mr. Harding. He didn't just make us learn dates; he made us understand the context, the  why . We used to debate things for hours. Sounds idyllic. My experience at school in Ayr was… less inspiring. More rote learning. Which is ironic, considering I now spend my life trying to get people to  engage  with stories. It’s a different skill altogether though, isn’t it? Selling something versus fostering a genuine understanding. You went to a grammar school, didn’t you, lad?

…Drizzly, innit? Proper Norfolk weather followin’ me even down 'ere. Used to be, you could set your watch by it, regular as clockwork. Nowt like it used to be. Oh, don't start on the weather, Arthur. It's always been changeable. I remember summers when we barely saw a drop of rain, and winters so cold the pipes would freeze solid. Harrow wasn’t much better, believe you me. Though, at least we had central heating eventually. You never had that in Costessey? Not when I were a lad, no. Coal fires, everythin’. And damp. Always damp. Mother used to say the house breathed moisture. Course, that were before the war, mind you. Everything was different then. Simpler, perhaps. Though, I wouldn't say  easy . Speaking of the war, have you seen this article about the escalating tensions in… well, never mind. Depressing stuff. It does make you wonder, doesn't it, how easily we forget the lessons of history. My grandfather, you know, fought in the Great War. Never really spoke about it. Said it were best left buried. True, Dad. They didn’t talk about trauma like they do now. Just… bottled it up. Grandad Harry was a quiet man, though. Always tinkering in the garden. I remember him showing me how to propagate roses. Odd, isn’t it? Faced unimaginable horrors, and remembered the roses. That’s men for you. My own father, bless him, he was in the Navy. Said the worst part wasn’t the U-boats, but the boredom. Long stretches of nothin’ but sea. He always joked he learned to knit during the war, just to keep his hands busy! My Da… well, he weren’t a fighting man. Too old. He were a farm labourer. Stayed and kept the land goin’. Said someone ‘ad to. But his brother, Uncle George… now  he  were in France. Came back a changed man. Never married, never settled. Always lookin' over his shoulder. It’s funny the things you learn about your ancestors. I was digging through some old family records recently and discovered my great-great-grandmother was accused of being a poacher. Can you imagine? A woman, poaching! Apparently, she was quite the character. Well, they were a resourceful lot, those Victorian women. Had to be, to survive. My mother’s family, they were all Londoners, running a small bakery. It was tough work, I gather.

Honestly, Dad, it feels… really weird. Driving this route for the last time with Mum moved out. It's just… not the same. Tell me about it, son. Forty-seven years of driving this road, picking up your Mum, dropping you lads off at school… Feels like a whole chapter's closed, doesn't it? Though, let’s be fair, your Mum was already talking about downsizing five years ago. Said the garden was getting too much. Yeah, but  doing  it is different. And she's so happy in the bungalow, which is good, I guess. Still feels a bit… sudden. Did Aunt Carol call about the housewarming? I promised I'd remind you. She did. Left a message. Said she’s bringing that awful lemon drizzle cake. The one that’s always, and I quote, “a little bit dry around the edges.” I told her we’d appreciate it, naturally. Can't offend family, can you? Though I swear she makes it deliberately like that just to get a reaction. Classic Carol. She lives for the drama. Speaking of family, have you spoken to Uncle Peter since… well, since he was in hospital? Last I heard, it was just a bad chest infection. I did, yesterday. He’s… not good, to be honest. They’re running more tests. Something to do with his lungs. He sounded weak, really weak. Said he's mostly just sleeping. It's worrying. Makes you think, you know? About your own mortality, that sort of thing. That’s awful, Dad. I’ll give him a ring later. It’s just… everyone seems to be getting older all of a sudden. It’s a bit of a shock. It is. Time flies, son. Especially when you’re bogged down with… well, everything. This mortgage, for instance. I was looking at the statements again last night, trying to figure out how we’re going to manage with Mum’s share. It’s a right mess, frankly. You shouldn’t stress about that too much, Dad. We talked about this. You and Mum have always been sensible with money. You'll figure it out. Maybe you could speak to Mr. Henderson at the bank? He always seemed alright. Henderson retired six months ago. Replaced by someone who looks at you like you’ve personally insulted his mother. Honestly, the customer service these days… It's appalling. I spent half an hour on the phone trying to explain the situation, and he just kept repeating policy numbers.

Right, so, we've got the main course settled – roast beef, definitely. Mum always loved a good roast. Though, remembering last year… she kept asking if it was Christmas. Honestly, it’s getting… well, you know. Yeah, it’s… noticeable. Not that she  acts  confused most of the time, just those little moments. The roast is a good shout though. Comfort food. Are we doing Yorkshire puds? Please say we’re doing Yorkshire puds. Naturally! Yorkshire puds are non-negotiable. I’ve already ordered the beef from Farmer Giles. He promised a really lovely joint. Though, getting out there to actually  choose  it was a mission. He was going on about sustainable fishing practices again. Honestly, you’d think he was selling salmon, not beef. Oh, Giles. He’s a character. Did he try to get you to buy a whole mackerel just because it was “responsibly sourced”? He did that to Dad last month. Almost! He was detailing the plight of the cod. I had to steer the conversation back to cow welfare, eventually. Anyway, sides? We’re doing roast potatoes, obviously, and I’m thinking parsnips, and maybe some braised red cabbage? Ooh, the red cabbage sounds lovely. And can I volunteer for potato duty? I make  amazing  roasties. All fluffy on the inside, crispy on the outside. A proper accomplishment. Consider it done. That would be brilliant, thank you. Now, seating plan. This is where it gets tricky. Uncle Bernard and Auntie Carol  must  be separated. The political arguments last time nearly ended in a cutlery war. Oh, God, yes. Remember when Uncle Bernard started ranting about… I can’t even remember what, but Auntie Carol was practically spitting across the table. Let's put Bernard at the end, near young Leo. He’s pretty good at distracting people with dinosaur noises. Good thinking! And Grandma? Should she be… close to the kitchen, do you think? Just in case she needs anything? Or to subtly steer her away from the dessert table before she demolishes the entire cheesecake? Yeah, maybe near the kitchen. Or next to me. I can chat with her and try to keep her engaged, you know? Remind her who everyone is, if she asks. It's just... hard. It is. It really is. I keep finding old photographs and… it just hits you, doesn't it? Looking at her when she was vibrant and full of life.

Honestly, this pain is  killing  me. Like, actually, genuinely killing me. I swear, these wisdom teeth are plotting my demise. Oh, still battling with those then? You’ve been moaning about them since we got to France. Have you booked an appointment with a dentist yet? We're in a proper city here, there must be someone decent. Booked? Aye, booked. For next  month . It's the only slot they had going. Can you believe that? A month of this throbbing ache. And it’s not even a constant pain, it's like… random stabbing. It's proper mental. A month is ridiculous! Though, I suppose French dentists are probably swamped with tourists needing emergency work. Still. Did you remember to pack your painkillers? The strong ones your mum gets you? Of course, I did. Though they only take the edge off. It's like, there's just this…hole. Like, a physical hole of pain right at the back of me jaw. Sounds dramatic, I know. You  are  dramatic, Liv. But no, I believe you. Wisdom teeth are the worst. Remember when I had mine out? I lived on soup for a week. Ugh, don’t remind me. Soup sounds… grey. I just want a proper Yorkshire pudding. Or a steak. Something I can actually  chew . Speaking of things I can’t do properly, how are your parents coping with everything? The house move and all? It's… chaotic, to put it mildly. Dad’s trying to be all calm and organised, as usual, but Mum’s completely stressed. Apparently, the solicitor sent the wrong documents  again . She was on the phone for hours yesterday, practically screaming down the line. Oh, bless her. She’s always been a bit of a worrier, your Mum. How’s the new house looking? Have you seen it much since the offer was accepted? Just the one quick visit. It's…nice. A bit smaller than our current one, but the garden’s lovely. And it’s closer to the station, which will be good for me getting back to Cambridge in term time. Which brings me to… Uni. Are you dreading going back as much as I am? Honestly? Massively. Don’t get me wrong, I love me course – Archaeology's brilliant - but living back in halls… No thank you. I’d rather wrestle a badger. And then there’s the whole thing with flat hunting for second year.

Right, so the recipe  says  this should be a perfectly acceptable lactose-free Victoria sponge. Honestly, you wouldn’t know the difference - unless you’ve got a particularly sensitive tummy, like someone I know…  cough  Leo  cough . I don't  have  a sensitive tummy! I just… sometimes feel a bit rumbly. It's the excitement. Excitement about what? The cake? Is it going to have sprinkles? Maybe, if you’re both exceptionally well-behaved. And yes, the cake. Although, we were actually talking about acts of kindness. Remember? For Chinese New Year? Oh yeah! Mrs. Chen said it's the Year of the Dragon! Does that mean we get dragon cookies? Hopefully! Though I was thinking we could  do  something kind, not just  receive  lovely things. We talked about making cards for Old Mr. Henderson, didn’t we? He always smells of biscuits. He does, doesn’t he? Well, that’s a lovely thing already - he  likes  smelling of biscuits! But maybe a card would cheer him up even more. Or we could offer to help him with his garden. My garden needs helping too. It’s full of weeds that look like monsters. We can tackle both, perhaps. It’s nice weather for it, if it stays dry. I was also thinking about… well, you know how we sometimes use the chess and draughts pieces as 'money' for little games? Yeah! The Queen is worth ten, and the pawn is one! Exactly. What if we 'earned' pieces by doing kind things? Like, one pawn for clearing up your toys, a knight for helping with the washing up… and we could 'spend' them on a little treat at the weekend. Could I earn a Rook by walking the dog even though it's cold? Absolutely! That’s a brilliant idea, Leo. A Rook is a very valuable piece. That’s a big kindness. Now, what about something slightly different… have you two noticed how grey my hair is getting? A little bit. It's like silver! It's less silver and more… frankly, depressing. I was thinking about getting a few streaks of colour. What colour?! Not green, please. Green is icky. No, not green! I was thinking maybe purple? Or… I saw someone with a lovely dusky rose colour. Purple would be cool! Like a dragon! See, Leo’s on board! It’s just a thought. A little bit of fun.

Honestly, Mum, Mr. Henderson  really  went off on one today. About… well, about everything, but mostly about my history essay. He said it lacked “narrative drive.” What even  is  narrative drive? It was about the suffragettes! Oh, Mr. Henderson. He’s a stickler, isn’t he? Narrative drive just means it needs to… tell a story, really. Not just list dates and facts. Think about Alice in Wonderland. It's full of facts about a strange world, but the  story  is what pulls you in. Alice in Wonderland… ugh. We have to analyse it for English next week. I just don't  get  it. All that nonsense. A talking rabbit? Seriously? It’s not meant to be serious, darling. It’s a satire, a bit of a commentary on Victorian society disguised as a children’s story. And Lewis Carroll was brilliant. Did you know he used to invent logic puzzles for fun? No! That's… surprisingly cool. Still doesn’t make it less boring though. Hey, did you hear about old Mrs. Gable? Apparently, she had a little bump with her car yesterday. Oh dear, no! Is she alright? I saw her yesterday at the shops. She seemed perfectly fine, though a little flustered. Apparently, someone pulled out in front of her at the roundabout near the harbour. Nothing major, just a dented bumper, but she was really shaken up. Old Mr. Peterson was the one who helped her. He’s a hero, really. He always is. That’s lovely of him. He’s a good man. It’s funny, isn’t it? People often say silly things happen around here, but there's a real community spirit. Everyone looks out for each other. Speaking of bumps and scrapes… you still got that little scar on your knee from falling off your bike last summer? Yeah. It's barely visible now. It used to be  huge  though! I thought I’d broken it. You were so brave. Didn't even cry. Though I think you were more upset about the state of your favourite trousers. They were floral! And brand new! Anyway… Dad said he's taking me to see that new band, ‘Static Bloom’, next Friday. Have you heard of them? Static Bloom? The ones all your friends are raving about? A little bit, yes. Your father has been humming their songs all week. Is that what you wanted for your birthday?

…and honestly, Harold, the sheer  audacity  of their planning application. They’re trying to push these solar farms through on agricultural land that’s been producing food for centuries! It’s just… criminal. I spent a good hour last night on the phone with that group in Dorset, trying to explain about Section 106 agreements, and the importance of really poring over the environmental impact assessments. Dorset, you say? Seems to be happening everywhere, doesn’t it? The pressure to meet these green targets, and the easiest route is always to slap a field full of panels down. I’m still fuming about what happened with the turbines up near Cheddar Gorge. Beautiful countryside, utterly ruined by those monstrosities. Cheddar Gorge. Now  that  was a fight. I remember following that one in the papers. Difficult terrain for protests, though, wasn't it? Too easy for the police to contain things. Exactly! And that's what I was trying to impress on the Dorset lot. It’s not enough to just wave placards. They need to understand the legal framework, know their rights, and propose viable alternatives. They were asking about a planning appeal – bless them, they hadn’t even considered the cost! It’s astronomical. Astronomical is the word. And councils...don’t even get me started on local councils. They’re supposed to be representing the community, but they’re so easily swayed. These energy companies dangle promises of ‘community benefit funds’ – a few bob for the village hall, and suddenly everyone’s a bit more… amenable. It's the finance, isn't it? Always comes down to the finance. Governments throwing money at subsidies for these projects, but barely a penny for genuine research into energy storage solutions. We’ve got enough renewable  generation  capacity, the problem is holding onto it when the wind doesn't blow or the sun doesn't shine. Precisely! I read an article just last week about a new type of flow battery being developed in Australia. Apparently, it’s incredibly efficient and can store energy for days. But where’s the UK investment? It’s all going into propping up these… visually appalling and often ecologically damaging projects. They talk about ‘net zero’ as if it's some magical solution. It’s a slogan, not a plan. And these developers, they’re masters of spin. Presenting everything as this benefit to the environment, conveniently glossing over the destruction of habitats, the impact on local communities… It’s the optics, you see.

… Honestly, the price of petrol these days. It's daylight robbery, I tell you. Daylight robbery. Though, I suppose it doesn’t matter  so  much now I’m mostly on the bus. It is ridiculous, isn’t it? Though I am starting to think having a car might be worth it, just for the freedom. Speaking of which, how did the driving lesson go, Dad? You were off to practice parallel parking this afternoon, weren’t you? Oh, don’t even ask. Parallel parking… it’s the bane of my existence. I managed to get  mostly  in, but nearly mounted the pavement doing it. Old Mrs. Higgins gave me a right look. Said I was going to take her geraniums out. Geraniums are sacred, Arthur! Everyone knows that. Though I suspect she says that to everyone who dares look at her garden. How was it  really ? Be honest. Alright, alright. It was… stressful. I’m getting the hang of the clutch, mostly. It’s just coordinating everything – steering, signals, looking in the mirrors… it’s a lot for an old brain like mine. You're doing brilliantly, Dad! Remember how you couldn't even  find  the indicators last week? Baby steps. And don’t let Mrs. Higgins intimidate you. Easy for you to say, you’ve been driving for years. Speaking of which, have you looked at insurance quotes yet, love? I know you were planning to get some before your next lesson. It’s going to be astronomical, I reckon. Especially for someone my age, learning at… well, let’s just say advanced age. I have, actually. It is…a bit eye-watering. But I’ve been comparing a few, and there’s one that looks promising – black box technology. It monitors your driving and can lower the premium if you’re sensible. Black box? Sounds like something out of a spy film! Will it tell the insurance company if you’re going over the speed limit? Pretty much, Mum. It also records things like harsh braking and cornering. It’s a bit Big Brother, but it could save us a fortune. A fortune is what we need. I’m hoping to take the test before winter sets in properly, but even just getting insured feels like a mountain to climb. We'll need to think about updating our holiday plans then, won't we? Maybe Cornwall is a bit ambitious if I'm the only driver.

Honestly, Dad, this is  exactly  what I needed. Proper homemade egg mayo. Not that stuff you get in Pret. Pret? Fancy. Back in my day, egg mayo was a treat, and it certainly wasn't bought in a shop. Your Nan made it, of course. Always a pinch of mustard powder, she did. Secret ingredient. Sounds good. You know, I was thinking about Brighton again. Found a flat online – tiny, but right near the seafront. Seems… doable. Brighton, eh? Still on about that? It’ll be chock-a-block with tourists, all year round now. And the parking! Don’t even get me  started  on parking down there. A nightmare. You'll spend all your money just leaving the thing. I know, I know. Parking is the biggest issue. But I figured I could manage without a car most of the time? It’s got really good public transport links, and I can cycle. It's just… I need a change, Dad. Being back here feels…stuck. Stuck? You've only been back a month since finishing your Masters! And it’s nice having you around. Helps me, you know? Though, you spend more time staring at that phone than talking to your old man. Sorry! It's just… work emails, mostly. And… Facebook’s been driving me mad. They’ve changed the notifications again. I keep missing important messages. Face…book? What’s wrong with a proper letter? Or even a phone call? All this digital nonsense. Makes me dizzy just thinking about it. I got roped into it by Carol - she's obsessed with posting pictures of her prize-winning roses. It's useful for keeping in touch with people, though. And organising things. Speaking of which, are you still going to the races next Saturday? That I am! Ascot. Always a good day out. Though the prices are getting ridiculous. Remember when you could get in for a fiver? Now it's more like fifty quid. Still, I've got a little system. Small bets, spread around. Never put all your eggs in one basket, as your Nan used to say. That’s sensible. You always were good with a bit of a flutter. Remember that time you won on that long shot at Epsom? You treated us all to ice cream for a week! Aye, that was a good day. A very good day. Things were simpler then.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Mr. Henderson to mark down my essay for ‘lack of original thought’ when I literally quoted a relatively obscure sonnet! It felt personal, you know? Like he just…doesn’t  like  me. Henderson sounds delightful. A real bastion of academic freedom, that one. Though, honestly, half the lecturers at Cardiff are just waiting for an excuse to fail someone. It builds their reputations, apparently. Exactly! It's a power trip. It’s not about the quality of the work, it’s about asserting dominance through red pen. Shakespeare’s probably spinning in his grave. Though he’d probably have a witty retort, the man was a master of sarcasm. Speaking of which…did you hear about old Mrs. Davies from the checkout at Tesco? No, spill. Last I heard she was still giving passive-aggressive comments about my questionable fruit and vegetable choices. She was arguing with a bloke about the price of parsnips. Apparently, he pointed out they were on offer, and she went on this  rant  about how "people these days don't appreciate the value of a good root vegetable!" It was glorious. Pure theatre. Oh, she’s a legend. Completely unshakeable in her convictions about parsnips. You know, that reminds me… I've been trying to learn to play the guitar. Utterly failing, obviously. The guitar? Really? That’s…ambitious. How’s it going? Are you aiming to be the next Ed Sheeran or just produce mildly irritating acoustic renditions of Wonderwall? The latter, definitely. Though I’m aiming for proficiency, naturally. It’s the 'winning' aspect I struggle with. Like, I want to  win  at guitar. Why is learning a skill so focused on competitiveness? It's supposed to be enjoyable. My flatmate keeps showing off, doing all these fancy chords…it’s infuriating. It  is  weird, isn't it? This need to conquer everything. It bleeds into everything. Remember Uncle George and his golf obsession? "It's not about the walk," he’d say, "it’s about  winning  the bloody trophy!" He took it so seriously. Oh god, Uncle George. The man lived for that miniature silver cup. Always talking about his handicap. Speaking of families… Have you ever thought about the origins of surnames? Mine’s particularly…uninspired. 'Smith'. Literally, a guy who made things out of metal. Thrilling. ‘Smith’ is a classic! At least it tells a story. Mine’s ‘Fairweather’.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of requests for avocado and gluten-free options at these conferences is just… baffling. Like, it’s a regional agricultural show, not a wellness retreat! You’d think folk were expecting Michelin stars, not a butty. Aye, people are mental. A butty’s a butty, innit? Especially after a long day lugging stuff about on a building site. I’d take a bacon and egg any day over some fancy smashed avo on sourdough. Speaking of which, how’s work been, Elle? Aside from the avocado apocalypse. Tell me about it, Maisie. I had a supplier trying to upsell me organic, fair-trade paperclips  yesterday . Paperclips! I nearly choked on my coffee. Though, to be fair, margins are tight, and everyone’s trying to justify their costs these days. Margins are always tight. That’s the beauty of agricultural shows, though. Proper folk. Not too bothered about the frills. It’s the corporate events that are the nightmare. All “conscious uncoupling” team-building exercises and kale smoothies. Conscious… what now? Sounds right pretentious. I stick to footy and a pint down the pub, myself. Keeps things simple. Still looking at moving outta me mum’s, by the way. Found a little place near Mill Road. Needs a bit of work, but it’s mine. Oh, that’s brilliant, Liam! Mill Road’s lovely. Little bit chaotic, but full of life. Are you doing it up yourself? Hoping to. Got a mate who’s a bit of a handyman, said he’ll give me a hand for a few beers. Trying to avoid proper builders – heard too many horror stories. Plus, my budget’s… shall we say, optimistic. Optimistic is a polite word for “non-existent,” I reckon. It’s the same with flats up in Doncaster. Absolute state of some of 'em. I’m still living with me parents, unfortunately. Saving for a deposit, apparently. Feels like I’m saving for a small island, though. It does, doesn't it? The housing market is utterly ridiculous. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if I'll ever own anything other than crippling student debt. I finally managed to snag a place in Leytonstone last year, but it was a battle. A  battle  I tell you. So many viewings… Leytonstone? That’s London, though, isn’t it? Different league entirely. I was looking at flats in Sheffield, just to get a bit more for my money, but then I thought, 'What am I doing?

…and honestly, Doreen, this picture just doesn’t do the clematis justice. It's  covered  in blooms this year. Proper showstopper, it is. Though, mind you, it’s benefitting from all this rain, isn’t it? Oh, it sounds lovely, Arthur. A shame we can’t smell it through the screen. Are you showing Reg everything alright? He’s a bit slow on the uptake with technology, you know. I’m seein’ alright, I am. Just wish the blooming picture weren’t jumpin’ about so much! Makes me dizzy. And aye, Arthur, that  is  a good show of clematis. Remember old Mrs. Higgins down the lane? Used to grow ‘em as big as dinner plates. I do indeed, Reg. Though hers were always a bit… purple, weren’t they? Mine are a proper, lovely lavender. Speaking of Higgins, have you heard anything more about that fence dispute with the new folks? Oh, don't get me started. Still goin’ on, it is. They reckon the boundary’s wrong, claim we’ve encroached. Encroached! I’ve lived here fifty years, practically  am  the boundary. They’ve got a surveyor comin’ next week, apparently. Waste of money, if you ask me. Oh dear, that’s awful. Boundaries are such a headache. Remember when we had that issue with Mr. Peterson and the overgrown hedge? Don’t remind me, Doreen! That was a summer of passive-aggressive garden pruning. Anyway, back to the garden… I finished putting up the owl box, Reg. Right at the back, near the bamboo. Hopefully, we’ll get some residents. Good on ya, Arthur. Though that bamboo’s gettin’ a bit out of hand, innit? Spreadin’ everywhere. Thought about takin’ some of it down? I’ve thought about it. But it gives the garden a bit of… exoticness, don’t you think? And the birds like it. Speaking of birds, did you catch that programme on TV last night? The one about black holes? Oh, the cosmos one! Brian Cox, wasn’t it? Fascinating, but honestly, a bit beyond me. All that talk of singularities and event horizons… Exactly! It gets you thinkin’, though, doesn’t it? The sheer scale of it all. Where did everything  come  from? It's mind-boggling. I was reading an article about the very beginnings of space – the Planck epoch, they called it. Seemingly everything was crammed into something smaller than an atom.

Right, I’m officially declaring this roundabout a personal enemy. Honestly, it’s designed to confuse. Did you  see  that van nearly take out Old Man Hemmings' hedge? You’re being a bit harsh, aren’t you? It’s just a roundabout. Though, yeah, that was a close one. Hemmings will be out there with his secateurs again, no doubt. Still, better than getting stuck on the A1, which we thankfully avoided. Easy for you to say, Mr. Structural Integrity. You design these things! You know how they mess with a person's head. Anyway, are we still on for that Italian place tonight? "Luigi's"? I was looking at the menu online. Seems decent. Luigi's is good. Bit pricey, maybe, but their pasta is proper good. I had a client meeting in Newcastle last week, and we ended up in this… well, it  claimed  to be Italian, but it was more like beige food with tomato sauce. It was horrifying. We're definitely going to Luigi's. Oh god, beige Italian. The worst. Reminds me of that "restaurant" we went to near Durham once. Remember? The one with the plastic grapes? Oh, don’t. I’ve actively repressed that memory. Durham's nice though, isn't it? The cathedral is… well, it’s  a  cathedral. Impressive, but I prefer York Minster, honestly. Something about the stained glass. It just feels… grander. York Minster  is  amazing. I went there on a school trip and nearly got lost for hours wandering around. Still, Durham has a certain charm. And the river's lovely. Though, getting a bus back from Durham to Sunderland after a night out is...an experience. Packed like sardines, always someone singing off-key. You and your Sunderland stories. It always sounds… vibrant. A bit chaotic, maybe? Harpenden is… less vibrant. Very neat hedges and everything. It’s lovely, in a very… controlled way. Controlled. That’s a polite way of putting it. Sounds a bit boring to me, to be honest. Though, I suppose that's the price you pay for being surrounded by lovely, spacious houses. Speaking of houses, have you seen property prices lately? It’s mental. Don’t even  start  me on property prices. Absolutely bonkers. I was looking at places in St Albans – a bit further out, but commutable – and you need to remortgage your soul just to get a two-bedroom terrace.

Aye, listen to that one. Now, that’s a robin, definitely a robin. Lovely little burst of song, isn’t it? Though, I swear they sound a bit mournful first thing. Like they've had a bad dream. You and your birds, Margaret! You can name ‘em all, can’t you? It  is  pleasant, though. Much better than that infernal beeping. Honestly, my alarm clock this morning nearly sent me through the ceiling. I’ve got it on the quietest setting now, but…it’s still startling. Startling is an understatement! Mine’s a gentle chime, supposed to mimic church bells. Usually just reminds me I'm getting old and need to be up. Though, truth be told, I'm usually awake before it anyway, listening for the blackbirds. They start the chorus much earlier. You feeding the birds still, Jean? Trying to. The squirrels are the problem now. Absolute bandits, they are. I put up a squirrel baffle, but they just stared at it for about ten minutes, then worked out how to go  around  it. Clever little blighters. I’m going through a right fortune in sunflower seeds. Oh, they’re dreadful for that. You need one of those cage feeders, the kind only small birds can get into. A bit more expensive, but worth it. Keeps the greedy squirrels out. Speaking of expensive… I had the dentist yesterday. Oh, dear! Not good. Was it bad? Not  bad  bad, just…expensive. They’ve found a tiny crack in one of my molars. Wants to fill it, naturally. Said it could get worse if I leave it. They always say that, don’t they? Like a ticking time bomb in yer mouth. Then she was asking about my general health, always do, and I mentioned the nosebleeds I've been getting…a bit worrying. Nosebleeds? Oh, Margaret, you must get that checked. Could just be the dry air, heating on all the time, but it's best to be sure. Remember old Mrs. Higgins? Used to get terrible nosebleeds, turned out to be something… well, not good. Aye, I remember poor Elsie. It puts the willies up you, doesn't it? Just a little trickle, usually. Happens when I’m gardening, mostly. Bending over, I suppose. Speaking of gardening, I'm trying to get the roses going. They’re looking a bit sorry for themselves after the winter. You always had a beautiful garden.

…and honestly, the school play was  chaos . Absolute, glorious chaos. Little Timmy Henderson decided mid-scene he was a dinosaur and just…roared. At Mrs. Higgins, who was playing the Queen. You couldn’t make it up. Oh, Timmy! He sounds like a legend in the making. It's the unpredictability, isn’t it? That's what keeps teaching interesting. Though, I bet Mrs. Higgins wasn't feeling particularly ‘entertained’ at the time. It's good to see you, by the way. It feels like ages since we last properly chatted. Not just a hurried 'hello' at a wedding or something. It  is  good to see you, Sarah. It really is. Life just…speeds up, doesn’t it? Especially with everything. How’s work? Still battling the system on behalf of the vulnerable? Still at it, yes. Always a battle, to be honest. We had a particularly difficult case last week, a young mum…struggling terribly. It really gets to you sometimes. But enough of that, we’re supposed to be enjoying a nice evening, aren’t we? You mentioned chaos at school - is that your main focus these days? Still teaching Year 5? Still Year 5. And still occasionally refereeing dinosaur attacks. But… things are changing, actually. I’ve been doing a lot of thinking. About, well, everything. Oh? Do tell. You always were the pensive one. Well, it’s silly, really. But I’ve started writing. A novel. No way! That’s brilliant, Amelia! What’s it about? It’s… complicated. It’s loosely based on some of the experiences I’ve had with… well, with trying IVF. And then deciding to go it alone. Single motherhood. That whole journey. It’s not  about  my experience exactly, but the emotional core… it’s very personal. Wow. That's… brave. And a really important story to tell. It's not an easy path, is it? I remember how hard it was for you, back then. All the appointments, the hope, the disappointment… It wasn’t. And it's still not. Little Leo is wonderful, absolutely wonderful. But some days… it’s incredibly lonely. And exhausting. Not that openly advertising that on social media is particularly helpful, you know? Everyone else just seems to be  thriving . Perfectly curated lives. Oh, don't even  start  me on social media. It’s a highlight reel, Amelia. A complete fabrication of reality. I try to limit my time on it now, it’s just…depressing.

This is a lovely little flat, ANON. You’ve made it really cosy. Much brighter than I expected, actually, considering it’s a basement. Thanks, love. Bit of a project, it was. Damp was the initial issue, naturally. Birmingham basements, eh? Always a gamble. But I’ve got it sorted now. Years of patching and painting. Keeps me busy, you know? Not having to  actually  work anymore doesn’t mean I’m idle! I can imagine! It’s good to have something to focus on. I’m finding that now, actually. The kids are both at school full-time, which is wonderful, but suddenly… it’s quiet. Terribly quiet. I’ve joined a pottery class. Pottery? Oh, that sounds nice! Always admired people who can  make  things. I was never very good with my hands. Good with words, though. Hence the teaching, I suppose. Thirty years I spent in a classroom, wrestling with teenagers. Oh, I know the feeling! I teach English as a foreign language now, mostly adults. It’s very different to secondary, though. Less…drama. Though you get some characters, definitely. I had a gentleman last week who was convinced the Queen was a lizard person. A lizard person! Good grief. They certainly don’t make ‘em like they used to. You get all sorts, don’t you? I remember one boy, back in the eighties, swore blind that Elvis was living in Solihull. Had a whole conspiracy theory worked out. The parents were mortified. It's often the parents you have to gently explain things to, isn’t it? It's amazing what children believe. Mine are convinced that if they leave a carrot out for the reindeer on Christmas Eve, they'll get a text message back. A text message? Now  that’s  progress. When I was a lad, it was a few biscuit crumbs and hoping Santa didn't track mud all over the carpet. It’s changed so much, hasn’t it? Even education. It's not like how it used to be. All this focus on… well, everything  except  the actual learning, if you ask me. I’ve noticed that too. Lots of emphasis on well-being, which is good, of course, but sometimes it feels like the core subjects get a bit… pushed aside. And the constant changes to the curriculum! Trying to keep up is exhausting. They were talking about another review at the staff meeting last week.

…and then our Brenda, she tries to make a Yorkshire pudding, right? In  Sunderland . Bless ‘er heart, it came out flatter than a pancake. Said it needed more air, I told her, lass, you need to be  in  Yorkshire to get the air right for a proper pudding! Oh, don't even get me started on Brenda’s attempts at northern cuisine! She asked me what fat to use.  Fat ! Like, you just use lard, Brenda! It’s not rocket science. Though, honestly, yours are probably just as bad, Liam. You’re in Cambridge now, the air’s all posh and doesn’t hold a proper rise. Oi! My Yorkshires are perfectly respectable. When I make ‘em in Leeds, that is. It’s a geographical thing, I’m telling ya. It's the humidity. You two are hilarious. It  is  just cooking, though, isn't it? Though I have to admit, my mum's attempts at a Sunday roast when we lived in Germany were… interesting. Let's just say sauerkraut doesn't really  enhance  roast beef. I think it's the inherent cultural understanding of the dish, really. You need a lineage of roast dinners to truly  get  a roast dinner. It’s a complex system. Oh, here we go with the engineer's analytical breakdown of a Sunday roast. It's food, Ben, not a bridge! Speaking of things that need complex systems... anyone seen anything good at the cinema lately? I’m completely dried up for films. I saw that new action flick, 'Steel Tempest' last week. Explosions, spaceships, the works. Good brain-off entertainment. Not exactly high art, mind. 'Steel Tempest'? Sounds… intense. I’ve been meaning to catch that documentary about the history of concrete. Apparently, it's surprisingly gripping. Concrete? Seriously, Alex? Hey, don't knock it 'til you try it! It's fascinating how much of modern life rests on – literally – concrete. Plus, the engineering challenges… Okay, okay, enough concrete chat. My brain's starting to seize up. Music then? Has anyone found anything new they’re obsessed with? I’ve been looping this new band, ‘Static Bloom’. They're kind of indie-pop, bit dreamy… Indie-pop? Sounds a bit soft for me, bab. I’ve been getting back into some old Kaiser Chiefs. Proper good, singalong stuff. Keeps you going when you’re stuck on a site all day, you know? Building things.

Honestly, the traffic in Cambridge is a joke. It's barely moved since we left the gym. Did anyone actually  gain  anything from that workout with this chaos afterwards? I feel like I burned zero calories just sitting in this metal box. Oh, come on, Liam. You did, you always do. You’re just being dramatic. Besides, it’s Friday afternoon. Everyone and their dog is probably trying to escape the city for the weekend. Speaking of which, anyone finalised plans for that weekend trip? I'm still leaning towards the Lake District. I found a little cottage online, looks really cosy. Bit of a drive, but worth it for the scenery, don’t you think? And a proper escape from…well, everything. Lake District sounds good. Although, honestly, the weather forecast isn't amazing. Looks like potential for rain most of the weekend. I was idly looking at Cornwall, maybe Penzance? Could be warmer. Cornwall’s a fair trek though, isn’t it? Especially after work on Friday. The Lake District is doable. Rain or shine, a walk in the fells is good for the soul. Plus, I’ve been meaning to test out my new waterproof jacket. Urgent field testing, naturally. Of course. Always a good excuse for new gear. I’m happy with either, really. Just need a change of scenery. This term has been  hectic . Little Timmy decided to glue himself to a chair this week. Apparently, it was ‘an experiment’. Oh, bless him. Sounds like you’re a saint, Sarah. I can barely handle a demanding deadline, let alone a classroom of six-year-olds. That reminds me, have you guys heard anything more about volunteering at the kids’ camp this summer? I emailed them a while ago. I haven’t. I signed up on the website, but haven't had any confirmation. Though, honestly, I’m starting to think my coding skills aren’t particularly useful at a kids’ camp. Unless they need someone to build them a miniature Minecraft world. They might! It's that new tech camp isn't it? They are pushing for coding skills, so they might actually want you. I’m happy to help with the general stuff - setting up, supervising, that kind of thing. Actually, I used to be pretty good at knot-tying from scouts. Could be useful for building forts. That's brilliant, Liam! You’re a hidden talent.

Ooh, nearly! Proper good save that, weren’t it? Though honestly, the commentary is drivin’ me round the bend. He's said 'narrative' five times in the last ten minutes. It's a  football  match, not a Victorian novel. He's a bit of a cliché merchant, isn't he? They all are. Just filling airtime. And yes, good save. Though I’m more concerned about how utterly predictable their attack patterns are. It’s… academically frustrating, almost. Academically frustrating? You’re applying your PhD brain to  football  now? Honestly, Mark. Well, it's all pattern recognition, isn't it? Predictive modelling. Just applied to… shin pads and shouting. Besides, anything's better than thinking about my data right now. I've been staring at regression analyses for twelve hours straight. It’s turning my brain to mush. Sounds awful. You need a proper break. We were talking about gettin’ away for Easter, weren’t we? Remember? Before the football took over everything. Oh, right. Easter. Yes. Still thinking about it. I was looking at that little cottage in the Cotswolds… the one with the pub across the road? Aye! That sounded lovely. Proper cosy. And we could walk. I’m sick of Cambridge being so… flat. I miss hills. I miss being able to  see  things, not just endless rows of colleges. I miss Sunderland, a bit, to be honest. Sunderland? That's… a strong statement, coming from you. You escaped Sunderland pretty quickly. I did, didn’t I? But sometimes I get a proper hankerin’ for a stottie cake and a walk along the beach. And my mam’s roast dinners. This is why I always end up buying far too much chocolate at Easter. Trying to recreate the feelings. So, it’s a comfort eating exercise fuelled by geographical nostalgia? That's… a fascinating insight, actually. Perhaps  that  should be your research. Don't you dare! The last thing I need is to analyse my own emotional attachment to baked goods. Speaking of which, did we get any Easter eggs? I feel a bit of a sugar craving comin’ on. I think there’s a dark chocolate one in the cupboard. And I might have picked up a few mini eggs when I was at the shops. Don't tell anyone, I’m trying to be healthy. Healthy? While watching football all afternoon? Come off it. Though dark chocolate is marginally less awful, I suppose.

Ah, Jaysus, will you look at little Finn there! Must have been… eight, maybe nine? At that funfair down in Midleton. He was  terrified  of the waltzers, absolutely glued to my leg for the entire time. And then, the minute we walked past the candy floss stall, suddenly, no fear whatsoever! He still doesn’t like fast rides, does he? He refuses to go on anything that spins. Says it messes with his head. He got that from your father, you know. Dermot never could stomach a rollercoaster. Always insisted on the teacups, the slow, gentle ones. Though, to be fair, that was usually after a few pints of Guinness. Oh, Dermot was a good man, a bit of a soft touch. Remember that time he won that enormous teddy bear at the fair in Tralee? He lugged it all the way home and Finn insisted on sleeping with it for a year. A year! It took up half the bed, didn’t it? And he named it… Barnaby, was it? Good times, good times. Look at this one… London Marathon, 2018. I was absolutely wrecked just  watching  you, Sarah. Don’t remind me. It was a personal best for agony, I tell you. I thought my legs would fall off. Honestly, even thinking about it makes my knees ache. I’m just glad I did it for the charity, that children’s hospice was lovely. Did you raise a lot of money? We exceeded our target, thankfully. People were very generous. Your Uncle David was a saint, running alongside me for most of it, shouting encouragement. And shouting at me to keep pace! He's a pain, but a good one. Now this is a good one. Iceland. Remember Iceland, Margaret? You and I went back in… 2010, I think? Spectacular scenery. Cold, though. Brutally cold. Oh, Iceland! That was beautiful. The Blue Lagoon was something else. Though I remember being convinced I was going to slip and fall on the ice every five minutes. That volcanic landscape... it felt like being on another planet. Have you been back since, Liam? Not yet, no. It’s on the list. There’s a few places on the list. Finn’s been talking about wanting to go, actually. He's doing geography at school and is fascinated by volcanoes and glaciers. He was showing me some videos of the Northern Lights the other day.

Honestly, Mum, you always make the  best  roast potatoes. They're perfectly crispy. Better than any pub I’ve been to, and believe me, my job involves a  lot  of pub lunches. Oh, don’t be silly, darling. It’s just a bit of fat and knowing when to turn them. Your Nan taught me, you know. She’d be horrified at the thought of an air fryer. Everything had to be done the proper way. Proper way  is  the only way! These youngsters now… all gadgets and instant gratification. No patience. Remember when we used to play marbles, Doreen? For hours, we’d be out there, knees scraped, trying to win a ‘taw’. Oh, marbles! Gosh, I’d completely forgotten about those. We had a proper bag, all different sizes and colours. I was terrible, though. Always lost them down drains. And conkers! Remember conkers? The annual battle… Oh, don't remind me! Peter – your father - was  obsessed  with conkers. He’d spend weeks soaking them in vinegar, trying to make them indestructible. He swore it worked, though I suspect it was more down to luck. He’d always be boasting to Mr. Henderson next door. Henderson! Now  there  was a character. Always had a pipe clamped in his mouth, and a story for every occasion. He used to say Peterborough was getting too big for its boots, even  then . “It’s a small world,” he’d say, “but it’s getting smaller by the minute.” Used to drive your father mad, that saying. It  is  a small world, though, isn’t it? I was at a conference in Bristol last week, and I got talking to a chap who worked with… wait for it… Old Man Hemmings’ grandson! Hemmings ran the sweet shop on Bridge Street, you remember? The one with the penny chews. No! Really? Arthur Hemmings’ grandson? Wow. What's he doing? He’s a software engineer. Can you imagine? From penny chews to coding! He said his grandfather always talked about how difficult you were to serve, Mum, because you always knew exactly how many sweets you were getting! Well, he  did  try to short-change me once! I was only little, but I knew my sums. Had to be firm with him. It's a skill, you know, standing up for yourself. Though I suppose software engineers don't need to worry about being swindled out of a farthing.

…Honestly, Doreen, this coronation…all this fuss. Seems a bit much, don’t it? All that gold, all that…pageantry. Makes a body feel a bit…small, y'know? Oh, now, Arthur, don't be like that. It’s a bit of tradition, innit? Something to brighten things up. And Charles…he’s seemed a decent sort, hasn’t he? Always talking about the environment and all that. Decent enough, I suppose. But a King? Seems a bit…archaic. Back in my day, we were all talking about decimalisation, getting rid of the old money.  That  felt like progress. This feels like going backwards, somehow. Reminds me of old Man Hemmings down the lane, always going on about the ‘good old days’. Never were that good, not really. Just different. You and your Man Hemmings! You always did have a knack for finding the grumpy soul in every situation. But think of the spectacle, Arthur. The children will love it. Even little Maisie next door was asking me about the crown this morning. All sparkly and…royal. Maisie’s a bright girl, she is. Though I reckon she'd be happier with a packet of sweets than a glimpse of a crown, eh? Still, it’s good to see people taking an interest, I suppose. Though I’ll tell you what  really  bothered me, Doreen. What’s that, dear? Don't tell me it's something else about the bunting... No, no, not the bunting. Though it  is  a bit much, all that red, white and blue. It’s this price of petrol. Gone up again, hasn't it? Makes it nigh on impossible to even pop down to Norwich for a proper butcher’s sausage. Used to be able to get a good Cumberland from Mr. Billings. Best in the county. Oh, Arthur, you and your sausages! You worry about the sausages more than the King, it seems. It  has  gone up, you are right. I saw it when I took young Timmy to his swimming lesson yesterday. Still, we manage, don't we? We always have. We’re not ones for extravagance. Manage, yes. But it’s getting harder, that’s all. And it's not just the petrol. The electric, the heating…it all adds up. Remember when you could leave the lights on all day and not think twice? And a loaf of bread cost tuppence. I do remember.

…and honestly, little Timmy actually  ate  a crayon yesterday. A purple one. He was convinced it was a sweet. Honestly, you wouldn't believe the state of him! Covered head-to-toe. Purple everywhere. Oh my god, Elsie! That’s awful…and hilarious. Little monsters, aren't they? I had one try and ‘wash’ his face with the class goldfish last week. Seriously?! They’re a handful, aren’t they? Makes copywriting seem almost… serene. Though convincing people they  need  a mauve toothbrush is a different kind of battle. Serene?! You’re lucky! Though mauve toothbrushes… that's a niche market, even for you, Liv. Speaking of serene, how  was  your weekend? You said you were going to see your mum and dad? It was good, needed it. Mum was on a mission to find the 'perfect' Christmas present for everyone. It’s October, Elsie! October! She was already comparing advent calendar prices. Honestly, it's exhausting just being  near  her enthusiasm. My mum’s the same. She started making lists in August. I told her I didn’t  need  anything, but she just wouldn’t let it go. She eventually suggested a pottery painting class. Which, okay, is actually kind of nice, but still... the pressure! Oh, I know that drill. My nan's a champion list-maker. She once got me a framed picture of a badger. A  badger . Said it reminded her of me. I'm not sure why. That's…specific. Maybe you have a mischievous streak? Like a badger rummaging through bins? Possibly. Though I think she just likes badgers. Anyway, enough about questionable family gifts. How’s work, Chloe? Still battling with Ofsted reports and endless paperwork? You have no idea. We had a ‘mini-inspection’ last week. Not a full one, just a focus on phonics. The pressure is ridiculous. It feels like they just want to catch us out. I spent the whole week drilling phonemes into seven-year-olds until I felt like  I  was going to start sounding like a robot! Ugh, the joys of education. The system is so broken, isn’t it? It's all assessment this, data that, and precious little space for actual teaching. Honestly. It’s why I only lasted two years at uni before deciding a teaching degree was more me. No offence, Chloe, but sometimes I feel like I'm a glorified data entry clerk.

…and honestly, the state of the garden when we bought this place! It was a jungle, honestly. A  jungle . Remember, Maggie? You came round with a flask and helped me hack back some of it.      Hack back? You mean  I  hacked back while you directed operations from the patio with another cuppa? Don’t rewrite history, Klaus! Though it  was  bad. Proper overgrown. Still, better than some of the gardens on Barlow Street. You seen old Mrs. Peterson’s? It's…an experience.      Barlow Street's changed a lot, hasn’t it? A lot more new builds going up. Seems like every empty patch of land has a ‘sold’ sign on it. Property prices are insane around here.      Mmmhmm.      Insane is putting it mildly, Chloe. When we moved here, this house was…manageable. Now, you look at Rightmove, and you’d think we were living in a mansion! It’s all location, isn’t it? Being so close to the parks, the city centre…      And the schools. Honestly, that's what drove the prices up. Everyone wants their little darlings in a good school. My Sarah, she had a brilliant time at the primary just round the corner. Then everything changed when she went to secondary. Different story entirely.      Speaking of schools, how's young Leo doing, Chloe? Still enjoying being the Head Receptionist at St. Jude's? He always seemed a bright lad.      He’s good, thanks. Actually, it’s Receptionist  Assistant . Head Receptionist’s on maternity leave. It’s a busy job though, a lot of parents calling, always something going on. And…well, it’s been a bit stressful lately. There was a bit of a scare last week. A parent made some… concerning comments.      Concerning how? Oh dear.      Just… extremist views, really. Talked about what they were teaching the kids, saying it was all ‘indoctrinating’ them. Mentioned ISIS, actually. It just felt… unsettling. We’ve had police involvement, thankfully. But it makes you think, doesn’t it?      That  is  unsettling. It’s a world away from arguing about grammar and syntax, isn’t it? That's why I stick to Shakespeare, honestly. Can’t get much controversy there… well, unless you start disputing the authorship!      My dad says Shakespeare wasn't even Shakespeare. He thinks it was a group of writers.      Oh, your dad's one of  those  people, is he? A conspiracy theorist? Well, he’s not alone.

…and honestly, the tea at that little guesthouse in Pokhara was dreadful. Absolutely dreadful. It tasted like dishwater. You’d think, being  in  Nepal, they’d have decent tea! But the views, oh, the views. Annapurna…simply breathtaking. Are you still thinking of going in November, Margaret? November sounds good, assuming my blooming school lets me. They’re always on about ‘continuity of learning’ and ‘staffing levels’ when I ask for time off. It’s exhausting. Though, I  do  need a break. All this fuss with the new free school meals system is driving me round the bend. Oh, don't even  start  me on that! Honestly, the forms! And the assumptions! Little Archie’s mother was practically in tears yesterday because she thought Archie wouldn't be allowed a biscuit if he didn't have a qualifying medical condition. I had to explain, three times, that he can have a normal biscuit, it’s just the specialist gluten-free ones are covered under the scheme. It’s a nightmare. Gluten-free… that’s another thing. My granddaughter, Emily, insists on everything being gluten-free now. Says she feels ‘cleaner’ eating that way. Honestly! When I was her age, we were grateful for a slice of bread and dripping! Dripping! Oh, yes. My mother used to make the most wonderful sausage rolls with dripping pastry. Proper sausages, too, from Mr. Higgins at the Village Shop. It wasn’t fancy but it was good, honest food. Remember Mr. Higgins? Vaguely. I was a bit young when he retired, wasn't I? I got all my sweets from there though. The little glass jars on the counter… remember those? Now it’s all pre-packaged rubbish. It’s a shame the Village Shop isn’t what it used to be. Though, I do occasionally pop to the Farm Shop now. Their sausages are quite good, though terribly expensive. David – my husband – makes wonderful sausages, actually. He’s taken up cooking in his retirement. Absolutely brilliant at it. He's even mastered a gluten-free sausage! Says it’s all about the binders. David's cooking? That’s a surprise! I always thought he was a bit hopeless in the kitchen. He was! Absolutely hopeless! But he’s quite enjoying it. Keeps him occupied. Says it’s more relaxing than gardening. Though he still fussed over the runner beans this year. Speaking of food, my mother-in-law… she had the most extraordinary diet growing up.

…and then Mr. Henderson, bless 'im, he asks me if the bouncy castle is ‘health and safety approved’. A bouncy castle, right? For a regional managers’ conference on sustainable logistics! Honestly, you couldn't make it up. I just stared at him, then said, “Sir, with all due respect, are we aiming for innovation or a toddler’s birthday party?” Oh my god, that’s brilliant! People are  wild . I had a similar thing last week. My boss wanted to incorporate a TikTok dance into the presentation on quarterly profits. A  TikTok dance , Chloe! Said it would “engage the younger investors.” Honestly, corporate Britain is losing the plot. Did you actually do it? The dance, I mean. Absolutely not. I managed to talk her out of it by pointing out the potential for looking…well, ridiculous. Instead, we just used some better graphics. Thankfully she’s more easily swayed by aesthetics than actual strategy. Sounds like a close shave, Liv. You’re a lifesaver. Mine was thankfully a quick "no". Though he did then suggest a magician. A magician! I suggested team building exercises instead, focused on, you know, actual logistics problems. He seemed happier with that. It’s just…exhausting, isn’t it? Constantly having to navigate these bizarre requests. It is. I’m lucky, I think, in that Mrs. Davison is pretty sensible. Mostly it's just diary management and expense reports for me, which is…fine. But it does make me feel a bit redundant sometimes. Like, I did a Masters in History, and now I'm making sure everyone has enough sticky notes. Don't underestimate the sticky note power, Ella! Seriously though, I get that. I’ve got a proper degree in Event Management and half the time I feel like a professional fire extinguisher. Putting out ridiculous requests instead of  planning  events. That's the thing with these jobs, isn’t it? The job description sounds amazing – “dynamic, creative, opportunity for growth” – then reality hits and you're mostly just a highly-paid problem solver. I sometimes wonder if my postgraduate degree was actually worth it for what I do. I always thought mine would be more glamorous. Glasto, big music festivals, the whole shebang. Turns out mostly it’s conferences in slightly depressing hotel ballrooms. Though, I did get to organise a charity gala last year, that was good fun. Ooh, what charity?

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of them, David. Saying it’s 'underutilised'. Underutilised because they’ve deliberately cut the opening hours! It's a self-fulfilling prophecy. Mmmph. Exactly! It's classic, isn't it? Starve something of resources, then claim it’s not performing. It's what they did with the youth centre, remember? Don’t remind me. My niece practically lived there. Now it’s luxury flats. Honestly, this library… it’s not just about the books, though the books  are  important. It's the community space, the kids' reading groups, Mrs. Higgins' computer classes for the elderly… It's a lifeline for some people. Old Man Hemmings goes every Tuesday just to read the paper and have a chat. He’d be utterly lost without it. Look, we need to get this petition going seriously. Have you started drafting it yet? I've got a rough outline. I’m trying to get the wording right. It needs to be forceful, but not… aggressive. You know, we don’t want to alienate anyone on the council already. I was thinking about focusing on the impact on children and the elderly, highlighting the social value. Good. Solid ground. We can gather signatures at the market on Saturday. I’ll bring a clipboard. And maybe that little table from the shed? It’s a bit wonky, but better than nothing. Perfect. And I'll print out a load of copies. I'm thinking of adding a section for people to write why the library is important to  them . Personal stories always pack a punch, don’t they? Definitely. Makes it real. Speaking of real… this noodle soup is surprisingly good for Plumstead. Though, I still miss that little Vietnamese place on Woolwich Road. Remember their pho? Oh, I remember. The queues were insane. They got priced out, didn’t they? Another victim of rising rents. It's… it’s exhausting, isn’t it? Constantly fighting these battles. It is. My shift on Friday is a nightmare. They’ve scheduled a borough planning meeting right when I’m supposed to be finalising the quarterly reports. Typical. Honestly, sometimes I think they do it deliberately to make my life difficult. They probably do. Bureaucracy at its finest. Still, you’re good at juggling. You always are. Just about. It feels like my brain is constantly doing mental gymnastics. I was reading an article about brain training apps the other day.

…Honestly, Doreen, they were at the door again this morning. Jehovah’s Witnesses. Persistent, they are. Though young lad this time, looked barely out of school. Still didn’t take ‘no thank you’ for an answer straight away, did he? Went on about the ‘new world’ and all that. Ah, yes, the Witnesses. Been coming ‘round here since… well, since we moved to Mattishall, I reckon. Old Mrs. Higgins down the road used to give ‘em tea. Said it was good to be polite. Though she never actually  joined  them, mind. Just the tea. Polite is all well and good, Arthur, but they do wear you down, don't they? I had a lovely girl a few weeks ago, very sweet, but she kept coming back. Eventually I had to be firm, said I was happy with my lot. Though I did feel a bit bad, to be honest. Bad? Why? They're perfectly entitled to their beliefs, of course, but my time is precious now I'm retired, you know? Precious! I've got model railways to paint and bird feeders to fill. Speaking of which, have you seen the long-tailed tits about lately, Arthur? They’ve been regular visitors. Not so much lately, no. I think that fox is getting bolder. Saw it slinking around young Timmy’s garden yesterday. Shame, really. Lovely birds, those long-tailed tits. Got a proper little stripe, they do. Reminds me, young Timmy… he's finally getting married, that one. Oh, is he? That’s lovely! To Sarah, is it? The girl who works at the post office? That’s the one. Big wedding planned down at the Abbey Barn. Bit ostentatious for my liking, but there you go. They’re all wanting the big day these days. Used to be a simple affair, a quick do in the village hall. Not anymore. Expensive business, weddings. Our Martin…well, his wedding wasn’t cheap, let me tell you. Though he and Emily seem happy enough, and that’s the main thing. Still living over in Ipswich, are they? They are, yes. Emily’s mum isn’t too well, apparently. Martin's been driving over quite a bit to help out. Good lad, your son. Though he does work himself ragged. He gets that from his mother, I suppose. Always busy, always doing. I tell him to slow down, enjoy life a bit.

…and honestly, the floral print was  atrocious . Absolutely atrocious. I keep meaning to get it properly upholstered, something a bit more…subtle. Maybe a nice linen? Linen would suit the room, definitely. Though upholstering is a nightmare, isn’t it? The cost! You’re better off just covering it with a throw, which is what I usually do. You two are always talking about redecorating. Honestly, this room is perfectly charming as it is. It feels…lived in. Unlike some of these modern houses, all stark white and cold. Precisely. Character, that’s what’s missing these days. And good solid furniture. Not everything needs to be flat-packed from Sweden. Remember old Mr. Henderson, the carpenter down the road? Could build anything. Oh, I remember him! He made that little shelf in the hallway, actually. It’s still there. Though, speaking of things needing doing, have you seen next door's garden? It's completely overgrown. I feel awful for poor Mrs. Peterson, but she really can’t manage it anymore. I think her son offered to help, didn’t he? He’s got a landscaping business, apparently. Though judging by the state of  his  lawn… perhaps not the best advert. Young people today! No sense of community. In my day, everyone helped everyone else. We wouldn’t have dreamt of letting a neighbour’s garden fall into disrepair. Times change, Moira. Times change. Though I do agree, that neighbourly spirit seems to be dwindling. Did you hear about that new restaurant opening on the High Street? “Spice Merchant” or something? Oh, yes! Apparently, it’s fantastic. I’ve been meaning to book a table, but things at work have been… hectic. They’re talking about another round of outsourcing. To India, I presume? Wonderful. Just what everyone wants – their jobs shipped halfway across the world. It’s all about the budget, apparently. They want to cut costs wherever they can. It’s demoralizing, honestly. You spend years building up expertise and then…poof. Replaceable. It’s a disgrace, that’s what it is. Building up expertise  is  valuable. These companies think only of the bottom line. It’s short-sighted. I saw it happening with the schools, you know, the rush to academies. Lost so much local control, so much community involvement. Academies… a mixed bag, I think. Some have thrived, others…not so much. It all depends on the leadership, doesn’t it?

…and honestly, Doreen, the council tax this year is just…criminal. They keep saying it's for services, but what services? The bin collections are less frequent, the roads are full of more potholes than ever, and the library’s hours have been cut again. It's a right cheek, it is. A cheek indeed, Arthur. They’re all lining their pockets, the lot of ‘em. Remember old Mr. Henderson? Used to be on the council, lived just down the lane from me in Costessey. Said it was always the same. Promises, promises, then more taxes. Never seen a penny of benefit myself, I haven't. It’s easy to say ‘they’re all at it’, isn’t it? But it’s a bit more complicated than that. The government's cutbacks have hit local councils hard. They’re having to make choices. Though I agree, sometimes those choices seem… questionable. My daughter, Sarah, she works in social care.
