Oh, this is lovely, isn’t it? Just gliding along. Though honestly, Polish roads… a bit more…characterful than Cambridge, wouldn't you say? Characterful is one word for it. “Pothole paradise” is another. Glad you’re enjoying the scenery though. You seemed a bit… apprehensive about the campervan life at first. Apprehensive is putting it mildly. I’m used to a rather… static existence, let’s say. And well, bathrooms on wheels felt a bit futuristic for a Cambridge girl. But honestly? It's rather liberating. No endless dusting. No worrying about the garden. Just…go. Although, my back is starting to complain a little. This seat isn’t exactly orthopaedic. We can stop soon, there’s a services area about twenty minutes on, according to the sat nav. You can stretch your legs. You  did  remember to bring your walking shoes, right? Unlike last time? I did, yes! They’re… somewhere. Honestly, you'd think after all these years I'd have mastered the art of packing. It's a skill, you know. A life skill. More important than… well, than some of the things I spent three years studying at university, actually. Right, because knowing the intricacies of 18th-century French literature is  definitely  less useful than fitting walking shoes into a rucksack. Speaking of useful, have you spoken to Mrs. Kowalski recently? About the extra TEFL classes? Oh, her. Yes. She’s keen, apparently. Wants me to do three evenings a week. It’s… tempting. Honestly, the thought of actually  earning  money again is… foreign. But three evenings feels a bit much. I’m trying to get back into a routine, you see. And that routine involves a significant amount of… nothing. Which is rather pleasant. You need structure, Mum! You said so yourself. You've been "doing nothing" for far too long. It's not healthy. You were always so sharp, so full of ideas. You could volunteer somewhere, you know? There's a language school in Rzeszow, maybe? Volunteering… now there's a thought. Though I'm not sure anyone would want my semi-rusty French skills. And honestly, the thought of dealing with…people… all the time. It's exhausting. Especially young people. You're a natural with them, obviously, teaching abroad and all. But I prefer books, really. It's a different skillset, for sure. It’s just… I see you sometimes, and I worry.

…and honestly, the detail they put into those Neolithic sites, Newgrange and Knowth… it just blows your mind, doesn’t it? Considering they were building them  before  the pyramids, practically. People always focus on Egypt, but Ireland's got its own ancient mysteries, y'know? It is incredible. I saw a documentary about Newgrange recently. The alignment with the winter solstice...so precise. But pyramids  are  impressive though, aren’t they? The sheer scale of it. And the engineering! How did they move those stones? Aye, the scale is something else alright. But it feels…different. Newgrange feels  connected  to the land, to something…older. The pyramids feel…imposed. Like a statement. Though I suppose both are about legacy, a sort of attempt at immortality, aren't they? Immortality. That's a big topic. You’ve been reading about telomeres again, haven't you? You were on about lengthening them last week. A fella can dream, can’t he? I was reading an article about advances in gerontology. Seems there’s a growing belief that cellular senescence isn't inevitable, just...manageable. And telomere lengthening is one avenue. It's all about energy, really. How cells utilize it. Sounds… complicated. It all feels a bit sci-fi to me. I’m more concerned with getting through the next toddler tantrum fuelled by a lack of energy! Speaking of energy though, did you see that article about exploring for Helium-3 on the moon? Apparently, it could solve all our energy problems if we could just get it back here. Helium-3? Now that's a bit ambitious. Space mining... It’d be cheaper to switch everyone over to geothermal, I reckon. Or put a massive solar array in the Sahara. Though, the Sahara's shifting. All that sand, tectonic plate movement... it’s fascinating how even seemingly stable landscapes are in constant flux. You always go back to tectonics, don't you? It’s like you're always imagining the earth breathing. I read something interesting about comets actually delivering water to Earth, billions of years ago. Imagine! We’re all made of star stuff, literally. Ah, now there’s a thought. And those comets...they’re remnants from the early solar system. It makes you wonder about the risks, doesn't it? Another big one heading our way… the impact events. That’s one way to  really  shorten life expectancy. Don’t! You’re making me anxious.

Honestly, this coffee's alright, but it’s not  proper  coffee, is it? Like, not like you get at that little place in Lytham. Remember ‘The Fig & Olive’? Oh, I loved The Fig & Olive. Their carrot cake was divine. But it's a bit of a trek now, isn’t it? Especially with everything going on. And we  are  trying to save a bit, aren't we? Save? Save for what, exactly? Seems like everything’s just…going out. Bills, the cost of a loaf of bread… it’s mental. I swear, it was cheaper when I was a lad. Dad, you  always  say that. But seriously, Mum's right. We need to be a bit sensible. I was looking at those vouchers for Marco Pierre White's place, the one in Blackpool. Could be a treat if we used one. But still… fancy. Marco Pierre White is… a character. We went there years ago, before you were born, when we first started dating. He wasn’t  in  the restaurant, thankfully. But it was overpriced for what it was. We’d be better off getting a takeaway and putting the money towards… well, towards the baby stuff. Aye, the baby. Speaking of which, have you lot sorted the high chair yet? I saw a right good one in Argos, adjusts for all heights, proper sturdy. We’re having a look online, Dad. Mum found one that converts into a booster seat as well, so it’ll last longer. It’s that cream colour she likes, though. EVERYTHING has to be cream. It’s a calming colour, darling! Better than bright pink, don’t you think? We're trying to create a peaceful nursery. Though honestly, peaceful might be optimistic. Peaceful? With  you  two? Nah. Still, a nice chair’s important. Makes life easier. Reminds me, I need new sunglasses. Mine are scratched to bits. Went to that garden centre last week, the one near Preston, and they had a massive sale. Oh, that’s a good idea. I need some new ones too. Though I'm trying to figure out what shape suits me. Round ones? Cat-eye? It’s a whole  thing . Then there is the budget... Maybe when your Auntie Sheila sends that birthday money. She’s very generous, your Auntie Sheila. Speaking of family, did you hear what Uncle George said about the referendum, again? Apparently he's convinced everything would be better if we just went back to how things were.

…and then old Mrs. Higgins, bless her, she actually tried to offer Derek a mince pie  through  the letterbox! Can you imagine? He was quite startled, poor thing. Though he did eat the pie, apparently. Oh, Mum! You’re making Mrs. Higgins sound like a villain. She just gets a bit… festive. Speaking of festive, have you even  thought  about the Christmas tree yet? Last year was a disaster, remember? Too big for the living room. Don't remind me! I kept tripping over it. This year, definitely a smaller one. Maybe a six-footer? Although, I did see a lovely pre-lit one at B&Q last week. Bit pricey, though. Pre-lit is good. Less faff. Though, admit it, half the fun  is  the faff. And untangling the lights. It's a tradition! A tradition I could happily live without, thank you very much. My back aches just thinking about it. How's work going, by the way? Still beating those deadlines? Yeah, it's… hectic. They’ve given me the new ‘Eco-Friendly Living’ campaign. It's a big one, loads of social media content, blog posts, the whole shebang. It’s interesting, but demanding. Trying to make washing-up liquid sound revolutionary is harder than you think. I can imagine! It all sounds very… clever. Still, make sure you’re taking breaks, love. Remember what happened last time you burned the candle at both ends? The nosebleeds weren’t pretty. I know, I know. Mum always looks after me. Actually, Liam wants to take me to that German Christmas market in London next month. Have you ever been? He's really keen, says it’s amazing. Oh, lovely! I haven’t been for years. Not since… well, not since your father and I went on that trip to Germany. Berlin, it was. Fascinating place, full of history. We went to Checkpoint Charlie, you know. It was only a few years after the Wall came down. Really? Wow. You hardly ever talk about that trip. It was a long time ago. And a bit…heavy, in places. Learning about everything that happened, during the war, and after. The resilience of the people, though. That was something. Liam’s really into history, isn’t he? He is, yeah. He's been reading a lot about the Weimar Republic lately, actually. Driving me mad with the facts! Says it's the key to understanding a lot of modern political divisions.

Right, so… this is officially a disaster zone, isn’t it? Boxes everywhere. I swear I packed strategically, but it just looks like chaos unleashed. It’s not  that  bad, Liam. It’s a new flat! It’s supposed to look a bit chaotic for the first day. Besides, it’s a really lovely flat. So much brighter than your old place. And look, proper floorboards! Proper floorboards that are probably full of dust mites. Honestly, I’m already regretting agreeing to move to Sussex. Bedford was… predictable. Predictably beige. Come on, you needed a change! And I’m here to help, remember? Okay, mugs are done. What's next on the ‘urgent needs’ list? Internet, I presume? I can handle that if you like. I’m pretty good at arguing with broadband companies. You’re a lifesaver. Honestly. I tried calling them earlier and got put on hold to a looped recording of panpipe music. It was aggressively relaxing. Yes, internet is priority number one. Then maybe figuring out the rubbish collection? I didn’t see anything about it in the tenancy agreement. I’ll tackle the internet. Rubbish… hmm. There should be bins around the back, I noticed when we were unloading. I’ll have a proper look after this mug situation is sorted. Did you manage to get the banking sorted? Switching over your address and all that? No, that’s on the ‘tomorrow’ list. I figured I’d deal with it after battling the internet demon. It feels… adult, doesn’t it? Suddenly having to worry about council tax and bin days. Very adult. Although, thinking about adult things, we definitely need to get some food in. I’m starving. I had a granola bar at 7 this morning and that was it. Good point. There’s a little supermarket just down the road, I scouted it out yesterday. We could walk there later? They might even have some decent seasonal produce. I saw some lovely looking plums in the window. Plums sound amazing. Actually, maybe we should plan a proper grocery shop for tomorrow? Stock up on essentials. And things to  make  things. Like actual meals. That’s a terrifying thought. My cooking skills peak at scrambled eggs. Oh, come on. We can learn together! I’m not exactly a culinary genius myself, but I can follow a recipe. Although, speaking of essentials, did you remember to bring the…  thing ?

…and honestly, the carbonara was  criminal . Like, swimming in cream, barely any pancetta. You know I’m a purist, right? It needs to be a proper guanciale situation. Oh, Chloe, you and your food standards! Seriously though, Bills is usually pretty good. I went for the halloumi and roasted vegetable skewers – safe choice, I know. But it was decent. It’s just… really nice to actually  sit  somewhere that isn't my desk or the kitchen table, you know? Absolutely. This is exactly what I needed. University feels like a lifetime ago now. Remember that disastrous attempt at a ‘sophisticated’ dinner party in second year? The one where the pasta caught fire? Don’t even  remind  me! Priya still brings it up every Christmas. She says it smelled like burning rubber for a week. And Ben tried to put it out with sparkling water! Oh god, Ben. He just panicked. He’s still like that, actually. Still perpetually stressed about  something . Last I heard he was convinced his sourdough starter was sentient. Classic Ben. Seriously though, how are things with work? You’ve been a Project Co-ordinator for… what, nearly a year now? Is it as terrifying as you thought it would be? Terrifying is a strong word. Organised chaos, maybe? It’s… busy. A lot of spreadsheets, a lot of emails, a lot of convincing people that deadlines are actually important. But it’s good. It’s challenging. It’s a million miles away from writing essays about Victorian literature, which is, frankly, a relief. What about you? How’s the placement going? Still at the marketing firm? Yeah, still there. It's… okay. It’s definitely given me a much clearer idea of what I  don’t  want to do, which is something, I guess. It’s a lot of social media scheduling and data analysis, which isn’t exactly inspiring. But the people are nice, and I'm learning a lot about the industry, I suppose. I'm starting to think I might want to go down the creative route, actually. Maybe something in content creation. That suits you! You were always brilliant at storytelling. Remember that short film we made for the film society? It was wonderfully weird. Oh, ‘The Existential Teapot’! That was a masterpiece. Pure genius. Mostly thanks to your editing skills, though. I just ran around screaming on camera. It needed the screaming!

…and honestly, the traffic getting  out  of Cambridge this morning was a nightmare. Felt like I was going to be late for ages, even though I left with what I thought was plenty of time. You wouldn't get that in Sunderland, you know? Everything’s just…closer. You and your Sunderland. You make it sound like some idyllic, traffic-free paradise. Last time I visited your mam, getting to her house from the station felt like a proper expedition. All those roundabouts! Aye, well, our roundabouts are  efficient . It’s just Birmingham drivers wouldn't understand the subtle art of yielding without causing complete chaos. No offence. None taken. Birmingham drivers are a breed apart, that’s true. Though I think Cambridge is giving it a run for its money on the congestion front. So, how was the meeting anyway? Still battling with getting the funding sorted for the new project? Ugh, don't even get me started. It’s like pulling teeth. Professor Davies is being incredibly difficult. He wants a much more…detailed methodology. As if I haven't already spent the last six months outlining every single step! It’s research, not building a Lego set. Sounds stressful. Is it the actual research he’s questioning, or is he just being a bit of a gatekeeper? Some of them enjoy that power dynamic, you know. Honestly? I think it’s a bit of both. He likes being seen as the ‘big brain’ and he’s worried the project won't deliver ‘significant’ results. Like anything that doesn’t immediately cure cancer isn’t worth doing. Classic. PhD life prepared me for a lifetime of justifying my existence to people who haven’t read a single paper. Speaking of which, mine's going…slowly. Really slowly. I keep getting stuck on this one particular algorithm. It feels like every time I fix one error, three more pop up. Oh, that’s the worst. The endless cycle of debugging. You need a distraction. Fancy going to that new vintage shop I saw on Mill Road tomorrow? They apparently have a massive collection of 90s stuff. 90s? You know I can’t resist a good 90s throwback. Although, I’m not sure my wardrobe can handle any more oversized denim jackets. I’m trying to cultivate a slightly more…sophisticated look. Sophisticated? You? Come on, admit it, you secretly love a bit of Britpop fashion.

Right, Gran, you won’t  believe  what Mr. Harrison was going on about in Politics today. Honestly, the man's a walking headline. Oh, aye? Mr. Harrison, is it? Still spoutin’ off then? He always did have a big mouth for a small man. What’s got ‘im riled up this time? Something about that lot in Westminster, I wager. You got it in one. He was going  on  about the new tax rises. Said it’s all the young people fault, spendin’ all our money on TikTok and…and avocado toast, apparently. Can you believe it? Avocado toast! Like  that’s  breakin' the bank. Avocado toast, eh? Bless 'im. They always need someone to blame, don’t they? In my day, it was long hair and rock ‘n’ roll. Before that, it was flappers and jazz. Always somethin'. Tax rises are a bother, mind. Everything's goin' up. Pension barely stretches these days. He was sayin’ it’s Labour’s fault, said they'll ruin the country if they get in. Proper Conservative stuff. But like, half the class reckon he's just repeating what he reads on Facebook. Facebook! . That's a dangerous place for proper information, lad. My Elsie – that's my daughter, your mum – she's always tellin' me about all the nonsense on there. People believin’ anything and everything. Now, I’ve always voted Labour, you know. My dad was a miner, down the pit at Evenwood. Labour was  the  party for workin’ folk. Mum says the same, about Dad always votin' Labour. But Mr. Harrison says Labour always spends too much money, and doesn't know how to manage the economy. He was goin' on about nationalisation too, like that's some terrible thing. Nationalisation… well, there's two sides to every coin, that. When they nationalised the railways, back in '48, it was a good thing. Proper service, decent prices. Before that, it was all about the profit, and the lines were fallin’ into disrepair. But then, they messed things up later on, didn’t they? It’s never simple, is it? Exactly! It's like, no one just agrees on anything anymore. It’s just… shoutin’ at each other. And then everyone gets all worked up. Even the teachers try to avoid talkin' about it in class, 'cause it just ends up in an argument. They’re sensible, those teachers. Best to keep things calm.

Now, Liam, love, elbows off the table, alright? It's grand to see you enjoying yer dinner, but we don’t want ye knockin’ over the gravy boat, do we? But it’s  comfortable  like this, Dad. And the gravy boat's, like, really far away. He's just growing, isn’t he? All limbs and angles. Though your Da is right, pet. It’s just polite. Think of Granny here, watching you. Wouldn’t want to make a bad impression, would you? Och, don't mind me, dear. I've seen worse manners in a classroom full of seven-year-olds! Though it  is  good to have a bit of decorum, even at your age, young man. It shows respect. Respect for gravy? No, respect for everyone at the table, Liam. And for the person who  made  the gravy, which, might I add, is mighty fine today, thanks to your mother. Thank you, love. It’s nice to actually sit down together as a family. It doesn’t happen often enough, does it? Everything's so rushed these days. Tell me about it. Work's been mad, deadlines creepin’ up on me like sneaky little goblins. But nights like this… these are important. Especially with your mother taking a break. Speaking of which, did yer wee one, Rosie, behave herself today? Mostly. She had a bit of a meltdown over a purple crayon, naturally. But Granny stepped in. Absolute lifesaver, she is. A Granny’s job is  never  done, is it? Though I do enjoy spending time with Rosie. She’s got a wee sparkle in her eye, that one. Reminds me of her grandfather. Was Grandad mischievous? Mischievous? Oh, he was a terror! A lovely terror, mind you. Always up to something. He could charm the birds out of the trees, he could. And he  loved  a good story. I used to tell him tales of the craziest things my pupils got up to. He’d roar with laughter. He’d have loved to see you now, Liam, all grown up. He always said young people today were a smart bunch. Did he know about computers and stuff? Not exactly. He reckoned the best computer was a good book and a sharp mind. But he was always curious. He’d ask me all sorts of questions about what I did. Speaking of curious things, did anyone see the news about the blood moon tonight?

…and honestly, the whole thing with the Scottish referendum all those years ago, it still rankles. All that energy, all that debate… and for what? Seems like a lot of fuss for another vote looming, doesn’t it? I mean, haven't they got more pressing things to worry about? Like, you know, the state of the NHS? Aye, you’ve a point, Arthur. A lot of hot air, wasn’t it? Though, I always understood wanting a bit more autonomy. We South Coast lot, we’ve always felt a bit… overlooked, haven’t we? Stuck between London and everything else. Doesn't mean I wanted to break away, mind you. Too much fuss. Too much uncertainty. Overlooked is putting it mildly, Derek! Brighton’s practically another planet to those Londoners. Anyway, enough about politics. How did the interview go with young Thomas? The one for the marketing position at that tech firm? Oh, that. Well, it was… an experience. He seemed to think he was interviewing  them  more than they were interviewing him. Lots of questions about company culture, work-life balance, mindfulness workshops. I mean, good questions to  ask , but after ten minutes of that, he hadn’t actually said anything about his qualifications! Sounds like your Thomas. Always had a knack for turning the tables. Remember when he tried to negotiate with Mrs. Higgins about extra biscuits with his tea when he was eight? Oh, don’t remind me! She was not amused. No, this was different. It felt… entitled. I told him afterwards, ‘Thomas, you’ve got to sell yourself. They need to know what  you  can do for  them , not the other way around.’ I’m not sure it sunk in. These youngsters, eh? Different breed. Speaking of youngsters, how’s Eleanor doing? Still enjoying her time volunteering at the animal shelter? She loves it. Absolutely adores it. Says it’s the most fulfilling thing she's done in ages. She’s got a real knack with the nervous dogs, apparently. Spends hours just sitting with them, quietly reading. It's lovely to see her so content. Makes a change from the drama with her ex, at least. Good. Glad to hear that. That relationship was… well, it was a bit of a mess, wasn't it? She's much better off without him. Actually, reminds me of old Graham at the school. Absolute nightmare. Graham?

Right, so I’ve been lookin’ at student accommodation for September. It’s… eye watering, innit? Like, genuinely. A room in a shared house near campus is more than my rent here, and that’s sayin’ somethin’. Oh, love, don’t get yourself stressed already. It always  seems  worse when you’re just lookin’. There’s always deals to be had, and you’ve got time yet. Your Dad’s got a mate who works at the council, hasn’t he? Maybe he knows of somethin’. Might do. Old Barry. He’s a bit of a gossip, that one. Though mostly about the allotments. Still, worth askin’. Though frankly, I’m more worried about the tuition fees. They just keep goin’ up and up. Feels like robbin’ Peter to pay Paul, does it? It  is  ridiculous, honestly. The whole system's designed to keep people in debt for decades. I mean, I'm lucky, I've got a scholarship, but even so... It's a proper weight, you know? Exactly! And the ‘experience’ they bang on about? Half of it's just tryin’ to afford beans on toast. Speaking of food, you two had lunch yet? I'm starvin'. This move is makin’ me peckish. I had a little sandwich before we left, but I could manage somethin’ more substantial. Your Dad insisted on gettin’ us all those biscuits though, didn’t he? Figured we’d need sustenance for the journey. Someone’s gotta keep your strength up. And they’re nice biscuits, Digestives. Can’t go wrong with a Digestive. Besides, you two were moanin’ about bein’ tired after all that box liftin’. They  are  good biscuits, I'll give ya that. But a proper lunch… maybe a pub on the way? Somewhere with a decent Ploughman's? That sounds amazing, actually. This is a pretty route, isn't it? We don’t often get out this way. Are we near St. Neots, Ann? You were born around here, right? Just past it. Used to be lovely countryside all around here. Though they're building houses everywhere now, aren't they? It changes so fast. I remember when the only supermarket was a tiny Co-op. Now it's a huge Tesco! Everything's a supermarket these days. Used to be proper butchers and bakers, proper shops with personalities. Now it’s all… corporate. It's a shame, yeah.

Right, are we all comfy? Grandad, you’ve got your blanket, haven’t you? Don’t want you getting a chill even with the heating on. Aye, lass, I'm reet. Plenty warm enough. Though this newfangled heating… it’s not like a good coal fire, is it? No smell. No  character . You and your coal fires, Grandad. You’d heat a palace with one if you could. He would! Honestly, last winter he was near lecturing the neighbours about their gas central heating. Anyway, how  are  you feeling, Grandad? Not too travel-sick, are you? This A-road’s a bit bumpy in places. Nah, not at all. Used to worse in the war, you know. Spending hours in the back of a lorry… Now  that  was bumpy. And smelled of petrol. This is luxury. Though, I must say, you drive a bit fast for my liking, Sarah. Slow down a bit, eh? I  am  doing the speed limit, Grandad! Honestly! It’s 60 on this stretch, and I’m at 58. I’m a conscientious driver, you know. She is, Grandad. She's always careful. You worry too much. A man’s allowed to worry, isn’t he? Especially when a granddaughter's whisking him off to see sheep. Sheep! I haven't been near a sheep since… well, since your grandmother and I used to go courting up in the Peak District. That sounds lovely! We should do that again, maybe? Although, maybe not  courting  - that’s a bit past it now! We're just going to see Farmer Giles' new lambs, remember? He promised me I could get some photos for the corpus. Tiny little things they are, apparently. The corpus needs photos of lambs? It’s for a project I'm working on. Linguistic variation in animal names. Apparently, different regions have totally different words for lambs. Like, some places call them "hoggets" and I had no clue! It’s fascinating. Hoggets? Aye, we called ’em hoggets back home. A good, strong word. “Lamb” sounds a bit…soft, doesn’t it? These modern words. Everything's got to be simplified. It’s interesting how language changes. I mean, I grew up with 'lamb,' but even I've heard 'hogget' occasionally. It feels…older, definitely. More rural. Exactly! And that’s what the project’s about. Preserving those older terms. It’s really sad when words disappear.

Honestly, I don't know  why  I bother with these parsnips. Nobody ever touches them. They just sit there, looking all… orange. Oh, don't say that, Mary. I might have one later. I'm pretty full from that Yorkshire pudding, though. You've outdone yourself, as always. It’s wonderful being able to just…  be  here, you know? Away from the blinking cursor and endless audio. Aye, it is good. Proper food, proper company. Beats staring at spreadsheets about North Sea pipelines any day of the week. Though, I sometimes miss the sheer… complexity of it all. This is simpler, thankfully. And tastier. You and your pipelines, David. You’d find complexity in a bowl of custard if you put your mind to it. Speaking of complex, how’s young Leo doing with his GCSEs? Have you heard anything from his mother? She texted earlier. He’s… stressed. History is the big worry. He says his teacher, Mr. Harrison, just  reads  from the textbook. No stories, no context, just droning on. Apparently, half the class are struggling. Oh dear. A dreadful teacher can ruin a child’s love of a subject. I remember Miss O’Malley, back in primary school. God rest her soul, she was a saint, but her maths lessons were… let’s just say they weren’t known for their dynamism. I think I actively  blocked  most of it out. Sounds like my experience with French. Monsieur Dubois. Beloved by some, feared by most. He’d slam the desks if you mispronounced a single syllable. It put me off languages for life. It's crazy how much influence teachers have. Leo’s always been good at history, he loves documentaries, but this… it’s making him anxious. I told him to talk to Mr. Harrison, but he’s shy. A good idea, but easier said than done with some teenagers. Perhaps a quick word with the Head of Department? Sometimes a gentle suggestion can work wonders. I always found a polite but firm letter was the best approach. Though, that was in the days  before  emails and constant communication. It feels like everything is instant now. Instant, and expected. No one has any patience anymore. Remember old Mrs. Higgins down the street? She was always late for everything, church, bingo… everything! But she always had a good reason, and people were kind about it. Now, five minutes late and you're getting texts.

Right, so, Mrs. Davies said the same thing as Mr. Harrison. You’re… enthusiastic in class, Leo. Very enthusiastic. And Elsie, you’re a little quiet, still. Though apparently, you did a  fantastic  drawing of a badger last week. A very fluffy badger. With stripes. But I  am  enthusiastic! I just… I like to ask questions! And explain things! To everyone! I know, darling. And that’s lovely. But Mrs. Davies said it sometimes means other children don’t get a chance to answer. It’s about letting everyone have a go. Oh. Like sharing? A bit like sharing. Sharing the talking. Now, eat your shepherd’s pie. It’s getting cold. And Elsie, just a few more peas, please. It’s yummy, Mummy. But I want to be Matilda when I dress up for World Book Day. I’m going to be… Atticus Finch! From  To Kill a Mockingbird ! Atticus Finch? Where did  that  come from? I read some of the book. It’s about being fair. And a lawyer! And he’s really clever. Very good choice, Leo. A bit ambitious for Year 4, but excellent nonetheless. Elsie, Matilda is wonderful. You’d make a brilliant Matilda. She's rather… determined. I  am  determined! Especially when I want chocolate. That’s true. Right, back to parent’s evening. Maths is… a concern. For both of you, actually. Though in different ways. Elsie, it’s more confidence. You know the answers, but you don’t always put your hand up. And me? And you… well, you rush. You get the right answer  eventually , but you don’t always show your workings, and you make silly mistakes because you’re so eager to get to the next problem. It's about slowing down, Leo. But it’s  boring  showing your workings! I know it feels that way. But it helps you check your answers. And it helps your teachers understand where you might be going wrong. We need to work on that. Maybe some extra practice with Miss Jones after school? Ugh. But I have circus club on Thursdays! We can rearrange it. Or maybe Tuesdays? They’re starting aerial silks, you know. You were so excited about that. Ooh, aerial silks! Can I try them too? Perhaps when you’re a bit older, darling. It takes a lot of strength. Speaking of after school, I need to confirm with Auntie Carol if she can pick you both up on Wednesday.

Ah, Jaysus, will ya look at little Mikey down the road? Old Man Hemmings has him working in that curtain shop now, of all places. A lad of eight! Though, to be fair, Hemmings isn’t exactly running a sweatshop, is he? Still, seems a bit…much. It  is  a bit much, isn’t it? And Hemmings always did favour the little ones. Though Mikey’s a bright spark, he should be playing football, not measuring drapes. Speaking of bright sparks… Oisin’s been on a one-man show all afternoon. "Dadda, look, big truck! Mummy, juice now!" It's utterly relentless. Juice! Juice! Och, that’s just them at that age, dear. Pure force of nature. Reminds me of wee Hamish when he was learning to speak. Used to demand ‘More biscuit!’ with the authority of a headmaster. He's a character alright. Though sometimes I swear he’s already negotiating. Tried to barter a biscuit for ten minutes of screen time earlier. Ten minutes! He’s learning all the tricks. Right, about his birthday… Are we still on for the bouncy castle at the hall? We are, but I'm starting to panic about numbers. Everyone and their mother seems to want to come. I sent out invites to thirty kids and I reckon we'll get at least thirty-five, plus all the adults. Are you sure the hall is big enough? The hall’s grand. Plenty of space. It’s more the logistics of keeping track of them all that worries me. I was thinking maybe we could get one of those students from UCC to lend a hand? They do volunteering, don’t they? I know a fella in IT there. Could pull some strings. That's a good idea, dear. Two adults for every five children is a good rule of thumb. You'll need all the help you can get. They're like little whirlwinds, those ones. That would be brilliant, actually. It's just… organising everything feels overwhelming. And then there’s the cake. Auntie Maureen volunteered, which is lovely, but…her floral decorating skills are…enthusiastic. Last year's cake looked like a particularly aggressive garden. Oh now, Maureen's heart is in the right place. We can subtly steer her towards a simpler design, eh? Maybe a plain chocolate one with a digger on top. Oisin’s obsessed with diggers at the moment.

…and then me mam, she goes, “Aye, but is it  actually  a palindrome if you ignore the spaces and punctuation?” Honestly, she’d ruin Scrabble for charity, she would. It's supposed to be a bit of fun, you know? Your mam sounds… thorough. My own attempts at linguistic pedantry are usually reserved for work, thankfully. Though, actually, she has a point about punctuation in palindromes. Technically, “A man, a plan, a canal: Panama” really relies on a generous interpretation. Generous is an understatement. It's a classic, but it feels like cheating a bit. We were having this debate at the lab actually, about whether you can count capitalization in a palindrome. Someone was trying to argue 'Racecar' and 'racecar' are  different  palindromes. Oh, don’t even  start  me. That’s just… needlessly complicated. It's the  concept  of reading the same backwards and forwards, innit? Not the specific formatting. It’s like arguing about whether a cat’s still a cat if you give it a hat. A philosophical feline conundrum. But I see your point. It’s the underlying structure, the symmetry. Which, now that I think about it, relates beautifully to some of the algorithms I'm working on. Mirroring data structures… Right, clever clogs. Don't go bringing your engineering stuff into our word games. We’re here to relax, not dissect the fundamental principles of reverse engineering! Speaking of games, anyone fancy a quick round of Twenty Questions? Actually, I’ve been meaning to ask you both about something a bit different. I was reading about lipograms the other day - writing something deliberately  excluding  a certain letter. A… what now? A lipo-… thingy? That sounds difficult. A lipogram. L-I-P-O-G-R-A-M. It’s a stylistic constraint. Like, trying to write a whole paragraph without using the letter ‘e’. Now  that  is a challenge. Though, I suppose it’s a good exercise in forcing you to be creative with your vocabulary. Avoiding common letters like ‘e’, ‘t’, or ‘a’ must truly test your linguistic agility. Sounds like a right headache, to be honest. I can barely spell ‘accommodation’ right on a good day, let alone write a whole chunk of text avoiding a vital vowel. Is there a point to it, other than making life hard? Well, historically, it’s been used as a form of protest, or to make a stylistic statement.

Right, that’s  better . Proper job. Honestly, I think I actually fell asleep on the bus coming back from uni today. Like, full-on head-bobbing, almost drooled-on-the-window sleep. Mortifying. No way! You? Miss ‘Always-On-The-Go’ Amelia? Actually napping in public? Should’ve got a picture. Think of the blackmail material. Don't you  dare . It was exhaustion, okay? Dissertation stress is a real thing. And that lecture on post-structuralism this morning… I swear, Professor Davies actively tries to induce sleep. He's a lovely bloke, but his voice is a weapon. Post-structuralism, eh? Sounds… thrilling. I’m stuck neck-deep in stats for my project. Numbers just swim around like confused goldfish. I'd trade places with you and your sleepy lectures any day. Don't complain too much, you chose Engineering! You knew there'd be maths involved. Speaking of confused, have you seen what Liam’s been posting on Instagram? Another picture of him “grinding” at the gym. Honestly, it’s getting a bit much. Oh, Liam. The man’s entire personality is now based around protein shakes and bicep curls. Remember when he used to be obsessed with obscure indie bands? What happened to that? Good question! I think he discovered weights and suddenly forgot everything else. We need to stage an intervention. Force-feed him a Joy Division album. I’m in. Maybe we could dig out those old photos from sixth form? The ones where he’s got that awful gelled hair and is wearing a band t-shirt three sizes too big? Oh my god, yes! And the one of you trying to skateboard and faceplanting into Mrs. Peterson’s flowerbeds? That was gold. I think I still have it somewhere… on a floppy disk, probably. Floppy disk?! You're showing your age now. Honestly, you've no right to call  me  old. I bet your mum's got those photos printed and framed. She loves embarrassing you. Don’t even go there. Mum’s been on a mission to show off my baby pictures to anyone who'll stand still. She cornered old Mr. Henderson from next door last week and made him look through the entire album. He looked thoroughly traumatised. Classic. She  lives  for that. Remember that time she tried to set you up with her friend’s grandson? The one who collected porcelain dolls?

Honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Old Man Hemmings. He actually suggested our extension would ‘ruin the character of the street’. Ruin it! It’s a semi-detached, all the houses have extensions now, it's practically a requirement for family living in this area! Hemmings is Hemmings. He complained when Ms. Davies painted her front door blue, remember? Said it wasn't 'in keeping'. He’s a professional objector. Did you get a chance to look over the updated plans I printed out last night? The ones with the visualisations? Briefly. I glanced. I was too busy drafting a strongly worded response to his initial objection. Something about ‘preserving architectural integrity’ while simultaneously having a PVC conservatory bolted onto the back of  his  house. The hypocrisy! But the plans… they looked good, didn't they? You did a good job with the rendering. It genuinely looks less imposing now with the pitched roof matching the neighbours’. Thanks. I spent a fair bit of time on it. I thought softening the visual impact was key. And shrinking the patio slightly. Hopefully, that addresses some of Mrs. Peterson’s concerns about losing her sunlight. She’s a bit of a sun worshipper, isn’t she? She is. And perpetually gardening, which frankly, I admire. But yes, good thinking on the patio. It’s the planning committee meeting next Tuesday, isn't it? I’m still dreading it. I know it’s probably irrational, but I get so nervous speaking in public, especially when it feels like you're defending something so… personal. You’ll be brilliant. You always are. Remember the university budget cuts presentation? You eviscerated Professor Davies’ arguments with just a few well-placed facts. This is Hemmings and Peterson, not academic titans. And I'll be there, backing you up. We've rehearsed, we’ve got all the documentation prepped. It's just a formality, honestly. Easy for you to say! You thrive on that stuff. You  enjoy  a good debate. I just want to get this approved and move on with it. Think of the extra space! The playroom for Leo… a proper guest room. We’ve been talking about this for ages. Exactly! And it’ll add value to the house. Which, let's be honest, is also a consideration. Have we finalised the list of things we’re taking to the antiques valuation tomorrow? Old Mrs. Higgins said she’s expecting a good turnout.

Honestly, this day has been  monumental  in its awfulness. Mr. Henderson tried to ‘suggest’ I re-prioritise the entire marketing schedule…again. As if I haven’t got enough on my plate already. Oh,  him . Still trying to micromanage everyone, is he? You'd think after six months he’d realise you know what you’re doing. Did you tell him to politely… well, you know? I bit my tongue so hard I nearly drew blood. I just said, “I’ve already factored that into the timeline, Mr. Henderson,” in my most sweetly condescending voice. It  almost  worked. He then proceeded to explain the timeline  back  to me. Men. Honestly. Speaking of which, how’s that date with… what was his name? Liam? The one you met at Sarah’s birthday? Oh, Liam. Disaster. Absolute disaster. He spent the entire evening talking about his miniature train set. A  fully functioning  miniature train set. Apparently, it’s his ‘passion project.’ No! Seriously? A train set? That’s… a choice. A horrible choice! And he kept trying to show me pictures on his phone. Close-up pictures of the engines! I made up a sudden emergency phone call from my ‘ailing aunt’ after the main course. It felt brutal, but necessary. You’re ruthless, I love it. Though, perhaps you need to broaden your dating pool slightly. Maybe avoid guys who willingly advertise their hobbies involving tiny locomotives. Don’t even. It's exhausting. I think I'm just destined to be a crazy cat lady. Have you seen old Mrs. Gable next door again? She was trying to ‘advise’ me on the best way to prune my roses. Like I asked for her opinion. Oh,  her . She’s a constant source of amusement, isn’t she? She thinks she’s Capability Brown. I saw her shouting at a squirrel the other day for ‘disrespecting her petunias.’ It’s genuinely bizarre. Anyway, enough complaining about work and neighbours. How was your shift? Anything exciting happen on the ward? Relatively calm, thankfully. We had a new patient admit, a young lad struggling with anxiety. It's heartbreaking, honestly. But rewarding when you can see them starting to cope. We had a lovely art therapy session this afternoon, actually. Someone painted a brilliant sunflower. That sounds… grounding. It’s nice to hear something positive. I need some grounding. Fancy doing something this weekend? We haven't done a proper day out in ages.

Right, so I'm thinkin', next weekend, car boot sale? Me nan’s been decluttering again, says she’s got boxes of stuff she wants rid of. Proper gold dust, apparently. Might be able to fund that weekend away we were talkin’ about. Ooh, yeah, that’d be good. Though, honestly, car boot sales are…intense. Remember last time? That bloke practically  wrestled  me for a chipped teapot? And the smell of old dust… Aye, that was a belter. Old Mr. Henderson, weren't it? He reckoned it was antique. Turned out it was from Home Bargains, ten years ago. Still, good fun. Better than watchin' all this…penguin poshness. D’you ever wonder who decides what gets advertised during these things? It’s always luxury holidays or fancy cars. Who’s watchin’ a penguin documentary and thinkin’, “Right, I need a new Range Rover”? It’s all about target audience, isn’t it? They’re layering the ads. People who watch nature documentaries are probably considered…affluent, environmentally conscious, maybe. So they hit ‘em with the ethical car ads, or holidays that boast ‘sustainable tourism’. It's manipulative. Like that one for the diet pills that came on earlier. Honestly, the lengths they go to… Proper awful, those adverts. Makes ya feel dead bad, like yer not good enough as ya are. Speaking of feelin’ bad, I saw Mrs. Davies down the street today. She’s tryin’ one of them juice cleanses again. Said she felt “nourished but miserable”. Oh, poor woman. She’s been doing those for years. It’s the cycle of dieting, isn’t it? Promise of quick results, miserable implementation, then back to square one. I was reading a paper on cognitive biases the other day – all about how easily we fall for stuff like that. It's linked to NLP actually, how advertising uses anchors and framing to influence behaviour. NLP, eh? You and yer brain stuff. You always manage to turn everything back to psychology. I swear, you look at a biscuit and analyze its subconscious implications. It’s a hazard of the job! Though, seriously, it's fascinating. And it explains so much about why people do the things they do. It also explains why I spend so much time online shopping, probably. Targeted ads everywhere… it's designed to be addictive. Tell me about it. I fell for the noise cancellin' headphones last week.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of emails I get now, just asking for grammar checks on student essays. It's relentless! I love teaching, I really do, but sometimes I feel like a walking, talking style guide. Tell me about it. My inbox is a battlefield of project updates, budget requests, and vaguely worded demands from upper management. At least yours is…intellectually stimulating? You’re lucky you get vaguely worded demands. I get demands phrased entirely in corporate jargon. “Synergise the content deliverables to maximise audience engagement.” Honestly, I spend half my day translating what my boss  means . Oh god, the jargon. It’s a plague. I had a PR person try to explain a campaign to me using the word "disruptive" approximately seventeen times. I nearly walked out. Though, to be fair, the campaign  was  disastrous. You lot sound like my Tuesday. I was interviewing this amazing folk musician for a piece, proper authentic stuff, then my producer calls wanting me to “inject some digital sparkle.” Digital sparkle! What does that even  mean  for a banjo player? It means they want TikToks, doesn’t it? Everything is TikTok now. Even… Shakespeare. I saw a production advertised with the tag line "Shakespeare, but make it relatable." Oh, please no. That’s… sacrilege. Though, I did download one of those language learning apps recently. Duolingo, I think? Just to try and brush up on my rusty Spanish before the holiday. It's oddly addictive. The little green owl guilt-trips you into practicing. Duolingo is brilliant, isn't it? Properly gamified. I tried Babbel for German, but it felt a bit…stodgy in comparison. Speaking of apps, has anyone tried that 'BeReal' thing? Oh, BeReal. The one where you get a random notification and have two minutes to take a photo? It feels… performatively authentic. Like, “look how normal my life is!” It stressed me out. I deleted it after a day. I get it. It’s exhausting trying to capture ‘real life’ on a timer. I’d rather just...live it. Though, speaking of capturing things, I’ve been trying to get back into writing fiction. It’s been years. Ooh, that’s fantastic! What are you working on? Just a short story, really. Trying to recapture that spark, you know? It’s harder than I remembered. I keep getting bogged down in world-building instead of just…writing. That’s always the way.

…and honestly, the whole estate was mud. Just churned mud, everywhere. We moved in ‘63, you see, after I’d finished my training at Rolle College in Plymouth. Almondsbury hadn’t really  happened  yet. Everything was fields, practically. Did either of you find it quite a shock coming here, settling in? A bit, yes. Though Ramsgate wasn’t exactly a metropolis either, mind you. But Bristol…it felt bigger. I came for an interview at what was then Clifton College in ‘66. Dreadful journey, honestly. Train was packed, and the signalmen were on strike, I think. Took me nearly six hours! Six hours? You were lucky! I came up in ‘62 to interview for a position at the hospital. Lovely hospital, still is, but finding somewhere to live was a nightmare. They showed me a little flat near Cotham Hill. Tiny! And damp. Apparently, it had been bombed in the war and ‘patched up’. Patched up is putting it mildly. It was like living in a biscuit tin. Oh, Cotham Hill. I remember that area. I was at Manchester University, and came down here in ’64 to take up a lectureship at the Poly. Had the same problem, though. Everything was either terribly expensive, or, well…not terribly desirable. Ended up renting a room in Bishopston for ages. A bit bohemian, Bishopston was then. Lots of artists and…interesting characters. I ended up in Redland. Found a little terraced house on Elgin Park. It wasn’t much, but it was ours, eventually. Mortgage rates were horrifying, of course. 13% I think it peaked at. Still, better than paying rent. We eventually bought in Patchway. It was…new. One of those post-war estates. All identical. But affordable! And a garden, which was vital. I couldn’t bear the thought of not having a garden. Though getting the roses to grow in that clay was a battle. What about you, David? You and Margaret found something quickly, didn't you? Relatively. Margaret’s father was a builder, fortunately. He’d picked up a plot of land in Bournville, and we managed to get a house built. Modern, you know. No character, but very practical. And a proper garden. Though, thinking back, the plumbing was questionable for years. We met, you know, at a dental conference in Bournemouth. Terribly cliche, I suppose. All those gleaming white teeth. A dental convention! That  is  a cliché.

…and honestly, darling, that little table? Found it at a car boot sale near Glastonbury, all covered in dust. Nearly didn’t bother, but something about the carving…it whispered to me, you know? Spent a good week cleaning it up, though. The things people just  discard . It’s lovely, Marion. You have a real eye for these things. It does look like it has a story to tell. My husband, bless him, never understood the appeal of ‘old junk’ as he called it. He was a very…practical man. An engineer. Everything had to  work . Oh, engineers! Bless ‘em, too. My brother was one. Built bridges, he did. Said it was all about physics and logic. Never could grasp a brushstroke, poor thing. Though he did try to commission a portrait of his boat once... disastrous. Absolutely disastrous. I can imagine! It's funny how we all have our strengths. I spent my life helping people  find  their voices, really. Speech therapy. A very different kind of building, I suppose – building communication. That sounds…rewarding. More useful than painting landscapes, perhaps? Though I always argued art  is  useful. It feeds the soul, don’t you think? Oh, absolutely. I wouldn’t diminish it for a moment. It’s just…sometimes you feel a more immediate impact. Seeing a child finally say their first word, or helping someone regain their speech after a stroke… those were very powerful moments. What made you decide to be an artist, Marion? Was it something you always knew you wanted to do? Oh, dear. Always. As a little thing, growing up in Well, Somerset, I used to spend hours sketching in the fields. Old Farmer Giles didn’t mind, as long as I didn't bother his sheep. Mum, she encouraged it. Not a terribly artistic soul herself, but she saw something in me, she did. My father… well, he was a bit…reserved. Thought it was a frivolous pursuit for a young lady. Wanted me to be a teacher, you see. Sensible. I grew up in Sydney, so it was a vastly different landscape. Lots of beach and sunshine. My mother, she was Scottish, very strict. Always pushing me towards…something respectable. She'd have hated the thought of me fiddling with paints. She wanted me to be a doctor. Respectable! That’s always the cry, isn’t it? What  is  respectable, anyway? I remember being sent to art school in Bath.

Right, so, this is officially the most ambitious shepherd's pie I’ve ever attempted. Like, proper layers, all the trimmings. You sure you’re alright to just… supervise? You're usually the culinary genius. Relax, Leo, it smells amazing already. Honestly, after a ten-hour shift surrounded by sugar and flour, the thought of active cooking is… traumatic. Besides, you know I'm a master of quality control. I’ll tell you if it needs more nutmeg. Nutmeg is  essential , don’t even joke. Speaking of essential things… I was thinking about getting another tattoo. Oh? Another one? Where are you thinking? Not on your face, surely. No, no face tattoos. I was thinking… maybe on my forearm, something small. I’ve been looking at constellations. Sagittarius, maybe? It feels…right, you know? That’s actually really nice. Subtle. Not like that dragon you almost got back in uni. Remember that phase? Don’t remind me! Thankfully, you talked me out of it. It would’ve been a disaster. Still regretting the eyebrow piercing though, that was a bad call. A  very  bad call. Anyway, how’s the dissertation going? Still wrestling with post-structuralism or have you finally slain the beast? Slowly but surely. It feels like it’s consuming my entire life. I swear, if I read another Derrida quote, I might scream. Oh! And speaking of consuming things... remember Mrs. Higgins from the bakery? She asked if I wanted to buy some discounted candy canes. Apparently, they're a bit wonky looking, but perfectly good. Candy canes already? It’s still November! People are getting a bit overzealous, aren’t they? But yeah, discounted candy canes... I could definitely use those for the Christmas display. I'm starting to plan it out. Thinking a sort of Victorian Christmas vibe this year. Hello, lovelies! Smells incredible in here. Shepherd’s pie? You two are spoiling me. Chloe! Perfect timing. We’re just plotting our Christmas domination. And I’m contemplating permanently marking my body with tiny stars. It’s been a productive evening. Stars sound lovely, Leo. Christmas domination, eh? What are we thinking? I’ve already started taking pre-orders for Christmas cakes at the café. It’s madness! I’m aiming for maximum festive cheer with the bakery. I want it to feel like stepping into a snow globe. I was thinking a huge Christmas tree, obviously, and loads of garlands.

Right, Cambridge is officially in the rear-view. Honestly, felt like I was living in a postcard for the last three years. A  very  stressful postcard, mind you. Stressful, you say? You always did thrive under pressure, Leo. More so than enjoying the beautiful scenery, it seemed. Did you at least manage a punt on the Cam before leaving? For the photos, if nothing else? Mum, please. Don’t remind me of the punting. Nearly ended up in Grantchester Meadows, honestly. And yeah, photos were taken. For…evidence. Look, the thesis is  finally  submitted. That’s the main thing. No more all-nighters in the library fuelled by lukewarm coffee and existential dread. Good, good. That's a weight off both our shoulders, I imagine. So, the big question… what  now ? You've been remarkably vague, deliberately so I suspect. You know you can't drift indefinitely, even if you  could  afford to. I’m not drifting! I’m… evaluating options. It’s a crucial stage of life, Mum, self-discovery and all that. Self-discovery usually involves a job, Leo. Or at least a plan approaching one. You didn’t mention anything about applying for anything during the term. I had a thesis to finish! And look, some of the professors were suggesting I consider a doctorate. It wouldn't be right away, obviously. A year out, maybe. To, you know, solidify things. A doctorate? Goodness. That's… serious. And expensive. Even with funding. Are you  sure  that's what you want, or is it just… the path of least resistance? Staying in academia feels safe, doesn’t it? It’s not about safe! It’s a genuine intellectual pursuit. I actually enjoy researching this stuff. It's not like I'm aiming to be a professor or anything, but… continuing the work, adding to the knowledge…it feels good. Hmm. I understand. Your grandfather would’ve approved, certainly. He always believed in the power of knowledge for its own sake. But let’s be realistic. Where would you  live  if you decided to pursue that? Cambridge is lovely, but it’s not exactly brimming with affordable accommodation. And coming back here… well, space is a bit tight as you know. That’s what I’ve been thinking about. It’s not just the course itself. It's everything else. I was looking at some flats in Leytonstone, actually. They’re… reasonably priced, and it’s on the Central Line, so pretty easy to get into town.

…and honestly, the train was  packed . I swear, everyone with a Cambridge connection decided to descend on the city this weekend. It took me nearly three hours from Aylesbury just to get to King’s Cross, and then another hour on the local line. Worth it though, isn’t it? Seeing the faculty again, even if it's just for a chat. Tell me about it! I drove down from Lincoln, thinking I was being clever avoiding the rail chaos. Ended up stuck in roadworks just outside Huntingdon for almost an hour. Cleverness spectacularly backfired. Still, it’s lovely to be back. Though I feel terribly underqualified suddenly, surrounded by all this… legal brainpower. Don’t we all, dear? Don’t we all. I find the feeling never quite goes away, even after forty years lecturing in this very building. Name’s Arthur Penhaligon, by the way. Archaeology, predominantly, though I’ve dabbled in a bit of linguistic history over the years. Oh, hello! I’m Elodie, and this is Maya. I’m a Language Research Coordinator, actually. It’s nice to meet you, Dr. Penhaligon. Archaeology sounds fascinating. Maya here. Research Administrator. And yes, it does! I always secretly wished I’d gone down that route instead of the more… administrative one. Digging things up sounds far more exciting than filling in forms. Exciting and infuriating in equal measure, my dear. I spent a summer excavating a small village site in Shropshire – near my birthplace, as it happens, Oswestry. We were convinced it was a Roman settlement, spent months carefully sifting through soil… turned out to be a rather substantial Anglo-Saxon one. Rewrites the whole local history, naturally. And the locals weren’t best pleased to have their neat Roman narrative disrupted! Oh, that's incredible! It’s amazing how much history is just…underneath our feet. You must come across the most interesting things. Do you find that language skills are particularly useful in archaeology? I mean, deciphering inscriptions and so on? Absolutely essential! Latin, of course, is foundational. But increasingly, understanding the development of regional dialects – the  vernacular  – is crucial. It can tell you so much about trade routes, migration patterns, even social structures. I was working on a project a few years ago looking at Arab influence in medieval Spain, and the linguistic connections were absolutely key. Tracking loanwords, analysing grammatical structures… revealing a far more complex cultural exchange than previously understood.

…So then, the bloke  actually  tried to pay with a five-pound note that was clearly a Monopoly one. Honestly, the audacity. You get all sorts at the student union bar, you know? Sounds about right. People are…optimistic, shall we say, when they've had a few. Beats dealing with a broken croissant machine at 3 AM though, believe me. That’s a whole different level of stress. Oh, don’t get me started on broken appliances. My milk steamer decided to pack it in mid-morning rush yesterday. Total chaos. Had to resort to frothing with a whisk! Customers were looking at me like I'd lost the plot. Whisking milk? Sounds artisanal. You could charge double for a 'hand-frothed latte'. Honestly, the things people will pay for these days… I was scrolling through TikTok earlier and there's this video of a guy reviewing  different types of water . Like, seriously? No way! Different types of water? Is he going full Gwyneth Paltrow on us? Oh, I saw that! Apparently, the mineral content and the source make a massive difference. I mean, I just drink tap water, seems to do the trick. It's amazing what goes viral, innit? It makes you think about what I could do on TikTok… maybe ‘Baking Fails of the Week’? I’ve got  plenty  of material. That could be good, actually. It's all about authenticity, isn't it? People are tired of perfection. Though, thinking about authenticity... I was reading an article about how the pressure to constantly 'brand' yourself as young people is ridiculous. Everyone needs a 'side hustle' and a perfectly curated Instagram. It  is  exhausting. I've been trying to get a documentary off the ground about exactly that – the performative nature of youth culture online. Funding's a nightmare, obviously. Everyone wants ‘content’, but nobody wants to pay for investigative stuff. It's all about shiny, fast things. Tell me about it. I’m just trying to finish my dissertation. It's on the socio-economic impact of streaming services on the music industry. Thrilling stuff, truly. My mum keeps asking when I’m going to get a ‘real’ job. She doesn't understand why a Masters degree doesn’t automatically translate into something… lucrative. Oh, mums. Mine’s been subtly suggesting I take over running the family hardware shop. Says baking’s ‘nice’ but ‘not a career’.

Honestly, this week has been…a lot. The students are particularly draining at the moment. It's not even the content, it’s just the  energy . So much entitlement. Tell me about it. Mine are obsessed with getting extensions for everything. “Grandma’s goldfish died,” “The wifi was down during essay writing hours,” it's endless. Though, I did have one genuinely heartbreaking story about a flatmate stealing someone’s dissertation research… that one actually warranted a bit of sympathy. Oh, that’s awful! But the goldfish? Really? It feels like they think we’re just here to tick boxes on their path to a first. And don’t even get me  started  on the marking. Mountains of it. It’s the joy of academia, isn’t it? Relentless assessment. Though, I'm starting to think about applying for that research grant we talked about. It would get me out of teaching for a bit, you know? Focus on something  I  actually want to do. That’s a fantastic idea, darling! You should definitely go for it. You’ve been talking about your work on the social mobility aspect of post-war housing for ages. It’s brilliant, you really should put your energy into it. How are the initial applications looking? Slow going, honestly. The form is monstrous. And because it’s related to social policy, it’s all interwoven with the current political climate. Which, frankly, is terrifying. Sunak's latest pronouncements on welfare… I mean, honestly, where do they come up with this stuff? It’s like they’re deliberately trying to make things worse. Don’t even. I saw that interview with him yesterday. Utterly tone-deaf. It’s all this performative ‘tough on benefits’ rhetoric, designed to appease the right wing. It's dehumanising, and it doesn't even address the  actual  reasons people need support. Exactly! They keep talking about ‘getting people back to work’ as if jobs are just… magically available. And the cost of childcare! It's a joke. No wonder people are stuck. Speaking of costs, have you looked at the energy bills again? I swear they jumped up another fifty quid this month. Don’t remind me. I had a mini-panic when I saw the direct debit go out. I’m trying to be sensible, turning everything off at the wall, shorter showers… but it feels like a drop in the ocean.

Honestly, this is lovely, ANON. You always did make the best sponge. Reminds me of my mother’s, though hers was always a bit…drier. She insisted on using self-raising flour even when it wasn't strictly necessary. Stubborn woman. It  is  good! You've really outdone yourself. Though I’m already feeling slightly guilty about the chocolate biscuit I snuck before lunch. Don’t tell Dad. Oh, he knows. He always knows. He’s got eyes in the back of his head, that one. Though I suspect he pretends not to notice just to keep the peace. You always were a little biscuit pilferer, weren’t you, Lizzie? Hey! I was a child! And it's a perfectly reasonable pre-lunch snack. It preps the palate. A very scientific explanation, dear. Speaking of science, how’s work going, Lizzie? Still surrounded by people talking about things that fly over your head? Pretty much, yeah. It's…interesting. We’re currently gearing up for a big push on a new journal about bio-luminescence. It’s fascinating stuff, really, all about creatures that make their own light. Deep sea stuff mostly, but some insects too. Bio-luminescence, you say? Now, there's a thought. I remember reading something about fireflies as a lad. Magical creatures, they seemed. Did you know they used to use them in lamps, historically? Before electricity, of course. Really, Arthur? That  is  interesting. I never knew that. It’s funny, isn’t it? All these things we didn’t learn at school. We taught so much English Literature, but very little actual…natural history. Though to be fair, the curriculum was different then. More Dickens, less deep-sea creatures. It's amazing what people used to do. Makes you wonder what things  we  do now that future generations will look back on and think are completely bizarre. Like… doomscrolling on TikTok. TikTok? Is that one of those…internet contraptions? I still can’t get my head around the internet, to be honest. I tried ordering some bird seed online last week. Took me an hour, and I’m still not sure if the order went through. Oh, dear. You and technology have never been the best of friends. I can help you with the birdseed, Arthur. I’ve gotten quite adept at navigating those online shops. It's a necessary evil, really. Though I must say, I do miss browsing the shops in town.

So, Leo, you were glued to that PlayStation all afternoon. What grand adventure were you having this time? Rescuing the princess, I presume? Dad, seriously? It's not ALWAYS rescuing a princess. I was building a city in  Cities: Skylines . It’s… complicated. You wouldn’t get it. It's all about traffic flow and zoning and… stuff. Sounds remarkably like trying to get a toddler to eat their dinner. Strategic placement, diversionary tactics… Aye, you'd know all about strategic placement, wouldn't you, love? Though Finnigan usually responds better to just throwing the food. Wooo! See? Exhibit A. Leo, is it one of those games where you spend hours and hours and then it resets if the power goes off? I remember your cousin Mark being distraught about something like that once. No, it saves automatically. It’s pretty good. I designed a whole rail network. It was brilliant, until… well, there was a massive pile-up near the industrial district. Apparently, I needed better road connections. Road connections, eh? Sounds like a bit of the M8 around here some days. Absolute chaos. Did you ever think of learning to code, Leo? You're rather good at building things… digitally, anyway. It's a good skill to have, you know. Lots of money in it. I dunno. Coding sounds… boring. This is more about being creative. Planning. Making something look good and  work . It's different. He’s got a point, Michael. It’s not all just lines of code. It's problem-solving, and Leo's always been good at that. Though, honestly, I’m more impressed he hasn’t blown up the TV yet with all that gaming. He gets that from his mother’s side of the family. A bit of a fiery temper, you have. Just kidding, darling! Oh, ha ha. Very funny. Speaking of fiery tempers, Finnigan was having a meltdown earlier when I tried to put Mr. Snuggles in the buggy. Apparently, Mr. Snuggles  needed  to walk. Mr. Snuggles? Isn't that the ridiculously fluffy bunny? The very same. He’s Finnigan’s best friend, apparently. Takes precedence over even Daddy sometimes, if I’m being honest. We had a long walk up to the park, did we not, love? And Mr. Snuggles had to be ‘in charge of the steering’. He gripped that bunny so tightly the whole way. It was adorable and slightly terrifying.

Well, I still say your sprouts last year, Marjorie, tasted like… well, like something the cat dragged in. No offence, dear. Oh, don't start with the sprouts again, Arthur! They were perfectly cooked! You just don't  like  sprouts, that's all. You'd rather have a plateful of Yorkshire puddings, wouldn't you? Now, now, let’s not descend into the annual sprout debate. It's lovely to be here, Anon. House looks lovely, all festive. Are the girls upstairs still engrossed in… whatever it is teenage girls do? We're doing TikToks, Mr. Davies! Don’t judge! It's research for a school project! Honestly! TikToks, is it? Sounds like a dreadful waste of time to me. Back in my day, we used to… well, we used to talk to each other. Face to face. Oh, Arthur, you're such an old stick in the mud. They’re having fun, leave them be. Speaking of fun, are we still managing the drive to Auntie Brenda’s on Boxing Day? It’s a fair old trek, isn’t it? I offered to drive, Marjorie, if Arthur's not up to it. Though, knowing Brenda, she'll want to tell us every single detail about Percy’s latest fall from a horse. Honestly, that woman and those animals… It's a miracle Percy hasn't broken every bone in his body. Percy fell  again ? He needs to retire! Seriously! Old Man Percy and his stubbornness. Stubbornness runs in families, doesn't it? He loves those horses, darling. It’s his life. Though, yes, it does cause us all a bit of worry. What about you two, any plans for the holidays beyond Brenda's and potentially offensive sprouts? I'm… um… going to see Ben. Ben? That’s the young man you’ve been seeing, isn’t it? Is he coming to Anon’s for Christmas dinner? Oh, just a friend, Mr. Davies. Nothing serious. Yet. “Yet”? Oh, my goodness. Teenage romance. It's all so… dramatic. Do be careful, love. And make sure he treats you properly. Proper treatment involves not wanting to spend all day staring at one of those TikTok contraptions. Arthur, really! Let the girl have her fun. Has anyone thought about getting the car serviced before the Boxing Day journey? I’d hate for us to be stranded halfway. Good thinking, David. I meant to call the garage.

Honestly, Derek, I don’t know what’s happened at the hospital. It feels like everyone’s just… running on empty. Old Mrs. Higgins was in again last night, convinced her cat was plotting against her. It’s always something. Sounds like a typical Tuesday, love. You always get the characters at night, don’t you? The day staff miss all the fun. Though, a plotting cat… that’s a new one. Is she on any new medication? No, same as always. I think she just gets lonely. And then starts watching too many spy films. It's draining though. Especially when you’ve got young Liam, bless him, constantly needing his hand holding because he's only just started on placement. Liam’s still finding his feet, is he? Poor thing. It's a proper baptism by fire, isn't it? First proper taste of the real world after uni. Oh, absolutely. He’s a good lad, really is. Just…a bit green. Keeps asking me things like ‘what do I  say  to a patient who’s crying?’ I tell him, “Just listen, Liam. Honestly, sometimes that’s all they need.” Wise words, Sarah. You've seen it all, haven’t you? Speaking of seeing it all…did you manage to get through to Fiona about your birthday? I know you said she wasn't picking up. No, still nothing. I’ve left two messages. It’s fine, really. She’s probably just busy with the kids and that new job. Though, it  is  my 45th next week. A girl can hope for a little acknowledgement, can't she? Forty-five! That’s a big one. I’m on present duty, remember? Don't worry, I've got something lined up. It's…different. Different how? Don’t tell me you’ve bought me another pottery painting kit. I still have three unfinished cherubs from the last one hiding in the garage. No, no cherubs! Definitely not. This is…an experience. Something we can all do together. Honestly, it'll be fun. I was thinking… maybe that escape room down in Maidstone? The one with the Victorian mystery theme? Ooh, that sounds good! I’ve heard good things about those escape rooms. Though, knowing us, we'll probably spend the entire hour arguing over where the candlestick is. That’s highly likely. You and your obsession with candlesticks, Derek. Remember Aunt Mildred’s house?

…and honestly, Doreen, you wouldn't  believe  the price of a loaf of bread now. Used to be, a shilling got you a decent sized one. Now? Blimey. It's gone mad. Tell me about it, George. Everything's gone up. Though I haven't bought a loaf in ages, mostly it's biscuits for me now. Easier on the teeth, you see. And cheaper. Inflation’s a beast, isn’t it? The Bank of England is trying to wrangle it, but…well, it's a complicated situation. Though frankly, all this talk of percentages doesn't help a pensioner much, does it? Found a little something at the market, Dad. Some decent apples. Thought we could have a crumble later. Though, honestly, getting there was a nightmare. Parking is atrocious. Apples are lovely, John. Thank you. Always reminds me of your mother, bless her. She made the best apple crumble. Though she used to sneak a bit of brandy into it. Don’t tell Doreen. Brandy, you say? Always did have a mischievous streak, that woman. Not like some, all pious and going to church every Sunday. Now, Doreen, that's a bit harsh. Church provides a community, a sense of belonging. Something we all need, especially as we get on. Belonging. It's all very well. But old man Hemmings, at the church, kept looking at me funny last week. I swear he thinks I'm…well, he thinks I’ve been up to no good. Silly old fool. Up to no good, Dad? What on earth are you talking about? Oh, nothing. Just…rumours. People talk. Especially about a bachelor like me. They always presumed I had a…a lady friend. Never did, mind you. Not seriously. There was Mabel, down at the social club, but she liked a bit too much gin for my liking. Mabel! She was a character, wasn't she? Always had a story. Though most of them were likely…embellishments. You know, a little here, a little there to spice things up. Speaking of spices, are we still on for the bridge club party on Saturday? I’ve been meaning to get some smoked salmon. Absolutely, Dad. Mum and I are happy to help set up. Though, honestly, I'm starting to worry about the heating. It's getting cold, and this house…it’s drafty. Drafty? It's a palace compared to the cottage I grew up in!

Right, I think that’s the curry base done. It smells proper good, doesn’t it? Though, not as good as me Nana’s, mind. Nobody makes a curry like Nana Elsie. It  does  smell amazing, honestly. You’ve really outdone yourself, Liv. And I agree about Nanas, they’re all just…curry wizards. Mine makes a decent one, but it's always a bit…precise. Not enough chaos, you know? Chaos is the secret ingredient! She just chucks things in and it  works . I’ve tried to get the recipe out of her for years, but it's always “a pinch of this, a handful of that.” Honestly, it's infuriating and brilliant all at once. You alright with the veg there? Need a hand? All good! Just reminiscing about my Mum trying to recreate Nana’s recipes. Similar story. It never quite hits the same. Speaking of family… how’s your brother, Ben? I haven't spoken to him in ages. Last I heard he was still travelling? Oh, he’s back! Been back a few months now. He’s… trying to be a proper adult. It’s going alright, I think. He’s found a little flat in Sheffield and started a job at some tech company. Being all sensible. It’s weird seeing him like that, after all the backpacking. Sheffield, huh? That’s… close-ish. Good for him, though. It’s scary, that transition, isn't it? Going from ‘finding yourself’ to ‘finding a mortgage’. I’m still firmly in the ‘avoiding mortgages’ phase, thank you very much. Tell me about it! My Mum keeps dropping hints about me needing to “settle down” and “think about the future.” Like I haven't already got a future sorted with this job, and trying to avoid all adult commitments for as long as humanly possible! Oh, the mothers! Mine’s started asking about my five-year plan. A  five-year plan ! I barely know what I'm having for dinner next Tuesday. Speaking of… this curry sounds perfect. What are we watching after? You said you had something lined up? I was thinking ‘Shaun of the Dead’. It’s been ages. And, honestly, I just need something silly. Work's been mental. This conference next month is massive – six hundred delegates! The venue keeps changing things on me, the AV guy is a nightmare, and apparently, someone’s requested a ‘gluten-free, vegan, nut-free, soy-free, fun-free’ buffet.

…and honestly, young lad, I just don’t understand the rush for another referendum. Seems like only yesterday we had the last one, didn’t it? All that fuss, all that debate… and for what? To end up back at square one? Well, Mum, things  have  changed since 2014. Brexit’s happened, innit? And loads of people in Scotland voted to stay in the EU. It feels… different now. Different, aye. But is ‘different’ enough to rip the United Kingdom apart? That's what I keep thinking. My grandad, he fought in the Second World War. He believed in the Union, fought for the Union. He'd be turning in his grave. Grandad fought for freedom, didn't he? Maybe Scotland wanting to decide its own future  is  a kind of freedom. Mr. Davies, our History teacher, was saying that. He said it’s about self-determination. Self-determination… It sounds grand, doesn't it? But it’s not that simple, is it? All this talk of borders and currency and… well, everything. It’s a right mess, and it will affect all of us, even down here in North Yorkshire. Think about trade, think about travel… I was talking to Liam, his dad's Scottish, from just outside Glasgow. He reckons it will be brilliant. They’ll have their own NHS, their own rules, no more being told what to do by Westminster. He said it’ll be like… like being free. Liam’s dad’s allowed to think that, he’s living it. But being ‘free’ comes at a price, love. I remember when they first started talking about devolution, back in the nineties. Old man Henderson down the pub, he was convinced it would be the end of everything. He was a bit of a doom-monger, mind you, but he had a point. Once you start dismantling something… it’s hard to put it back together again. But isn’t Scotland different? They feel… connected to Europe more than England does. And everyone keeps saying how Nicola Sturgeon is really good at arguing their case. Oh, Sturgeon's a clever one, I'll give her that. A politician through and through. She knows how to play the game. But I still think it’s a risky gamble. Remember all the arguing about the oil? Back in the 70s when they first had a wee referendum about it?

Oh, honestly. Look at ‘em, already at each other’s throats. It’s not even 9:30! Tell me about it. It's like they  try  to find the most chaotic people in the country. Though, I am slightly invested in whether Sharon’s actually his mum or not. It's always 'he says, she says' isn’t it? And the lie detector. Oh, the  lie detector . Like that’s even remotely reliable. It just gives everyone an excuse to shout louder. It's a national embarrassment, this show. But… I can’t look away. It's awful, but it's like car crash TV. Proper train wreck. Though I was listening to Bethany earlier, she was saying her nan  loves  this. Says it makes her feel better about her own life. Well, that’s… grim. But I suppose there's a certain comfort in knowing other people are having a worse time, innit? Still, the accents on this show are… something else. Listen to that bloke now. It’s like he’s trying to swallow his Ds. You’re talking about Liam, yeah? He's from Manchester, isn’t he? They do that a lot, drop the ‘t’s and the ‘d’s. It's just how they speak. It's elision, right? That's what my linguistics lecturer called it. Cutting out sounds to make it flow quicker. We all do it, just different sounds.
