This tea’s lovely, Mum. Proper brew, this. Not like the stuff they try to pass off at the office. It’s all instant rubbish these days. Oh, instant. Don’t get me started. Your grandfather, bless his soul, would have a fit if he knew anyone drinking that… powdered nonsense. Always loose leaf, him. Proper Yorkshire Tea, mind. Though, back in my day, we didn’t  have  a choice, did we? It was just… tea. You always say that, Mum. "Back in your day..." Everything was harder back then, according to you. It  was  harder! Don't you go contradicting your grandmother! We didn’t have these fancy microwaves, or dishwashers, or… whatever it is you project managers do all day staring at screens! It’s… a bit more complex than just staring at screens, Grandma. I manage teams, budgets, timelines… basically, I try to make sure things get done on time and without falling apart. It’s stressful. Hence the craving for a proper cuppa at your place. Sounds exhausting. I had a right nightmare with a client today, actually. Trying to convince them that the turquoise sofa  definitely  clashes with the orange wallpaper. Honestly, some people… no taste at all. Turquoise and orange? Ouch. That’s… bold. Bold is one word for it. Awful is another. Though, I remember a dress I had in the fifties, a sort of coral colour… with a little turquoise trim. It was all the rage, you know. Fashion goes round in circles. I'd rather not revisit coral and turquoise, thank you very much. Speaking of revisiting things, did you see that old film was on last night, Mum? 'Brief Encounter'? Oh yeah! I caught the tail end of it. Classic. Trevor Howard and Celia Johnson, right? Proper tearjerker. Oh, it broke your heart, that film did. The longing… the repression. Times were different then, you know. You couldn't just…  leave  a marriage. People didn't. You suffered in silence. It was a good film, though. Very British. It's amazing how different things are now. People just up and leave without a second thought. Makes you wonder about commitment, doesn’t it? It's a different world, definitely. Though, maybe it’s just easier to be  seen  to be unhappy now. Social media and all that. Everyone's broadcasting their feelings. Broadcasting their feelings? Sounds exhausting. I used to keep my feelings to myself.

Honestly, Leo, you’ve barely touched yours. And Elsie, is that  all  you’ve eaten? It’s Pancake Day! It’s practically a national requirement to consume your weight in batter. It’s…squidgy. And the lemon makes my face do a funny thing. I’m building a rocket. In my head. It needs very specific fuel. Pancakes are not the right fuel. A rocket, is it? Well, perhaps a tiny little bite for the engine then? Just one? Elsie, a little lemon  is  good for you. It has vitamin C, you know. Vitamin…see? Like seeing things? Sort of. It helps you see  better . And stay healthy. You had a sniffle yesterday, remember? My rocket needs unicorn glitter for fuel! That's definitely better than pancakes. Unicorn glitter… right. We’ll add that to the shopping list. Speaking of lists, did either of you remember to tell me what you thought about the school assembly this morning? Mrs. Davies said you both were very well-behaved. It was loud. And Barnaby sniffed. A lot. I liked the singing! But Oliver kept kicking my chair. Oh dear, Oliver again. Honestly, I had a little chat with his teacher last week. He's a lovely boy, truly, but needs a little guidance with personal space. It makes me think about little Thomas in my class... such a sweet boy, but he comes to school sometimes without a proper breakfast. It breaks your heart, doesn't it? Seeing children who aren't getting enough. Why doesn’t he eat? It’s… complicated, darling. Sometimes families don’t have enough money for food. It’s not his fault, and we try to help at school. It just… makes you think. It makes me think about my own childhood, being silly and worrying about what game to play next. Did you have pancakes when  you  were little? Oh, yes! Mum always made them, and Dad would try to flip them and usually end up with batter everywhere. It was a mess, but a happy mess. Actually, it reminds me… remember when we talked about going to the Science Museum next weekend? The one with the big dinosaur? The very one! And the amazing space exhibit! We could go on Saturday, if that works. We’ll need to book tickets, mind you. It gets awfully crowded. Then maybe Sunday we could... oh, I completely forgot! Auntie Carol mentioned the Festival Hall has that children’s storytelling event on Sunday afternoon.

Oh my  god , this Kung Pao chicken is incredible. Seriously, best takeaway we’ve had in ages. Told ya! Golden Dragon always delivers. Though, last time they forgot the spring rolls, which was a tragedy. Proper tragedy. A tragedy? Dramatic, much? Still, spring rolls  are  important. They’re the structural integrity of a Chinese takeaway. They’re a good palate cleanser between the heavier dishes, I’ll give you that. Though, honestly, I’m more about the sweet and sour pork. It's a classic for a reason. You’re such a creature of habit, Liam. Always the sweet and sour. Speaking of habits… did you hear about Old Man Hemmings? Apparently, his funeral is next week. No way! Old Man Hemmings? The one who used to yell at us for playing cricket on the village green? The very one. Apparently, a short illness. Mum told me, she runs the flower shop, so she’s doing the arrangements. Said he requested they play ‘The Great Escape’ theme tune at the service. Seriously? That’s… wonderfully weird. He always did have a rogue sense of humour. I remember he once told me my soil samples looked like Bob the Builder’s building site. Oh, bless him. He was a bit of a character. It’s a shame, though. Even when he was grumpy, he was… present. You don't get that much anymore. Yeah, it’s just… everyone’s disappearing, isn’t it? It feels like every other week we’re talking about someone’s grandparent, or a neighbour… It's getting to that age, I suppose. We're all getting older, and so are the people around us. It’s depressing, though, isn’t it? Especially when you think about… well, what happened with Sarah and Mark’s dog, Winston. Oh, don’t even  go  there. I'm still a bit raw about that. Poor Winston. That was… awful. They're taking it really hard, apparently. I saw Mark in the pub on Tuesday. He didn't say much, just stared into his pint. He was a good dog, Winston. Sarah was practically his mum. They've been trying to get a new one, haven’t they? I saw something on Facebook about a rescue pup. Good for them. A distraction will be good. It won't replace Winston, obviously, but... It’s something. Speaking of distractions, anyone seen that new sci-fi film, ‘Nexus’?

Oh, look at this one. Auntie Mabel at her 70th. She looks so… determined, doesn’t she? Even then. Remember how she used to insist on doing the Christmas dinner, single-handedly, for about thirty people? Determined is a polite word for it, dear. That woman was a force of nature. An absolute whirlwind. Your grandfather used to say she could argue a cat out of a saucer of milk. And the dinner  always  had to have bread sauce. Even if nobody wanted it. And the sprouts! Don’t forget the sprouts. Boiled within an inch of their lives. I swear, they’d bounce if you dropped them. They did! I vividly remember trying to hide them under the gravy. She always knew, though. Always knew. She had a sixth sense for rogue sprouts. And for anyone sneaking a second mince pie. She used to keep a tally, you know. Of who had what. Said it prevented greed. Oh, Mabel. She was… unique. Do you remember Old Man Hemmings next door to her? The one who collected gnomes? Vaguely. I was quite young. Wasn’t he a bit of a recluse? A recluse is putting it mildly. Never said a word to anyone, supposedly. Except to shout at the squirrels for disturbing his gnomes. Mabel used to leave him plates of rice krispy cakes on his doorstep, though. Said he looked “thin as a rake”. Rice krispy cakes! That’s lovely. He probably lived on those and squirrel-induced rage. It’s funny, isn’t it, how you remember these little things? It’s not the big events, it’s the tiny interactions. Absolutely. It’s the details that paint the picture. It’s why I try to get my students to really  observe  things, not just see them. To notice the small details. Good philosophy, that. Speaking of observations, I’m still trying to wrap my head around this psychological experiment I signed up for. It’s… odd. Oh? What’s it about? It’s about predicting people’s behaviour in hypothetical situations. They give you these scenarios, really mundane things - like choosing between supermarket checkouts, or deciding whether to take the stairs or the lift – and then they analyse your responses. Apparently, it’s connected to research on driverless cars. Driverless cars? Goodness me. I can barely trust  people  to drive, let alone a machine! They frighten me, those things.

Right, almost ready! Who wants to try and count how many spring rolls I’ve made? It’s a terrible game, I know, but it keeps little hands busy. Ooh, can I have one  now ? Please? They smell yummy. I’m drawing a dragon! It’s for Chinese New Year. It needs scales. Lots and lots of scales. Patience, Lily-Rose. Just a little longer. And that's brilliant, Leo, a proper dragon! Is he a friendly dragon, or a scary one? Scary! He breathes fire. And he’s guarding… a planet! Which planet? Is it sparkly? Like Saturn? I learned about Saturn at school today. It has rings! Saturn  is  very sparkly, you're right, Daisy. Leo, what planet is your dragon guarding? Um… the red one. Mars! It’s full of…dust and secrets. And the dragon doesn’t want anyone to take them. Very good! A secret-guarding, fire-breathing dragon on Mars. I love it. Right, spring roll count – anybody? I think I’ve cracked thirty. One… two… three… oh, there are loads! More than ten! More than ten is a good start. They're ready now, anyway. Careful, they’re hot. So, what did you both learn at school today, apart from fabulous facts about Saturn? We had music! And I played the piano! I played ‘Hot Cross Buns’ all by myself! That’s wonderful, Daisy! I’m so proud of you. You’ve been practising so hard. Leo, what about you? We talked about space… and then we did maths. Boring maths. Except Miss Periwinkle said if we all get ten right answers, we can build a rocket out of cardboard boxes. A cardboard rocket? Now  that  sounds exciting! Maybe you can design it to fly to Mars and deliver a message to your dragon. Can we have noodles with our spring rolls? I want noodles! And prawn crackers! Absolutely. Noodles are on their way. I was thinking, after dinner, maybe we could watch  Barbie and the Great Adventure ? It's not strictly Chinese New Year themed, but it’s got a lovely adventure in it. I don’t want to watch Barbie! I want drum lessons! Mr. Harris said I’m getting better at the snare drum. Drum lessons it is, Leo. We can alternate. Maybe Barbie one night, drums the next? Though, after all those spring rolls, you might have a lot of energy for drumming.

Honestly, this is… perfect. Just what I needed. Uni’s been a proper slog lately. Feels miles away from deadlines and dodgy student halls. Tell me about it. Though, swapping essays for early mornings and proving dough isn’t  exactly  a holiday, mind you. Still, Rome feels… different. Less pressure, yeah? And the sun! London was threatening rain the entire time we were packing. You two are always complaining! It's a holiday, enjoy it! And honestly, this bar is a find. Proper chilled out. Much nicer than that tourist trap we almost went to near the Trevi Fountain. Yeah, that place was mayhem. All selfie sticks and shouting. This one’s got character. And the Negronis are… well, they're  Negronis . You Brits appreciate a good bittersweet drink, eh? You know us too well, mate. Though, I'm finding the Italian appreciation for aperitivo is rubbing off on me. Bit of nibble action with your drink? Can get used to that. How’s the coffee been treating you, by the way, Liam? Still battling the espresso snobs? Always. They’re… passionate, let’s say. Constantly telling me my grind is too coarse or my tamp is off. It's like they've all secretly worked at a micro-roastery their whole life. It's a bit much, honestly. I miss just making a flat white without a lecture. Oh, bless you. You're dealing with  real  Italians, then. The coffee is a religion here. It’s not just a caffeine delivery system. Speaking of which, has everyone sorted their AirBnB situation properly? I had a slight panic this morning when I thought I’d booked it for next month instead of this one. Sorted, sorted. Found a cute little place just off Campo de' Fiori. Tiny, but right in the thick of it. Bit noisy at night, I suspect. But hey, we’re in Rome! Noise is part of the experience. I’m good too. Managed to snag a place near the Vatican. Bit further out, but the reviews said it had amazing views. Plus, it was suspiciously cheap… which always worries me slightly. Hope it’s not got a resident ghost. A ghost? Nah. Probably just dodgy plumbing. Or a tiny, very loud Italian family. Let's hope not. Right, dinner then. I was thinking we could try that Trattoria Isabella everyone’s been raving about. Apparently, they do the best Cacio e Pepe in Rome.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of glitter involved in some of these hen do ideas is terrifying. Like, how are they even cleaning that up? It’ll be found in their carpets for decades. Oh, you’ve been deep-diving into Pinterest again, have you? You know how it sucks you in. I swear, half my free time is spent scrolling through things I’ll never actually  do . It's the pressure, isn’t it? Everyone expects these mega-events now. It’s not enough to just go for a nice dinner anymore. It has to be…an experience. Exactly! Chloe's sister's hen do last year was a full-on weekend glamping thing, with a cocktail masterclass and a silent disco. It looked amazing on Instagram, but everyone was exhausted. And broke. That's what I'm worried about with Amelia's. She’s hinted she wants something "low-key", but her mum is already talking about hot air balloons.  Hot air balloons!  Amelia's terrified of heights. Oh, bless. Mothers, eh? They always have…visions. Maybe we need to subtly steer her mum towards something a bit more down-to-earth. I was thinking, maybe a baking class? Amelia loves baking. Ooh, good shout! Remember that disastrous attempt at a croquembouche we did for Ben’s birthday? We could relive the trauma…but in a controlled environment, with someone who actually knows what they’re doing. Oh god,  that  croquembouche. It looked like the leaning tower of pastry. I’m still finding caramel stuck in corners of my kitchen. But a baking class  is  a good idea. Or maybe a craft workshop? Like pottery painting or something? Pottery painting is good! Amelia did a pottery class ages ago and loved it. She made this…questionable vase. It was very…abstract. But she was so proud of it. The problem is, coordinating everyone. Sarah’s already said she’s got a work conference that weekend. Typical Sarah! Always working. Okay, so baking or pottery…what about the venue? Somewhere central, I guess? And not too pricey? There's that new studio space just off the market square; ‘The Craft Corner’ I think it’s called. I saw it on Instagram. They do all sorts of workshops. It's pretty reasonably priced, and they've got a little café too. Oh, perfect! I can check their availability. I’m pretty good at wrangling schedules.

Right, this sauce  should  be thickening up now. Honestly, feel a bit rough, though. Think that dodgy kebab last night finally caught up with me. Dodgy kebab? You and your late-night Bedford cravings. You  know  that place isn’t the best. Served you right, didn't it? You look a bit pale, actually. Not too bad, though, yeah? Just a bit of nausea? Nah, nothin' serious. Just... everything feels a bit wobbly. And my head's like a bass drum. Still, gotta keep goin’. Promised Mum we'd have this Bolognese ready for when she gets back from visiting Auntie Carol. She’s been going on about Carol's new conservatory for weeks. Honestly, a greenhouse in November… Sounds about right. Auntie Carol and her…  projects . She’s always got one on the go. Did you hear she’s thinking of doing a pottery course? At her age! No way! She's mad. Reminds me, I need to ask you about that weekend away you were planning. Italy, wasn’t it? How’s the planning going? Found a decent hotel yet? Yeah, Florence. Still looking at hotels, actually. Honestly, it's a nightmare. Everything’s either ridiculously expensive or looks like it hasn’t been updated since the Renaissance  itself . I wanted something a bit… charming, you know? Not just another sterile box room. I get that. Remember that hotel we stayed in in Barcelona? The one that smelled faintly of old socks and despair? Never again. You gotta read the reviews  carefully . Filter out all the Americans complainin’ about the tea bags, though. They’re impossible to please. Good point. I’ve been trying, but there are so many. I’m starting to think a hostel might be the way to go. Meet some people, experience the ‘real’ Florence… Hostels? You? Mr. ‘I require a minimum thread count of 400’? I can’t see it. Still, could save you some dosh. You’re gonna need it, Florence isn't cheap. You planning on doing any cooking over there, or relying on pasta and pizza solely? I was thinking a mix. I’ve been trying to learn some basic Italian dishes. Mum gave me her old ‘Italian Cooking for Beginners’ book. It’s terrifyingly detailed. Apparently, there's a  right  way to make Bolognese. Oh, I bet. Every Italian nonna has a secret ingredient and a lifetime of judgement.

Right, shopping list. We’re definitely out of biscuits, aren’t we? And I need more of that lavender hand wash - the one that smells proper lovely. Oh, and don't forget the cat food, Elsie. Winston's giving me  looks . Biscuits, lavender wash, cat food. Got it. Though honestly, Winston could give a masterclass in manipulative glances. He’s a fluffy tyrant, that one. You know, it's funny… I was looking at Brenda’s birthday card the other day and it had her age on it. Such a thing! We never did that, did we? Just wrote ‘Happy Birthday’ and a little sentiment. Goodness no! It felt… gauche. And slightly alarming, to be honest. Knowing precisely how old someone is. Though, people are much more upfront about it these days. Still, I wouldn’t dream of putting my age on a card. It feels terribly… American. Exactly! It just feels… unnecessary. Speaking of Brenda, I need to get her something. She mentioned wanting one of those little calendar fobs for her handbag. With the year on it. Do you think they still  do  those? Oh, I’m sure they do. Maybe at Clintons? Or even a little gift shop. They’re the sort of thing you find everywhere leading up to Christmas. I remember making those at school, actually. Though ours were dreadful – bits of cardboard and glitter glue everywhere. Oh, the glitter. It got  everywhere . Mrs. Higgins used to threaten to ban it completely after every craft session. It was in the ventilation system for weeks! Remember those awful felt tip pens that always smelled of chemicals? The purple ones were the worst. Oh, don’t remind me! They stained everything. And the paper always went see-through if you used too much. But we were blissfully unaware of the chemical dangers, weren’t we? Everything was just… fun. Do you remember practicing hockey at primary school? That was a nightmare. Hockey! Absolutely dreadful. I was hopeless. Always getting clocked with a stick. I think I spent more time hiding behind the goalposts. You were alright though, weren't you? Quite sporty. I wasn't  that  good! Just… less afraid of the stick. It's funny what you remember. Thinking about school always makes me wonder what I'd have studied if I'd gone to university younger. I always fancied something to do with sound, actually. Sound?

…and honestly, it’s a blessed relief to be  away  from Southend. Don’t get me wrong, it's home, always will be. But… the sheer  volume  of people. Constant noise. Here… it's just… peaceful. Though, I must say, these Devon lanes are a bit narrow for my liking. Nearly met a tractor coming around that bend yesterday. Oh, you get used to the tractors, Dad. It's part of the charm. And the lanes  are  narrow, but everyone’s pretty considerate. Most of them wave as you go by, which is nice. Have you met many of the neighbours yet? A few. Old Mr. Henderson next door seems a decent sort, bit of a gardener, apparently. Offered me some runner beans. Said he’s been growing them for… well, longer than you've been alive, I reckon. And that Mrs. Tremaine across the road, always has a smile and a wave. A bit nosey, perhaps, but harmless enough. She asked about…well, everything. My age, my health, what I used to  do . Oh, Mrs. Tremaine! She knows  everything  about everyone in Holsworthy. She’s a lovely woman, though. She organises the village fete, apparently. Always needs volunteers. You could offer to help with the raffle, David. It's a good way to meet people. Mum, don’t put him straight into volunteering! Let him settle in first. He needs to  enjoy  retirement, not be running raffles. I appreciate the thought, honestly. But I'm still finding my feet, so to speak. Though, Henderson did mention something about a local walking group. Might be good to get out and about a bit. Doctor’s been on at me about exercise. Getting a bit…stiff, you know. That's a wonderful idea! The Holsworthy Harriers, I think they're called. They do walks of all lengths. I saw a poster for one next Saturday, up at the village hall. Apparently, it goes along the River Waldron. That sounds lovely. Though, knowing you, Dad, you'll have a map and compass and be plotting a completely different route within five minutes. Now, that is unfair! I am perfectly capable of following a marked trail. Mostly. Although, I did get us a bit lost on that coastal walk in Norfolk a few years back… remember that, Amelia? How could I  forget ? We ended up in a field of sheep, Dad. And it was pouring with rain.

Honestly, this is ridiculous. Another 'limited time offer' that’s been running for a month. They’re taking the Mick, aren't they? Who is? What’s wound you up now, Liam? Don’t tell me you’re falling for another one of those “miracle” cleaning products advertised all over TikTok. Nah, not that. Though Brenda next door swears by one that smells like bubblegum. No, it's this jacket. Been wanting it for ages. Keeps going up and down in price. It’s like they’re deliberately messing with ya, playing mind games. That  is  annoying. Price fluctuations are the bane of online shopping. Algorithms, Liam, pure algorithms. They track what you look at, see you're interested, and subtly increase the price knowing you're more likely to bite. Algorithms… right. Sounds fancy for ripping people off. I just want a decent jacket that doesn't cost the same as a small car. And it’s not just the jacket, is it? Everything feels… over-inflated. Even the things I’m not even looking at. It’s everything, yeah. Rent, food, petrol… everything. It’s a proper mess. Still, you gotta look for the deals. I found some alright stationery for uni online the other day. Saved a few quid. Stationery? You and your stationery. You’re like a magpie for pens and highlighters. I’m trying to find something to  do , not just things to write with. Still no luck with the jobs, then? Still nothing concrete. Sent off a couple of applications yesterday – one at the Spar, another at that new cafe in the town centre. Doubt I’ll hear back, though. They always want experience, don't they? What experience am I supposed to have at 18? Besides A-Levels, obviously. Tell me about it. I've got a degree… a  degree … and I'm still staring at a phone screen waiting for someone to offer me anything. Even stacking shelves. It's… demoralising, to be honest. I know. Mum keeps saying I should just get a part-time job anywhere, “build up my CV”. Easier said than done when everything's so competitive. And she doesn't understand the pressure of exams coming up. She never does, does she? Always got a suggestion, always thinks she knows best. Remember when she tried to get me to take that job delivering leaflets? “Get off your backside, Liam!”

Right, well, this is a proper improvement, isn't it, love? Still a bit…sparse, mind you. Needs some  life . Though I suppose that’s the fun bit, isn't it? Filling it up. Though goodness me, new furniture prices these days… highway robbery, I tell ya. It is a bit bare, yes, but I wanted to get the big stuff sorted first – fridge, washing machine, cooker. That was the priority. And honestly, after the move, I was completely wiped out. Furniture can wait a bit. Though I was eyeing up that little dresser in Antique Barn yesterday… Oh, good! Sandwiches are ready. Ham and pickle for you two, and I made myself cheese and tomato. You  must  try the pickle, Sarah, it’s from that farm shop near Hatherleigh. Proper stuff. And yes, Antique Barn is dangerous! You’ll come out with something you absolutely don’t need. Remember that ceramic goose you bought last year? Oh, don’t remind me! Poor Gertrude. She’s currently residing in the shed, staring into the abyss. But the dresser  is  lovely. And reasonably priced, I thought. It would fit perfectly in the dining room. Priced reasonably? Honestly, you two! Everything's overpriced. Still, a bit of browsing never hurt anyone. More importantly, are we still on for that coastal walk next week? The weather forecast looks…decent. Absolutely! I've been looking at routes around Hartland Quay. There’s a fairly easy one, about six miles, with a lovely pub at the end. We could fortify ourselves afterwards. Perfect for a bracing winter walk. Sounds brilliant! I’ve been needing to get out and stretch my legs. School’s been hectic, marking papers until my eyes cross. Although, I did have one student ask me today if the Romans had central heating. Honestly! They certainly didn’t have combi boilers, I can tell you that much! Though they weren’t half bad with hypocausts, apparently. I read a bit about it for a history project years ago. My degree was in management, obviously, but I always enjoyed a bit of history. It puts things in perspective, doesn’t it? Makes you realise how little time we actually have on this planet. Which reminds me, have you heard from Auntie Brenda lately? She’s getting on a bit now. I spoke to her last week. She's complaining about her knees again, but otherwise, she's as sprightly as ever.

Right, that was…pleasant. Your mum really outdid herself with the roast, didn’t she? Though I swear she tries to subtly interrogate me about my research every time we visit. She does, doesn’t she? It’s her way of showing she cares, I think. “Still poking around in people’s heads, are you, darling?” She always asks it with that slightly concerned look. Honestly, she thinks health psychology is just…navel-gazing. Navel-gazing with statistical analysis and ethically approved consent forms! It’s more complicated than that, Mum! I tried explaining the latest study – the one on the correlation between social media usage and anxiety in young adults – but her eyes glazed over after the first sentence about longitudinal data. Bless her. She’s a primary school teacher; her idea of data is marking little Timmy’s spelling test. How’s that study going, actually? Still hitting roadblocks with recruitment? It's… challenging. We're getting applications, but filtering for the right demographic is a nightmare. Wanting to participate is easy,  qualifying  is hard. And then half the people who do qualify don’t respond to follow-up emails. It's like trying to herd cats online. I spent half of yesterday chasing down participants who'd apparently changed their email addresses. Sounds exhausting. It’s similar with the teacher assessments I’m managing. Getting schools to submit everything on time is pulling teeth. Especially with all the new curriculum changes. Everyone’s stressed and overwhelmed. I spent three hours on the phone today trying to explain the new reporting framework to a headteacher who clearly hadn’t even  looked  at the guidance. It's all just… admin, isn’t it? So much time spent on things that aren’t the actual work. I end up feeling like a glorified email responder half the time. It’s incredibly demoralising when you’re supposed to be doing cutting-edge research. Tell me about it. I love the assessment side of my job – seeing how we can support teachers and help kids reach their potential. But the endless spreadsheets and data entry… it’s soul-crushing. I’m starting to feel like a data processor, not an education professional. Have you considered talking to your supervisor about it? Maybe someone could take some of the administrative load off? I have, briefly. He’s supportive, in principle. But he's already got a mountain on his plate.

Honestly, this is lovely, isn't it? Your mum’s roast is still the best, Maureen. Nothing beats a proper Sunday dinner. Though, I do miss having a dog under the table, hoovering up the scraps. Don’t start, Sarah. We’ve been over this. The flat simply isn’t suitable for a Labrador. Remember Buster and the chewed furniture? And the time he ‘redecorated’ Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning begonias? That was one time! And he was a puppy! Besides, a little chaos is good for the soul. This feels…  too  tidy. I saw a really cute video of a corgi trying to herd ducks online earlier. It was brilliant. Maybe a corgi would be a good compromise? Lower to the ground, less destructive potential? Corgis are alright. A bit yappy, though. Give me a good, solid working dog any day. Reminds me of old Rex, my dad’s sheepdog. Now  that  was a dog. Knew exactly what you were thinking before you did. Speaking of thinking... I had a right awkward moment at uni today. Trying to take notes in anatomy, and the lecturer was going on about the left hemisphere of the brain and… well, I’m left-handed. Everything felt backwards! I kept writing the labels on the wrong side of the diagrams. Oh, bless you, love! It must be a nightmare learning all that stuff then, being left-handed in a right-handed world. I always felt a bit awkward at school with handwriting, always smudging everything. There’s a surprisingly high percentage of left-handers in creative professions, you know. Artists, musicians… even some footballers. Something about spatial reasoning, I think. That’s fascinating. I didn’t know that. I’m right-handed, but I definitely struggle with spatial awareness. Building flat-pack furniture is my nemesis. It's all a bit of a con, innit? This whole 'left brain, right brain' business. My grandad, he was a dustman, not a scientist, but he could fix anything. Didn't need a fancy diagram for that. Just common sense and a bit of wire. Your Grandad was a clever man, George. They didn’t have all the advantages we do now. He built his own sheds, didn’t he? From scratch. He did. And the neighbours all asked him to fix their fences. He wouldn't charge them much, just a bottle of stout and a bit of company.

Aye, grandad, you wouldn’t believe the curry I had last night. Proper, proper hot. Nearly set me mouth on fire, it did. Not like yer mild stuff, eh? Mild? Lass, I remember curries that’d curl your hair. Back in the fifties, we had an Indian chap, Rajinder, worked down at the exchange. Used to bring in dishes… now  those  were curries. Not this watered-down stuff you get these days. Had a kick to ‘em, did Rajinder’s. Sounds intense. I actually tried making a vindaloo last weekend. Followed a recipe online, thought I could handle the heat. Turns out, my tolerance is… significantly lower than I estimated. Ended up needing a whole tub of yoghurt. Oh, I know that feeling! I thought I was proper hardy, growing up on spice blends mam used to make. Then I had a phall in Bradford. Changed me life. Bradford, you say? Now, I haven’t been to Bradford in… oh, sixty years, maybe more. Used to go with my father. He was a keen railway man, always chasing steam engines. Wonderful days. We’d get fish and chips, wrapped in newspaper, naturally. Never seen anything like the food options now. It’s all… different. It is. I was in Tokyo last month for a conference. The food scene there is just… wild. Everything from Michelin-starred restaurants to tiny ramen shops down back alleys. I tried fugu, pufferfish. Apparently, if it’s not prepared properly, it's rather deadly. Fugu?! You are brave, pet. I can barely handle a scotch bonnet chilli! Did it taste of anything, or just… danger? It was surprisingly delicate. A slight numbness around the lips, but not unpleasant. More about the experience, I think. It’s fascinating how different cultures approach food. It really reflects their history and values. I'm hoping to go to Morocco next year. The spices… I've been reading about them for ages. Morocco… that takes me back. We went there on our honeymoon, your grandmother and I. 1952 it was. Different world, then. Camels, marketplaces, the smell of mint tea... She loved mint tea. We travelled by ship, you know. Took nearly a week to get there. No aeroplanes, not like today. A week?! Grandad, that’s mad! I can get to Barcelona in like, two hours on a budget airline. It changes how you see places, doesn't it?

Right, so I’ve been thinking more about the ‘Postcolonial Literature’ module. I’m still slightly worried about how we’re going to fit Said  and  Spivak into a single semester without it feeling… rushed. Rushed is definitely the danger. Students will just end up skimming, making superficial connections. Have you considered dropping Auerbach? He’s brilliant, obviously, but might be the least essential for the overall theme. Ooh, that’s…tempting. I do love  Mimesis , but you’re right. It feels a bit tangential when we’re aiming for a focused exploration of postcolonial thought. It'd give us breathing room for more primary texts too – Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, perhaps? I was thinking a couple of short stories alongside  Half of a Yellow Sun . Excellent. Adichie is always a winner. Students respond so well to her. And sticking with short stories is smart, keeps the workload manageable. Did you get anywhere with the reading list for the introductory seminar? I was trying to brainstorm yesterday but kept getting distracted by… well, everything. Distracted by the lure of Chinese streaming services, I presume? You were engrossed in that historical drama about the Empress Dowager Cixi last night. Guilty as charged. It’s absolutely ridiculous, all the melodrama and exquisite gowns. But surprisingly addictive! Anyway, back to work. I sketched out a list – a bit of Chinua Achebe to get things moving, maybe some excerpts from Frantz Fanon... the usual suspects. I was hoping we could use it to gauge their existing knowledge, see where they're at before diving into the heavier theory. Sounds good. I was thinking we could start with a bit of a 'What  is  postcolonialism?' discussion. I've found in the past, they come with so many preconceived notions, or none at all, and it's better to establish some ground rules before we get bogged down in complex interpretations. Plus, it gives me a chance to slip in some Brecht. Brecht  and  postcolonialism? You're a glutton for intellectual punishment, aren't you? He’s relevant! Think about the alienation effect, the disruption of narrative… it resonates with a lot of postcolonial writing. Besides, it's been ages since I've talked about him. It feels like a skill needing dusting off. What about your ‘Modern Poetry’ syllabus? Are you still planning on focusing heavily on the Harlem Renaissance? Absolutely. It’s such a vibrant period, and there's a lot students don’t know about it.

Honestly, this coffee machine is the bane of my life. It makes a noise like a strangled badger every time, and half the time it just spits out lukewarm water. Remember the Bialetti we had back in Dublin? Simple, reliable… proper coffee. You've told me about the Bialetti. Repeatedly. It sounded idyllic. Though, knowing Dublin, you probably had a queue of neighbours wanting a cup. Aye, she’s a bit obsessed with that coffee pot. Though, to be fair, everything's better in Dublin in Bridie’s memory. That's not true! But a decent cup of coffee  is  a basic human right, isn't it? Anyway, more pressing matters. Have you two got any further with looking at removal and storage costs? We really need to get a handle on this before the house sale goes through. I’ve had quotes from a few places. It’s… grim. Everything’s gone up. Container storage is surprisingly pricey, and the removal companies are quoting like we’re moving the Crown Jewels. I think the best so far is ‘Man With a Van’ – shockingly unprofessional name, but the quote was reasonable. ‘Man With a Van’? Sounds…trustworthy. . We need to be careful, though. Remember what happened with old Mr. Henderson's antique clock? Vanished into thin air. Don't even  mention  Mr. Henderson. That was a scandal. Let's stick to quotes from reputable companies, shall we? I’m leaning towards self-storage. We could pack things ourselves, save on labour costs. Though, the thought of packing up a lifetime of…stuff…is utterly exhausting. We could do a bit each day. Spread it out. I’m happy to help, obviously. It’s just… finding the time between work. And trying to decipher what  is  worth keeping. You and Geoff accumulated…a lot. We did, didn’t we? Geoff always said you never know when you might need a spare set of encyclopedias or a collection of commemorative spoons. He was a hoarder, bless him. He was a character. A bit eccentric, maybe. So, packing ourselves… it’s an option. Honestly, I'm more worried about what to  do  once we're actually living in that tiny cottage. Limited garden, no proper workshop for me… We’ll make it work. It’ll be cosy. And peaceful. Away from all this…chaos. Speaking of chaos, did you see what Keir Starmer said about… well, everything?

Right, so you’re telling me ‘Old Man Tiber’ isn't just a cool name you made up for your nan’s goldfish? It's… an actual river? Honestly, Leo, you say the most things. Yes! It's the River Tiber. Rome, Italy. Very famous. It’s where Romulus and Remus were, like, abandoned and raised by a she-wolf. Basic history, innit? Though, admittedly, calling a goldfish Old Man Tiber  is  a bit much. Your aunt Brenda really has a flair for the dramatic. Brenda’s always been a character. Remember when she insisted on calling her chihuahua ‘Attila the Hun’? Said it was ironic. Didn’t seem ironic to the postman. G’day, folks. Lookin’ at me like I’m missin’ somethin’? Is this a history lesson I wasn’t informed about? And is that carbonara any good? Looks pretty rich. It’s alright, mate. A bit heavy on the pancetta for my liking. But we were just on Brenda and her… naming choices. Apparently, she’s sourced the most ridiculous pseudonyms for everything. I'm worried she'll start renaming  us . Oh, God, please no. I’m already ‘Poppy’ enough. I don’t need a Roman emperor title tagged on. She’s been obsessed with canals lately, too. Trying to convince my uncle to buy a narrowboat and name it ‘The Wandering Whelk’. The Wandering Whelk! That’s brilliant! He’d never go for it. Uncle Barry barely leaves Birmingham, let alone takes to the waterways. Though, thinking about canals... does anyone know anything about kosher law and canal boats? Kosher law… and canal boats? Now  that’s  a combo. What brought that on, Chloe? Old Mr. Goldstein down the street. He's thinking of getting one, but he’s worried about keeping kosher while living on the water. Something about needing separate sinks and… I didn't really follow. It all sounded very complicated. Blimey. That  is  specific. Guess it depends how strict he is. I mean, you can’t exactly pop to Tesco for a kosher chicken mid-canal trip. Though, there's that deli near Little Venice… maybe he could stock up? It's a niche market, definitely. Speaking of tricky logistics… Anyone fancy going to that new club, ‘The Static’, on Friday? I heard the DJ’s amazing, but getting in is a nightmare. They’re super strict with ID. The Static, huh? Sounds… loud.

…Honestly, I’m deleting Tinder. It's just a load o’ rubbish, isn’t it? All lads sendin’ the same three messages. “Hey,” “How’s it goin’?” an’ then somethin’ about me lookin’ nice. Groundbreaking. Oh, tell me about it! I had one lad whose entire bio was just a picture of his car. A  beige  car. Like, are you tryin’ to impress me with your sensible vehicle, mate? I… I don’t really get Tinder. I tried it once, lasted about five minutes. Felt a bit… weird. Like shopping for people. Nah, it's a laugh at first, innit? Just a bit of a scroll. But it gets exhausting. And the ones that  do  message back are usually… not worth the effort. Remember that lad, Liam, from last month, Sarah? The one who kept talkin’ about his crypto investments? Oh god, Liam! I remember! He tried to explain blockchain to me for a solid hour. I just nodded and pretended to understand. I think he thought I was impressed. He wasn't even attractive, was he? Just… passionately invested in digital money. Speaks volumes, that does. I’m seriously considering givin’ up on the whole ‘dating’ thing for a bit. Focus on uni, focus on not failin’ my dissertation. Good plan, honestly. Uni is stressful enough without addin’ potentially beige-car-owning crypto bros into the mix. How’s the dissertation comin’ on anyway, Sarah? Still strugglin’ with the primary sources? Strugglin’ is an understatement. I’ve spent the last three days starin’ at these old newspapers, tryin’ to make sense of it all. It's about the impact of the coal mines closin’ on Doncaster, right? And every article just makes me feel… sad. And it’s all handwritin'! My eyes are killin' me. That sounds really intense. My dissertation's about Victorian literature, so at least everything's typed. Though, decipherin' Victorian attitudes to… well, anything… is a whole other headache. You lot have proper essays to write, then. I’m doin’ a practical project. Buildin’ a website. Easy peasy. Though, now I’m regrettin’ pickin’ web dev when I don’t know the difference between HTML and a ham sandwich. You are hopeless, Chloe! Honestly. I’m helpin’ you with that, remember? We were gonna work on it tomorrow after our lecture? Oh, right! Thank god for you, Em. Honestly, I'd be lost without a proper Yorkshire lass to guide me.

Honestly, it’s just… bewildering. They’re talking about raising the state pension age  again . Bewildering, I tell you. After a lifetime of paying in, you'd think they'd let a bloke enjoy his retirement. Aye, it’s a cheek, isn’t it, Arthur? A proper cheek. They say people are livin’ longer, but that don't mean we  want  to be workin' till we drop. I’m lucky, mind. Managed to squirrel a bit away, enough not to rely entirely on the handouts. Though handouts is a harsh word, innit? It's what we're owed. It's all about numbers, isn't it, Bernard? They look at the spreadsheets and forget there are actual  people  behind those figures. People who’ve worked hard, paid their dues, and now just want a bit of peace. My Harold always said the government just fiddled with things till they suited themselves. Harold was a smart man, Gwen. He always had his finger on the pulse. Remember when they tried to change the bus routes? Absolute chaos. Said it was for efficiency, but it was just to line someone's pockets, if you ask me. This new pension thing feels the same. They say the economy needs boostin’ and… well, it’s always an excuse, isn’t it? It’s the young ‘uns, you see. They think we’ve had it too good. Too much benefit, too much… well, everything. They don't remember the war, or rationing, or having to graft for every penny. They expect everything handed to ‘em on a plate. Though, to be fair, it's not all their fault is it? The system’s geared that way now. Don’t get me started on the youth of today, Bernard. But it's not just them. It's the whole attitude. Nobody takes responsibility anymore. They all blame someone else. It’s this constant complaining, moaning… It's… it’s exhausting just  listening  to it on the telly. Speaking of which, did you catch that new drama on ITV? ‘The Long Shadow’? Grim stuff. Oh, I saw a bit of it. All those murders up in Yorkshire. Frightful. Makes you think, doesn’t it? All that darkness lurking just beneath the surface. Though, honestly, I find myself turning it off. Too much negativity. I prefer something a bit lighter. ‘Call the Midwife’, maybe. That's a bit of warmth.

Honestly, this leek and potato soup is refusing to thicken. I’ve added enough cornflour, I swear. It's just… watery. Sounds like my attempts at persuasive fundraising sometimes. All effort, no substance. Though, admittedly, soup doesn’t usually involve emotionally manipulative storytelling. How was your day, love? Apart from the rebellious soup, of course. It was…fine. Mrs. Peterson was on at me about the library book club again. Apparently, I ‘promised’ to organise a talk on Victorian novels. When did I  promise  that, I ask you? It feels like every time I step foot in that place, I’m signing up for another voluntary commitment. You have a good heart, that’s all. You can’t help wanting to contribute. Though, I can see why the relentless requests would get to you. My day was pretty much the usual grind. Had a disastrous meeting with old man Hargrave. He wants to donate, but only if we rename the wing after his poodle. A poodle?! Seriously? I wish I was making it up. Apparently, ‘Fluffy deserves recognition for her unwavering loyalty’. I tried to explain that the wing is for children undergoing treatment, not canine companions, but you wouldn’t believe the performance. I think I aged ten years just in that room. Oh, Roy, that's awful! You deal with some…interesting people. It's no wonder you come home drained. I keep thinking I should find something a bit more…fulfilling, you know? Something other than occasional freelance proofreading. But what  is  fulfilling these days? Don't start on that again, love. You enjoy your proofreading. It keeps your brain active, and it gives you flexibility. Besides, what would you do? Open a tea shop? Become a professional dog walker? Very funny. Though a quiet tea shop  does  sound appealing sometimes. No demanding library patrons, no poodles… Just scones and a good book. You and your scones. Though, remember your disastrous attempt at baking for the village fete last year? We’re still finding crumbs in the car. That was one bad batch! And it was the humidity’s fault, not mine. How’s your mum doing, by the way? I haven’t spoken to her in a couple of weeks. She’s alright, although her hip’s giving her gyp again. She hates going to the doctor. Says they just want to pump her full of pills.

Honestly, this Polish weather is… predictable. Grey. Just grey. Reminds me a bit of Cambridge in November, actually. Though at least there you expect it. Here, you sort of hope for a burst of sunshine. You’re telling me. I’ve been battling a cold since I got back from that training weekend in Kraków. Proper chesty one. Feels like it’s settled in for the long haul. This Tarnow air doesn’t help, does it? It feels damp, even when it’s… not actually raining. Oh, you poor thing. You really should rest. Not the kind of thing you want dragging you down when you’re trying to inspire grown adults to conjugate verbs, is it? Though, knowing my luck, I’ll probably catch it off  you . Don't worry, I'm being extra vigilant with the hand sanitiser. It's just… exhausting. Being ‘on’ all day for students, then coming home and feeling utterly rubbish. It’s making me question everything, actually. Question everything? Like what? The joys of TEFL? Well, not  just  TEFL. More… what I'm doing with my life, I suppose. It's a good job, it pays the bills, and I'm genuinely good at it. But sometimes I just long for… something different. Remember when I briefly tried to be a librarian? Vaguely. Lasted all of three weeks, if I recall correctly. Said the quietude was “suffocating.” It was! But even then, it felt… closer to what I  wanted . This feels… strategic. Like a sensible, adult choice. Not a passionate pursuit. It's weird, isn't it? I always thought I’d feel more settled by now. More… at home. Home. That's a tricky one. I’ve been thinking about it a lot since Mum… well, since everything. Going back for the funeral… Bury isn't  home  anymore, not really. Not for me, anyway. It hasn't been for a very long time. It just feels like… a place I'm obliged to feel things about. I can imagine. It must be awful. And I know you haven't been back for ages. It's hard when places change, and  you  change, and the connection feels… frayed. Exactly. And seeing all the old photos… Auntie Margaret’s been posting relentlessly on Facebook, naturally. Images of Mum as a girl, Mum with Dad, Mum with all the cousins. It’s… overwhelming. And it’s making me realise how little of that I actually  remember .

Honestly, this week has been  mental . Like, actually mental. I swear, if one more client asks me to "make it pop" I’m going to scream into the void. "Make it pop"? Oh, the life of a copywriter. Sounds…colourful. Still better than debugging survey logic though, believe me. I spent all yesterday tracking down why people were consistently answering "purple" to a question about their favourite number. Purple?! Seriously? That's...wild. See, that's the kind of illogical thing that would actually make my brain happy, because at least it’s  interesting . "Make it pop" is just…nothing. It’s corporate beige with extra steps. How’s the postgrad going, by the way? Still buried in data? Mostly. It's the tail end of data collection, thankfully. Then it’s just…analysis paralysis. Trying to make sense of what everyone thinks about… honestly, I can barely remember the initial research question anymore. It was something about consumer perceptions of sustainable packaging, I think. Vague, important, and deeply dull. Sound familiar. I did a campaign last month for a company selling…recycled cardboard boxes. Thrilling stuff. You wouldn't believe the amount of copy dedicated to the structural integrity of recycled cardboard. Oh my god. That  is  niche. Did anyone actually care about the structural integrity? Apparently! They were really keen to emphasise it. Like, “Strong enough to hold your memories!” or something equally…patronising. I fought hard for “Holds things. Responsibly.” but no. "Holds things. Responsibly." That's brilliant. You should’ve run with that. So, speaking of responsibly…have you managed to do a proper food shop this week? I'm operating on a diet of slightly stale biscuits and hope at this point. Don’t even  start  me. The supermarket is a battlefield. I tried on Tuesday, and it was absolute chaos. Everyone was grabbing reduced items like they were competing in the Hunger Games. I managed to snag some slightly-past-their-best avocados, but it cost me a minor emotional trauma. Oh, the avocado struggle is real. The window of perfection is so tiny! I need to brave it this weekend, I think. I’m thinking Borough Market. It's expensive, obviously, but at least you can actually  move  without being elbowed in the ribs. Borough Market is a good shout. Although, the samples can be a bit…aggressive. Remember Sarah trying to get a whole chorizo slice stuck in her mouth?

Honestly, I don’t know  why  you two are up so early. It's barely seven! Did someone decide to test the structural integrity of the house again last night? No! We were practicing our juggling! Remember, you said we could learn circus skills? I dropped all the apples. On the dog. Oh,  sweetheart . Did Buster mind? And apples on the dog is… not ideal. Right, okay. Juggling ambitions at this hour. What exactly were you juggling  with ? Please tell me it wasn’t the good crockery. Just apples! We got them from the fruit bowl. And Buster licked them up. He liked it! Good. Good for Buster. Though I suspect he’ll be a bit… energetic later. Right, tea. I need tea. What are we doing today, besides horrifying the family pet with fruit-based acrobatics? I was thinking a trip to Grantchester Meadows, maybe? Can we get ice cream? Perhaps. If you both behave. And no juggling ice cream. That’s a firm no. I’ve seen that disaster movie, it’s not pretty. But it would be  fun ! Fun and sticky. Very, very sticky. No. We'll stick to  eating  the ice cream. Speaking of which, have you two had breakfast? I want toast! With jam! Toast it is. Poppy, do you fancy toast too, or something else? And did you manage to get any more sleep after the apple-juggling expedition? I’m not hungry right now. And I did, but then I remembered what you said about that Neon Moon thing tonight! Is Uncle David coming? Ah, yes. Neon Moon. It's a good one. And yes, David should be coming. He said he was trying to get the night off work. It's meant to be a good band playing, I think. We'll need to head over a bit earlier than usual, though, to get a good spot. What's Neon Moon? It’s a sort of… a music and food event, darling. Like a little festival. Lots of people, good music, and yummy food trucks. Remember we went last summer when that amazing Mexican place was there? Oh! The one with the hot sauce that made my tongue tingle? That's the one. Now, I was chatting to Liam’s mum yesterday – you remember Liam from school? – and she was telling me about how she went to Australia last year. She kept using all these… strange phrases.

Oh, this is lovely, isn’t it? Proper countryside. Much better than battling London traffic, even for a Friday. Though, honestly, I think I’m developing a twitch just  thinking  about the M25. Aye, it's a world away, alright. Though give me a good rugby match in the city any day. This… this is restorative. And you needed restorative, after that manuscript you were telling me about. The one with the… questionable historical accuracy? Don't even  start  me on Bartholomew Finch's ‘A Noble History of the Earls of Essex’. Noble is… not the word I’d use. More like ‘fantastical nonsense cobbled together with a smattering of actual dates’. The author clearly believes Wikipedia is a primary source. Honestly, the debates we're having about historical narratives now…it's a worrying trend. You mean like, stuff being deliberately rewritten? I saw a thread online about that, about how history textbooks are changing. Oh, it's more subtle than outright rewriting, usually. It’s about emphasis, about what’s  included  and what’s left out. And about presenting opinions as fact. It's a slippery slope, isn’t it? Reminds me a bit of the… well, the whole Brexit mess, actually. So much spun narrative. Now, now, Elspeth. Let’s not bring Brexit into it. We've had enough debate on that particular subject to last a lifetime. Though I will say, it highlighted rather spectacularly how easily people latch onto narratives that confirm their existing biases. It’s true, isn't it? People don’t want nuance. They want simple answers, and someone to blame. It’s exhausting trying to have a rational conversation. Even with family, sometimes. Speaking of family… Grandad Rhys used to have  opinions . Strong ones. Used to say everything bad in the world could be traced back to… well, pretty much anyone not from Monmouthshire. Ah, Rhys. He was a character, your grandfather. A proud Welshman, to put it mildly. Though his view of England was… shall we say, less charitable after they closed the steelworks in Nantyglo. He blamed Thatcher, naturally. Everything was Thatcher's fault, according to Rhys. It was a particularly hard time for that area, wasn’t it? My father worked in similar industries, though further south. He never spoke about it much, a very stoic man. But I remember the anxiety, the uncertainty. It shaped his politics, certainly.

…and then the badger, right, he’d built this  enormous  fortress out of jam jars and old wellington boots! But it wasn’t to keep people  out , it was to keep the glitter inside. He was obsessed with glitter. Glitter! Why? Well, he thought glitter was magic. He believed if he collected enough, he could wish for a never-ending supply of raspberry ripple ice cream. Raspberry ripple is the BEST! Better than mint choc chip. No! Mint choc chip is! It’s green! Alright, alright. No need for a full-scale ice cream war. But back to the badger… So, this fortress, it’s wobbling, because jam jars aren’t exactly structural engineers, are they? And the glitter is… escaping. And then what happens? Does the glitter make everything sparkly? It does! But not in a good way. It gets EVERYWHERE. In the squirrels’ nuts, in the robin’s feathers, even inside Mr. Hedgehog’s prickly bits! He was  not  impressed. Oh no! Hedgehogs don’t like things stuck to their spikes! Exactly! It caused absolute chaos. We're thinking about maybe making the villain a slightly grumpy gnome? He's the one who accidentally knocks the fortress with his walking stick. A gnome! Yes! Can he have a really long beard? A  very  long beard. One that gets tangled in the glitter, perhaps? And maybe he’s trying to find a special flower for his grandma? Ooh, that’s brilliant, Lily! See, this is why I love story-building with you two. You always add the best bits. It's much more fun than trying to come up with everything myself. Speaking of stories, did you both remember I signed us up for that Helen Moss reading at the Linton Book Festival next week? The one about the adventures on the Norfolk Broads? That's the one. 'The Eerie Elevator' isn’t it? You both loved ‘The Mystery of the Missing Mummy’ ages ago. I do remember! The mummy had a secret message! He did indeed. Helen Moss is really good at those twisty plots, isn't she? I’m hoping she'll do a signing too. We can get a new book for your collection. Can we go on a boat after? Like in the book? We can look into it, Leo. It’s a Saturday, so maybe we can find a little boat trip somewhere around Cambridge.

Honestly, this lentil shepherd’s pie is taking  forever . I thought being vegetarian would be easier than this. Like, less… fiddly. Easier? You’ve been saying that since you went veggie, Liv. It’s only been three months! And shepherds pie is never easy, regardless of the filling. It's a commitment. She’s right, it’s a whole process. Though, I will say, the smell is incredible. Better than when you tried that butternut squash lasagne. That was… an experience. Hey! The lasagne wasn’t  that  bad. It was just… structurally unsound. And maybe a bit bland. Okay, it was pretty bad. But I was experimenting! Anyway, the point is, sometimes I miss just… chucking a chicken in the oven. It feels so simple. Simple, maybe, but at what cost, Liv? Seriously. Think about those chickens. The conditions they’re kept in… I  do  think about it, okay? That’s why I stopped eating them! It’s just… sometimes I wonder if all this, all the lentils and the tofu, is actually making a difference. Like, is it just me feeling morally superior, or am I actually mitigating animal suffering? It’s absolutely making a difference. Every little bit. Plus, there’s the environmental impact. All that methane. It's a huge problem. Have you looked into lab-grown meat at all? Oh, here we go. Shmeat time. Hey, don’t knock it ‘til you’ve tried it. Apparently, they're getting really good at replicating the texture and taste. It could be a solution – meat without the cruelty, without the environmental damage. It just sounds… weird. Like, fundamentally unnatural. A burger grown in a petri dish? I don’t know. I'd rather just stick to my lentils. Plus, it feels a bit… dystopian, doesn’t it? Like  Black Mirror  territory. I get the ick factor, honestly. It’s the same feeling I had when I first considered taking vitamin D tablets. Why would I need to  supplement  something my body’s supposed to produce naturally? But then, living in London, you barely see the sun for six months of the year. It's practical. And maybe shmeat will be too. Good point about the vitamin D. I religiously take those now. Dr. Sharma practically threatened me with rickets if I didn’t. Though, maybe I should also be taking B12… apparently that’s a thing when you cut out meat.

Honestly, this gravy is refusing to thicken. It's like water. Did I even put enough cornflour in? You always say that, love. It’ll be fine. Probably just needs a good whisking. You worry too much about the gravy. It’s never the gravy anyone complains about. Definitely not. It’s always Uncle Barry’s political opinions. Remember last Christmas? The whole debacle about Brexit over the Brussels sprouts? Oh, don’t remind me. And then Aunt Carol chimed in, saying it was all the young people’s fault. Honestly, a full-scale war nearly broke out over cranberry sauce. Carol’s a character, isn’t she? Says what she thinks, regardless. Though I swear, every year she gets a bit more…  firm  in her convictions. Firm is an understatement. Anyway, speaking of things refusing to work properly, this washing machine is making a noise like a distressed walrus. I'm convinced it's on its last legs. Oh no, not again! Didn’t Dad fix it just last month after it started vibrating like crazy? Fixed is a strong word. He  attempted  to fix it. He mostly just shouted at it and tightened a few bolts. It’s a temporary stay of execution, more like. We really should just get a new one. We really should. But then the question is  what  to get. I saw one online that does everything – steam cleaning, self-dosing detergent… it’s a marvel of modern technology. And wildly expensive. Everything's expensive these days. It's ridiculous. I was looking at new routers for the flat, and they're charging a fortune for something that should just… connect to the internet. Honestly! The internet. That's a whole other rabbit hole. Old Mr. Henderson next door was telling me he's convinced it’s all a conspiracy to steal people’s data. He's switched back to carrier pigeons, apparently. You're joking! I wish I were. He seriously showed me a little harness he'd made. Says it's more reliable. Though I pointed out the pigeons might struggle with bills. That's amazing. He sounds… committed. Speaking of things people are committed to, are we still on for New Year's Eve at the O’Malley’s? I think so. Though I am starting to feel a bit old for all that. All the loud music and the… enthusiasm. I’d rather be in front of the telly with a nice cuppa.

Right, supper's nearly done. Honestly, though, finding butterfly forks in Bury St Edmunds is apparently a quest worthy of Arthurian legend. Do they  not  exist outside of garden centres and terribly twee tea rooms? Butterfly forks? What even  are  butterfly forks? Sounds…fussy. They’re those little ones, aren’t they? All decorative and fancy. Mum uses them for parties. They’re a pain to actually  eat  with. Exactly! A pain! But Old Mrs. Henderson specifically requested butterfly forks. Said it would "add a certain  je ne sais quoi " to her quiche and cucumber sandwiches. Honestly. You’d think after 87 years she’d have accepted the superiority of a normal fork. Maybe she just likes butterflies. Possibly. Though I suspect it’s more about showing off. Anyway, it reminded me…did you two remember what we talked about for tomorrow? The two minutes silence? Oh, yeah. For…Ukraine, right? At eleven? That’s right. It’s important, even if it’s just a small thing. A moment to just…stop. To think. It’s horrible what’s happening over there. It’s just… hard to even understand, isn’t it? Like, Russia? Why are they doing that? Mr. Davies in History said it was complicated, something about NATO and…stuff. It  is  complicated, darling. Centuries of history, political tensions... Honestly, even I struggle to unravel it all. Mr. Davies is right to say it’s ‘stuff’, because ‘stuff’ is a vast understatement. But at its core, it's about power, sadly. And greed. And forgetting the value of human life. It’s… upsetting. Does it feel different now than when… well, when stuff happened before? Like, with other wars? That’s a really good question, actually. I think… yes. Because of how connected we all are. We see it  immediately  on our phones, on the news. It feels closer. And the scale of the displacement…the number of people having to leave their homes… it’s immense. My mate’s grandad fought in a war. He doesn't really talk about it. Says it was awful. Many don't. War leaves scars, both visible and invisible. It's why moments of silence, reminders…they matter. We  have  to remember. Speaking of remembering… has anyone given any thought to what they want to do for birthdays this year? Yours is coming up soon, isn’t it, Leo? Not really. Dunno.

Right, who wants pasta with pesto? It’s quick, and frankly, my brain is fried after marking essays all day. Honestly, Year 9…some of them clearly think a comma is a suggestion, not a rule. Pesto! Yes! Can I have loads of parmesan on mine, please? Like, a mountain? I just want pasta. No parmesan. It makes my tummy rumble funny. Alright, no parmesan mountain for either of you then. Sensitivity is the word, isn’t it? It feels like the whole world is discovering food intolerances. Remember Auntie Brenda’s drama last summer with the gluten? She was  so  cross she couldn’t have cake at Grandma’s birthday! She certainly was. Speaking of summer… we really need to nail down holiday plans. I was looking at Cornwall again. Remember how much fun we had last time? We could go back to that little beach near Padstow. With the rock pools? And the crabs? The very same! We spent hours catching crabs. Although, Dad nearly had a heart attack when you tried to bring a particularly grumpy one back to the car. He  was  grumpy! He kept pinching my finger! He did. And likely deserved a bit of space. Cornwall feels…safe. Easy. But I also had a thought. It's a bit ambitious, but… I saw an advert for an Adventure Island holiday. You know, the theme park in Southend? They do package deals with hotels nearby. Adventure Island?! Really?! With the Viper and the Inferno Falls? Oh, please, please,  please  can we go there? Is there a really big rollercoaster? There are several. Quite big. It would be…different. A bit more adrenaline fuelled than rock pools. It's just…it feels a bit…chaotic. I’m thinking about being a stressed teacher  all  day. But it's Adventure Island! It's in that book series we have! "The Adventurers"! We could pretend  we  are the Adventurers, solving a mystery on the rollercoaster! You've clearly thought this through. And you’re right, you're obsessed with that series. It is good, isn’t it? Good storytelling. I'm going to the V&A next week. There's a display on book cover art from the Golden Age of children's literature. Might be inspiring. Can we go to the beach  and  Adventure Island? That, my dear, is the million-dollar question. We’d need a very long holiday.

…and then Mr. Harrison  actually  said my essay was “lacking in… nuance.” Nuance! It’s a history essay about the Battle of Hastings, not a blooming poem! What nuance does a bloke need when William the Conqueror's just kicking everyone’s doors in? Harsh, mate. Harrison’s always been a bit… pretentious, isn’t he? I reckon he just likes using big words to make himself feel clever. Did you at least get a decent grade? A C. A  C ! I put ages into that thing. Honestly, I think he marks down anyone who doesn’t agree with his weird theories about Norman farming techniques. You doing alright with history? Yeah, Mrs. Davies is alright. She actually explains things, y’know? And she doesn't make you feel like you've personally offended the entire academic community if you ask a question. I'm hoping for a B on my coursework. It's on the industrial revolution, which is… marginally more interesting than Hastings, I guess. Marginally. Listen, forget history for a sec. Remember Benji said he was throwing a party this weekend? Yeah! At his place, right? His mum's usually pretty chill. Is Chloe going? Apparently. And Liam, and… pretty much everyone. Trying to convince my mum to let me go. She's got this whole thing about needing to know exactly who's going to be there, and what the adult supervision situation is. It's a party, not a diplomatic summit! Tell me about it. My dad's the same. He's all, "Are there going to be older students there?" and "Will there be alcohol?" Like I’m planning to smuggle in a distillery or something. Exactly! It’s just music and awkward dancing, innit? Speaking of awkward, did you see what happened with old Manvers and a Year 7 today? No! Spill. Manvers is a legend for unintentional chaos. Okay, so he was trying to be all firm and 'respectful authority' with this kid who was… skateboarding in the corridor.  In  the corridor. And he tries to grab the board, and completely loses his balance and nearly takes out Mrs. Peterson's prize-winning ferns. No way! Manvers, flattened by foliage? That’s brilliant. Poor ferns though. He really shouldn't be allowed near anything fragile. He's a walking health and safety hazard. Seriously! And then the Year 7 just scooted off, laughing his head off.

Right, this is doing me head in. Sat Nav’s sent us round the bloody houses again. Honestly, you’d think with all these new roads they’d sort the mapping out. It's like it  wants  us to end up in a field full of sheep. It’s rarely  that  bad, love. Just a slightly…optimistic interpretation of ‘shortest route’. Hertfordshire roads aren't exactly grid-system friendly, and you’re used to Sunderland where it’s basically straight lines and roundabouts, aren’t you? Straight lines and roundabouts that  work ! This is all…winding lanes and ‘unsuitable for HGVs’ signs. And don't even get me started on the cyclists. They just pop out of nowhere! They have right of way, you know. Though, I agree, some of them don’t help themselves. Saw one yesterday, just riding two abreast, taking up the whole lane, completely oblivious. Two abreast?! On a country road?! Honestly. It's just… asking for trouble. I'm not against cyclists, mind. My uncle Derek's got a proper fancy road bike, spends all his time training. He's always going on about cadence and… aero-whatever. I just don't understand the appeal. Give me four wheels any day. Derek's pretty dedicated. He was telling me about a new cycling event he's entered, some ridiculous hill climb in the Peak District. Says it's all about the mental fortitude. I suppose there's something to be said for that. It's like cricket, really. Long periods of nothing much happening, then a tiny burst of intense action. Cricket… Ugh. Don’t get me started. My dad is proper obsessed. Every summer, it's all he talks about. Scores, averages, who’s in and who’s out. I can barely tell a bat from a ball. He tried to get me into it when I was little, but all I remember is being bored stiff and covered in sunscreen. Sounds about right. It's a slow burn, cricket. It's not exactly a fast-paced thrill ride. Though, I enjoyed watching the Ashes last year. The atmosphere was incredible. Gets the whole nation going, doesn’t it? Gets  your  dad going, you mean. I was at work, classifying newspaper articles about…well, not cricket. I'm still dealing with the fallout from that article about the abnormally large marrow someone grew in Northumberland.

Right, this is impossible. Honestly, Golden Dragon’s online menu is a work of abstract art. Is that sweet and sour chicken… or just a picture of orange goo? Let me see. Oh, that’s definitely orange goo. They haven't updated their photos since… well, since I was still at school, probably. You know, they used to have decent specials. Remember the salt and chilli ribs? Ooh, yes! The ribs were  amazing . They stopped doing those when they redecorated, didn’t they? All minimalist grey and neon lighting. Ruined the vibe, completely. It did. It absolutely did. Right, okay. Ribs are off the table, sadly. So, what are we realistically ordering? I'm starving. I had, like, half a biscuit for lunch. Half a biscuit? Seriously, Amelia? You need to fuel yourself better than that. Okay, let's do the usual. Chicken chow mein for me, obviously. And spring rolls. Always spring rolls. Predictable, Leo. Shockingly predictable. You’ve ordered that same thing for the last… five years, minimum. Hey! Don’t knock it. It’s a classic. It's reliable. It's... sustenance. What about you, Liv? What are  you  fancying? I’m actually feeling something a bit spicier. Maybe the Kung Pao Chicken? I haven't had that in ages. Good shout! That  is  good. Okay, Kung Pao for Liv, chow mein for Leo… I think I’m going to be adventurous. I’m going to attempt the… Szechuan Beef. Woah, careful now. That stuff is  hot . Remember when Uncle Barry tried that? He was sweating for an hour and kept demanding milk. Oh god, yes! He turned bright red. It was glorious. I think I can handle it. I've built up a tolerance. Thanks to all those questionable chillies you get in those dodgy meal deals. It’s not a good tolerance-building strategy, Amelia. Just saying. Maybe order a side of egg fried rice just in case. A cooling agent. Good point. Okay, egg fried rice it is. Right, now the sauces… This is where it gets tricky. How many black bean sauces do they  need  to offer? They’re trying to give you a choice, Amelia! Be grateful. I always go for the sweet chilli. It goes with  everything . Sweet chilli is a bit basic, isn't it? I'm a plum sauce girl myself. See, this is why we can’t just  order  Chinese.

…and honestly, the waiting lists are getting absolutely ridiculous. Old Mrs. Higgins down the road, bless her, has been waiting six months for a hip replacement. Six months! She's in agony, can barely get around. You see it at the hospital, don't you, with your work? Oh, you have  no  idea, Hans. It’s… demoralising, honestly. We’re patching people up, sending them home with pain meds and advice to “manage”, knowing full well they need proper intervention. It’s not the care  we  want to provide. We’re swamped, understaffed, and the resources… well, they’re stretched thinner than filo pastry. It's not just hips, either. Routine appointments, specialists, even getting a diagnosis… it’s a battle. It's just...it feels like it’s been getting progressively worse, hasn’t it? I remember when the NHS felt… robust. Maybe I'm romanticising the past, being an academic and all, dwelling on golden ages that probably never truly existed, but it  felt  different. Now, it’s constantly on the brink, isn’t it? Always a crisis. It is. And the constant restructuring doesn't help. New targets, new initiatives...it feels like we’re endlessly chasing our tails. And it's not like people aren't trying. The staff are incredible. They're working extra shifts, taking on more and more, but there’s only so much anyone can do. I had a patient yesterday, young lad, asthma, kept ending up in A&E because he couldn’t get a timely appointment with his GP to review his inhaler. Completely avoidable. That’s… heartbreaking. Absolutely heartbreaking. It’s a systemic failure, isn’t it? It’s not about individual failings, it’s a crumbling system. Speaking of crumbling, have you had any more trouble with old man Peterson next door? Still complaining about the bins? Don't even get me started. He reported me to the council…  again . Apparently, the green bin was “slightly overfilled”. Slightly! It was a Tuesday, bin day! I mean, seriously? He’s got nothing better to do than scrutinise everyone’s waste disposal habits. He's always peering through his curtains. I swear, he's got a log book detailing my life. That’s… unsettling. Honestly, some people. I’ve had to bite my tongue more times than I can count trying to be neighbourly. He glared at me the other day when I was taking the recycling out.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of marking I’ve got this week is criminal. Essays on  Beowulf  – you’d think after all these years, students would have  something  original to say about a bloody Anglo-Saxon epic. It's all just regurgitated SparkNotes, isn’t it? Anyway, how are you doing, Mr. Davies? Still keeping well? Aye, alright lad, alright. Can’t complain, not really. Though me knees are giving me jip somethin’ fierce this week. Damp’s got into ‘em, I reckon. Feels like I’m ninety-nine, not eighty-seven. And don’t you go callin’ me Mr. Davies, makes me feel a right old fossil. Just Arthur’ll do. Arthur it is, then. Sorry about that. It's just habit, you know, being surrounded by formality at the uni. Damp is the worst, though. My mother swore by a poultice with mustard in it. Smelled horrendous, but she said it drew out the badness. Of course, she swore by a lot of things… mainly complaining, to be fair. Aye, mothers are good at that. Mine used to say a spoonful of treacle cured everything. Didn’t stop me gettin’ the measles twice, mind. Speaking of complaints...did you hear about young Mikey down the street? Got ‘is benefits stopped. Apparently, they reckon he’s fit for work. Fit for  what , I ask ya? He can barely tie ‘is own shoelaces! Oh, dreadful. I heard something about that, yes. It seems the whole system is geared towards finding reasons  not  to help, rather than the other way around. It’s barbaric, honestly. They talk about ‘dignity of work’ but what dignity is there in forcing someone into a job they are demonstrably incapable of doing? Then they moan about the cost of healthcare when the stress breaks them. It’s a vicious cycle. Exactly! And they’re all talkin’ about gettin’ people back into work, but where  are  the jobs? This area’s been bleedin’ dry since the docks closed. Used to be you could walk down here and trip over a job. Now? It’s all takeaways and betting shops. My granddad worked on the docks, a proper grafter he was. Built this city, he did. Liverpool’s history is so intrinsically linked to the port, isn’t it? It's a shame to see it diminished. Though, I suppose, that’s progress, they say. Though what progress looks like these days is anyone's guess.

Aye, honestly, this is a proper good cheese and pickle. Beats the stuff they had at that conference last week, hands down. Remember that weird sourdough with… what  was  that, Chloe? Beetroot and something else aggressively floral? Oh god, yes! It tasted like a garden centre. I think it was elderflower. And massively overpriced for what it was. You’d think a linguistics conference would have better taste, wouldn’t you? Pun intended. It’s the principle of the thing. Academics getting excited about niche food trends…it's a bit much. I just wanted a normal ham and cheese. You guys are hilarious. I’m still trying to adjust to British lunch habits. Everything feels so… deliberate. Back in the States, it’s usually just grabbing something quick at your desk. Though, I  do  appreciate a good sit-down meal. This is lovely, actually. Tell me about it! I spent a week in New York last year for a publishing event and the sheer  speed  of everything was mental. Like everyone was permanently chasing something. Here, it’s a bit more…relaxed. Though, obviously, we're all melting down about deadlines all the time regardless. Aye, deadlines. Always deadlines. Speaking of which, how's the pronunciation dictionary project going, Chloe? You were looking a bit stressed about it last time we spoke. It's…complex. We've hit a snag with the regional variations in vowel sounds, predictably. Trying to get a truly representative dataset for Received Pronunciation  and  accurately capturing all the nuances of, well, everywhere else is proving… ambitious. We’ve been discussing that actually, in the team. The issue of standardisation versus authenticity.
